about: Species table (R8) for the 12 featured species (F1). Names: pipeline/species_curated.json; facts: pipeline/facts_reviewed.json (decision R8f), sources verified by pipeline/verify_sources.py. Windows and regions: computed by pipeline/build_species.py from the tracked animals listed under 'tracked' (citations in data/catalog.json). Dates are MM-DD; 'from'/'to' span the middle half of the animals. Re-run before relying on the numbers.

en.text: In the Polish village of Żywkowo, storks outnumber people five to one.

source.title: Wikipedia, Żywkowo
source.quote: For 30 inhabitants accrue about 160 storks and 42 nests.

en.text: Too hot? A stork cools off by pooping on its own legs.

source.title: Cabello-Vergel et al. 2021, Scientific Reports
source.quote: Storks (Ciconiidae) frequently excrete onto their legs to prevent overheating, a phenomenon known as urohidrosis.

en.text: A stork called Prinzesschen has her own postage stamp and a bronze statue.

source.title: Volksstimme, Prinzesschens Reise (2016)
quote: Wie aber kam der Vogel, der über ein Dutzend Jahre für die Wissenschaft fliegen sollte, zu seinem Namen?
Die von der Künstlerin Heike Landherr entworfene Bronzeskulptur steht auf dem Storchenhof Loburg
Das Motiv zeigt Prinzesschen fliegend, die Marke gehört zur Serie „Bedrohte Tierarten“

en.text: Many storks in Spain and Portugal skip Africa and spend the winter at rubbish dumps.

source.title: Gilbert et al. 2016, Movement Ecology: Are white storks addicted to junk food?
quote: recently guaranteed, year-round food from landfill sites has facilitated the establishment of resident populations in Iberia.
Storks travelled up to 48.2 km to visit landfills during non-breeding

en.text: The legend of storks bringing babies is ancient; Hans Christian Andersen made it popular.

source.title: Wikipedia, White stork
source.quote: The legend is very ancient, but was popularised by a 19th-century Hans Christian Andersen story called "The Storks".

en.text: In 2020 wild white storks hatched chicks in England, the first in Britain for 604 years.

source.title: National Geographic, After 604 years, white storks are nesting in Britain again (2020)
source.quote: It was May 6, 2020, a landmark moment: It had been 604 years since the previous written record of white storks breeding anywhere in Britain.

en.text: Photos of white storks taken in 1884 are the oldest known pictures of any wild birds.

source.title: Wikipedia, White stork
source.quote: Ottomar Anschütz 's images of white storks, taken in 1884—the earliest known photographs of any wild birds

en.text: White storks can find frogs by listening for their mating calls.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), White stork
source.quote: Birds returning to Latvia during spring have been shown to locate their prey, moor frogs ( Rana arvalis ), by homing in on the mating calls produced by aggregations of male frogs. [ 102 ]

en.text: Shot by hunters, the Croatian stork Malena never flew again. Her mate Klepetan flew {13000 km|8000 mi} back to her from South Africa every year.

source.title: Wikipedia, Klepetan and Malena
quote: Between 2001 and 2021, Klepetan traveled from South Africa to Brodski Varoš , Croatia, each spring to mate with Malena
Croatian janitor Stjepan Vokić found Malena while fishing in 1993; she had been shot by hunters and was unable to fly.
Through a radio tracking band, it was determined that Klepetan made a 13,000-kilometre (8,000 mi) month-long journey from South Africa to Croatia to meet up with Malena each year.

en.text: In 1822 a stork turned up in Germany with a {80 cm|31 in} African arrow in its neck: the first proof that storks winter in Africa.

source.title: Universität Rostock, Schloss Bothmer: Der Pfeilstorch ist zurück
quote: als Bewohner von Gut Bothmer einen Weißstorch entdeckten, dem ein etwa 80 cm langer Stock am Hals hinunterhing.
Der Pfeilstorch lieferte somit den ersten Beweis für den Fernzug der Störche bis in das äquatoriale Afrika.

en.text: In 2013 Egyptian police detained a stork called Menes as a suspected spy. The suspicious device was a European wildlife tracker.

source.title: ABC News, Egypt's 'Spy' Stork Found Dead (2013)
quote: Egyptian police detained a stork in August when a resident in Egypt's Qena province, 280 miles southeast of Cairo, became suspicious after noticing a European wildlife tracker on the bird, The Associated Press reported.
A local conservation group said Saturday the stork, which it had named "Menes," had been killed.

en.text: No one knows why storks vanished from Britain 600 years ago. They appear on medieval banquet menus, so they may simply have been eaten.

source.title: National Geographic, After 604 years, white storks are nesting in Britain again (2020)
source.quote: No one knows for certain why storks disappeared from Britain, though their appearance on the menus of medieval banquets suggests that they may simply have been targeted for food.

en.text: White storks barely have a voice. Instead they clatter their bills, a sound like distant machine-gun fire. Even the chicks join in.

source.title: Wikipedia, White stork
quote: The adult white stork's main sound is noisy bill-clattering, which has been likened to distant machine gun fire.
Like the adults, the young also clatter their beaks.

en.text: A stork nest can be an apartment block: sparrows and starlings nest inside it, and sometimes even little owls move in.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), White stork
quote: Several bird species often nest within the large nests of the white stork.

Regular occupants are house sparrows , tree sparrows , and common starlings ; less common residents include Eurasian kestrels , little owls , European rollers , white wagtails , black redstarts , Eurasian jackdaws , and Spanish sparrows .

de.text: Die Loburger Störchin Prinzesschen hat eine eigene Briefmarke und ein Denkmal aus Bronze.

source.title: Volksstimme, Prinzesschens Reise (2016)
quote: Die von der Künstlerin Heike Landherr entworfene Bronzeskulptur steht auf dem Storchenhof Loburg
Das Motiv zeigt Prinzesschen fliegend, die Marke gehört zur Serie

de.text: Wird es zu heiß, koten Störche sich auf die eigenen Beine. Das schützt vor Überhitzung.

source.title: Cabello-Vergel et al. 2021, Scientific Reports
source.quote: Storks (Ciconiidae) frequently excrete onto their legs to prevent overheating, a phenomenon known as urohidrosis.

de.text: Im polnischen Dorf Żywkowo leben rund 30 Menschen und etwa 160 Störche.

source.title: Wikipedia, Żywkowo
source.quote: For 30 inhabitants accrue about 160 storks and 42 nests.

de.text: Nirgends in Deutschland brüten Störche so dicht wie in Rühstädt an der Elbe.

source.title: Berlin.de, Storchendorf Rühstädt
source.quote: Nirgendwo in Deutschland nisten so viele Störche auf so engem Raum wie im Europäischen Storchendorf Rühstädt nahe der Elbe.

de.text: 1822 kam ein Weißstorch nach Mecklenburg zurück, mit einem afrikanischen Pfeil im Hals.

source.title: Universität Rostock, Schloss Bothmer: Der Pfeilstorch ist zurück (2018)
quote: Der Storch wurde 1822 im Klützer Winkel erlegt und lieferte seinerzeit den ersten Beweis für den Fernzug der Störche bis in das äquatoriale Afrika.
Der vermeintliche Stock entpuppte sich dabei als ein aus Holz geschnitzter und mit einer eisernen Spitze versehener Pfeil.

de.text: Um 1990 gab es in ganz NRW nur noch drei Storchenpaare, alle in Petershagen an der Weser.

source.title: Tagesspiegel (dpa), Was klappert da? Darum gibt es so viele Störche (2026)
quote: Petershagen an der Weser im nördlichen Zipfel Nordrhein-Westfalens
da hatten wir in ganz NRW noch drei Paar Störche. Und die waren alle hier

de.text: Sein Schnabelklappern hat dem Weißstorch den Namen Klapperstorch eingebracht.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Weißstorch
quote: Die Stimme des Weißstorchs ist nur schwach ausgeprägt.
Er verständigt sich durch Klappern mit dem Schnabel , deshalb wird er auch Klapperstorch [ 2 ] genannt.

de.text: Nach einem Jägerschuss konnte Malena nicht mehr fliegen. Ihr Partner Klepetan kam trotzdem jedes Jahr {13000 km|8000 mi} aus Südafrika zu Malena.

source.title: Wikipedia, Klepetan and Malena
quote: she had been shot by hunters and was unable to fly.
Through a radio tracking band, it was determined that Klepetan made a 13,000-kilometre (8,000 mi) month-long journey from South Africa to Croatia to meet up with Malena each year.

de.text: Max Bloesch holte die Störche in die Schweiz zurück: Ab 1955 flog die Air France Jungstörche aus Algerien ein, gratis. 292 kamen so.

source.title: Beobachter, Wiederansiedlung: Mission Storch (2013)
quote: Die Aktion kostet keinen Rappen: Die Air France fliegt gratis, wohl aus PR-Gründen.
1955 geht der erste Flug.
292 Störche kommen so in die Schweiz.

de.text: Vor 2.000 Jahren lebten Weißstörche nur im Römischen Reich, bis an Rhein und Donau. Erst seit 1.000 Jahren geht es nach Nordosten.

source.title: Tagesspiegel (dpa), Was klappert da? Darum gibt es so viele Störche (2026)
quote: Den Erkenntnissen zufolge kamen Weißstörche vor rund 2.000 Jahren ausschließlich auf dem Gebiet des Römischen Reiches vor.
Die nördliche Grenze ihres Verbreitungsgebiets verlief demnach zu der Zeit entlang des Rheins und der Donau.
Seit etwa 1.000 Jahren breitet sich der Weißstorch dem Szenario zufolge Richtung Nordosten in Europa aus.

de.text: Den Kinder bringenden Storch gibt es erst seit etwa 1700. Als alles Sexuelle verpönt war, half der Storch beim Erklären.

source.title: Tagesspiegel (dpa), Was klappert da? Darum gibt es so viele Störche (2026)
quote: Das ist nicht älter als etwa um 1700.
Da sei alles Fleischliche und insbesondere das Sexuelle verpönt gewesen, sagt Bense.
Mit dem Storch hat man nun eine Möglichkeit zu erklären, wie die Kinder gebracht werden

de.text: Der Weißstorch verschlingt große Beute als Ganzes, weil sein Schnabel sie nicht zerkleinern kann.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Weißstorch
source.quote: Große Beutestücke bis knapp 1000 Gramm können nur als ganzes Stück verschlungen werden, da der Storchenschnabel für das Zerlegen von Beute und Aas nicht geeignet ist.

en.text: A crane's windpipe coils through its breastbone like a trumpet.

source.title: Naturpark Kyffhäuser, Kraniche im Blick (2021)
source.quote: Seine Luftröhre ist beachtliche 130 cm lang und durchzieht als Doppelschlinge das Brustbein.

en.text: You can hear a crane bugling from {5.6 km|3.5 mi} away.

source.title: RSPB, Crane
source.quote: Cranes are vocal birds, with a distinct bugling call which can be heard up to 3.5 miles away.

en.text: Unlike young storks, young cranes fly south with their parents.

source.title: Naturpark Kyffhäuser, Kraniche im Blick (2021)
source.quote: dass die Jungtiere das erste Mal mit ihren Eltern ins Winterquartier ziehen.

en.text: Crane couples can stay together for life.

source.title: Naturpark Kyffhäuser, Kraniche im Blick (2021)
source.quote: Verpaarte Kraniche können ein Leben lang zusammen bleiben.

en.text: Cranes dance, and even the chicks practice the steps.

source.title: Naturpark Kyffhäuser, Kraniche im Blick (2021)
source.quote: Schon Küken üben den Tanz

en.text: A banquet for an Archbishop of York in 1465 supposedly served up 204 cranes.

source.title: Wikipedia, Cranes of Great Britain
source.quote: A banquet to celebrate George Neville's enthronement as Archbishop of York in 1465 supposedly included 204 cranes.

en.text: The word 'pedigree' comes from French for 'crane's foot', after the lines of family trees.

source.title: Wikipedia, Pedigree chart
source.quote: The word pedigree is a corruption of the Anglo-Norman French pé de grue or "crane's foot", either because the typical lines and split lines (each split leading to different offspring of the one parent line) resemble the thin leg and foot of a crane

en.text: Cranfield in England is named after cranes: 'open country frequented by cranes'.

source.title: Wikipedia, Cranes of Great Britain
source.quote: English place names with the prefix "cran" are not infrequent, and derive from the bird, for example the name of Cranfield in Bedfordshire derives from the Anglo-Saxon crane feld - open country frequented by cranes.

en.text: Common cranes coat their feathers with mud, probably for camouflage.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Common crane
source.quote: In common with sandhill cranes (and no other crane species), common cranes "paint" their bodies with mud or decaying vegetation, apparently in order to blend into their nesting environment.

en.text: Carrion crows are cunning egg thieves: they put on a distraction display to lure nesting cranes away, then steal their eggs.

source.title: Wikipedia, Common crane
source.quote: The carrion crow ( Corvus corone ) is locally a successful predator of common cranes' eggs, trickily using distraction displays to steal them.

en.text: Medieval England prized cranes as the 'noblest quarry'. In 1212 King John flew his gyrfalcons at cranes in Cambridgeshire and killed seven.

source.title: Wikipedia, Cranes of Great Britain
quote: English people prized cranes as the "noblest quarry" for a falconer , and gladly ate them.
In December 1212 King John flew his gyrfalcons at cranes at Ashwell, in Cambridgeshire, and killed seven

en.text: At Britain's 'crane school', keepers in gray hooded smocks fed the hand-reared chicks with plaster crane heads on litter pickers.

source.title: Wikipedia, Cranes of Great Britain
source.quote: Although the cranes are hand-reared, all humans having contact with the birds wear special grey cover-all smocks, complete with hoods, and feed the cranes using plaster cast crane heads mounted onto litter picker handles.

en.text: In 1979 two wild cranes turned up in Norfolk and stayed. In 1982 they raised a chick: Britain's first breeding cranes in about 400 years.

source.title: Wikipedia, Cranes of Great Britain
quote: The origins of this population can be traced to 15 September 1979, when two birds appeared near Hickling Broad
these birds stayed throughout 1980 and 1981, and in 1982 raised a single young, the first successful breeding in Britain for around four hundred years.

en.text: Now and then a common crane from Eurasia veers off course and turns up in Nebraska among the half-million sandhill cranes on the Platte.

source.title: National Wildlife Federation, Great Gathering on the Great Plains (2003)
quote: With nearly a half-million cranes stopping here each spring, the placid Platte is transformed into the site of the greatest gathering of these birds in the world.
Add to this the occasional appearance of an endangered whooping crane or a Eurasian "common" crane that has veered off course

en.text: Migrating common cranes have been known to fly as high as {10000 m|33000 ft}. Among birds, only Rüppell's vulture has been seen higher.

source.title: Wikipedia, Common crane
source.quote: During these migratory flights, common cranes have been known to fly at altitudes of up to 10,000 m (33,000 ft) , one of the highest of any species of bird, second only to the Ruppell's vulture .

en.text: Crane chicks can swim soon after hatching and run with their parents a day later, long before they can fly.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Common crane
source.quote: New hatchlings are generally quite helpless but are able to crawl away from danger within a few hours, can swim soon after hatching and can run with their parents at 24 hours old.

de.text: Der Lufthansa-Kranich ist älter als die Lufthansa: Otto Firle zeichnete ihn schon 1918.

source.title: Lufthansa Group Newsroom, Lufthansa-Kranich feiert seinen 100. Geburtstag (2018)
quote: 1918 entwarf der Grafiker und Architekt Otto Firle für die Deutsche Luft-Reederei, einer Vorgängergesellschaft der Luft Hansa, einen stilisierten Vogel.
das Aktienbuch der ersten Deutschen Luft Hansa - so die damalige Schreibweise - vom 6. Januar 1926

de.text: Mitte Oktober zählten Beobachter in Linum bei Berlin einmal über 116.000 Kraniche.

source.title: wissen.de, Faszination Kraniche: Sie sind wieder unterwegs (2022)
source.quote: In Linum bei Berlin zählten Vogelbeobachter Mitte Oktober sogar über 116.000 Kraniche.

de.text: Die Luftröhre des Kranichs ist {130 cm|51 in} lang und liegt als Doppelschlinge im Brustbein.

source.title: Naturpark Kyffhäuser, Kraniche im Blick
source.quote: Seine Luftröhre ist beachtliche 130 cm lang und durchzieht als Doppelschlinge das Brustbein.

de.text: Kraniche tanzen gern, und schon die Küken üben die Schritte.

source.title: Naturpark Kyffhäuser, Kraniche im Blick
source.quote: Schon Küken üben den Tanz

de.text: Anders als junge Störche ziehen junge Kraniche mit den Eltern ins Winterquartier.

source.title: Naturpark Kyffhäuser, Kraniche im Blick
source.quote: dass die Jungtiere das erste Mal mit ihren Eltern ins Winterquartier ziehen.

de.text: Kranichpaare können ein Leben lang zusammenbleiben.

source.title: Naturpark Kyffhäuser, Kraniche im Blick
source.quote: Verpaarte Kraniche können ein Leben lang zusammen bleiben.

de.text: Kraniche schlafen stehend im flachen Wasser, sicher vor Füchsen und Wildschweinen.

source.title: wissen.de, Faszination Kraniche: Sie sind wieder unterwegs (2022)
quote: da sie dort stehend schlafen.
So sind sie vor Füchsen, Wildschweinen und streunenden Hunden sicher.

de.text: „Der Kranich nach der Heimat strebt“: Schon Goethes Faust schaute dem Kranichzug nach.

source.title: Wikipedia, Kranich
quote: Goethe lässt im Faust (Vor dem Tor)
den Protagonisten klagen: Der Kranich nach der Heimat strebt.

de.text: Der Preußenkönig Friedrich Wilhelm I. ließ Kraniche jagen, „wegen ihres großen Schadens“: Flussauen sollten zu Ackerland werden.

source.title: Wikipedia, Kranich
source.quote: In Preußen ließ Friedrich Wilhelm I. zur Kultivierung von Stromtälern und Flussauen die Jagd auf Kraniche „wegen ihres großen Schadens“ anordnen.

de.text: Kraniche leisten Geburtshilfe: Will ein Küken aus dem Ei, treten die Eltern dagegen, gerade so fest, dass nur die Schale bricht.

source.title: Wikipedia, Kranich
quote: Sobald die Jungvögel versuchen, das Ei zu durchbrechen, treten die Elternvögel mit ihren Krallen nach dem betroffenen Ei
Der Tritt der adulten Vögel ist allerdings nur so stark, dass er die Schale des Geleges beschädigt und der Nachwuchs dadurch nicht verletzt wird.

de.text: Sobald es hell wird, starten an den Rastplätzen Hunderte bis Tausende Kraniche aus dem Wasser und fliegen in langen Ketten zu den Feldern.

source.title: wissen.de, Faszination Kraniche: Sie sind wieder unterwegs (2022)
quote: Sobald es hell wird, werden sie unruhig und mehrere hundert bis tausend Tiere starten aus dem Wasser und fliegen beeindruckend in langen Ketten los.
Sie machen sich auf umliegenden Feldern auf die Suche nach Nahrung.

de.text: Kraniche fliegen oft Hunderte Kilometer am Tag, im Extremfall {2000 km|1240 mi} am Stück. Mit Rückenwind schaffen sie bis zu {100 km/h|62 mph}.

source.title: wissen.de, Faszination Kraniche: Sie sind wieder unterwegs (2022)
quote: im Extremfall sogar 2.000 Kilometer nonstop.
bei Rückenwind sogar 100 Stundenkilometer.

en.text: Honey buzzards eat no honey. They're after the wasp grubs.

source.title: RSPB, Honey Buzzard
source.quote: Despite their name, they do not eat honey but in fact raid bee and wasp nests in search of the grubs inside.

en.text: Honey buzzards wreck the nests of the invasive Asian hornet.

source.title: Martín-Ávila et al. 2025, Pest Management Science
quote: as an ally for the control of the invasive yellow-legged hornet
with 89.3% of attacked nests destroyed.

en.text: Young honey buzzards may dress up as common buzzards to fool goshawks.

source.title: Hawk and Owl Trust, Honey Buzzard
quote: It is thought that this could be a defense against potential predation by Goshawk.
a Goshawk is going to be more cautious against this well-armed species, than against the much weaker Honey Buzzard.

en.text: Young honey buzzards take a gap year: they roam Africa before they ever come back.

source.title: Strandberg et al. 2012, Movements of immature European honey buzzards in tropical Africa (Ardea)
quote: Immature European Honey Buzzards Pernis apivorus are believed to remain in tropical Africa during the first years of their lives.
They travelled between 2,430 and 3,990 km (minimum distances) during 13 to 14 months, in which they visited several sites.

en.text: Unusual for a big raptor: male honey buzzards have blue-gray heads, females brown ones.

source.title: Wikipedia, European honey buzzard
source.quote: The sexes can be distinguished on plumage , which is unusual for a large bird of prey; the male has a blue-grey head, while the female's head is brown.

en.text: Honey buzzards spend hours on the forest floor, digging out wasp nests with their claws.

source.title: Wikipedia, European honey buzzard
quote: It spends large amounts of time on the forest floor excavating wasp nests.
It is equipped with long toes and claws adapted to raking and digging

en.text: A honey buzzard's spring courtship includes wing-clapping.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), European honey buzzard
source.quote: The European honey buzzard breeds in woodland , and is inconspicuous except in the spring, when the mating display includes wing-clapping.

en.text: On 3 September 2012 counters at Batumi, Georgia, logged 179,342 honey buzzards in one day: a world record for the species.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, 1 million raptors pass Batumi, Georgia (2012)
source.quote: On September 3, counters recorded a one-day, world record 179,342 honey buzzards.

en.text: Adult honey buzzards detour via Gibraltar. Young ones on their first trip cross the Mediterranean anywhere, yet reach the same winter homes.

source.title: Hake et al. 2003, Age-dependent migration strategy in honey buzzards tracked by satellite (Oikos)
quote: All adults crossed the Mediterranean Sea at the Strait of Gibraltar
In contrast, the juveniles travelled in more southerly directions, crossed the Mediterranean Sea at various places, but still ended up in the same wintering areas as the adults.

en.text: 31 young honey buzzards set off from Finland, and the wind scattered them across {3340 km|2080 mi} of Africa, west to east.

source.title: Vansteelant et al. 2017, Proceedings of the Royal Society B
quote: satellite-tagging 31 fledgling honey buzzards
the birds eventually spread out across 3340 km of longitude.

en.text: Scale-like feathers around a honey buzzard's eyes are armor against stings, and its plumage may even carry a chemical that deters wasps.

source.title: Wikipedia, European honey buzzard
quote: Scale-like feathers around the eyes and forehead provide armour against the stings of its prey species.
Honey buzzards are thought to have a chemical deterrent in their feathers that protects them from wasp attacks.

en.text: An adult honey buzzard combines a magnetic compass with remembered rivers and mountain ranges to find its way south.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), European honey buzzard
source.quote: Being a long-distance migrant, the honey buzzard relies on magnetic orientation to find its way south, as well as (for adult birds) a visual memory of recognisable geographical features such as mountain ranges and rivers, along the way.

de.text: Weltrekord: Am 3. September 2012 zogen 179.342 Wespenbussarde über Batumi in Georgien.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, 1 million raptors pass Batumi, Georgia (2012)
source.quote: On September 3, counters recorded a one-day, world record 179,342 honey buzzards.

de.text: Wespenbussarde graben Wespennester aus, die bis zu {40 cm|16 in} tief im Boden liegen.

source.title: Staatliche Vogelschutzwarte Hessen, Steckbrief Wespenbussard (2007)
source.quote: Wussten Sie, dass er bis 40 cm tief im Boden verborgene Wespennester ausgräbt

de.text: Wespenbussarde scharren Wespennester auf wie ein Haushuhn. Ziel sind die fetten Maden.

source.title: Die Rheinpfalz, Ganz wild auf stechende Insekten (2018)
quote: dann scharrt der Vogel wie ein Haushuhn und öffnet mit Krallen und Schnabel die Insektenlöcher.
Sein Ziel sind die Waben mit den fetten Puppen und Maden.

de.text: Gegen die Wespenstiche tragen Wespenbussarde verhornte Federn um Augen und Schnabel.

source.title: Die Rheinpfalz, Ganz wild auf stechende Insekten (2018)
source.quote: Um Augen und Schnabel schützen ihn verhornte Federn.

de.text: Wespenbussarde haben fast gerade Krallen und ans Graben angepasste Beine.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Wespenbussard
quote: Die Beine sind vor allem an das Graben im Boden angepasst.
Der Tarsometatarsus ist kurz und sehr kräftig, wobei der unbefiederte Teil sehr dick beschuppt ist.
Die Krallen sind kaum gebogen.

de.text: Beim Partnerwechsel am Nest geben Wespenbussarde einen leisen Rasselruf von sich.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Wespenbussard
source.quote: Noch seltener wahrgenommen wird ein vergleichsweise leiser, klappernder und in der Tonhöhe variierender „Rasselruf“, der vor allem bei der Ablösung des Partners am Nest eingesetzt wird.

de.text: Alte Wespenbussarde fliegen über Gibraltar. Junge queren beim ersten Zug das Meer irgendwo und landen doch im selben Winterquartier.

source.title: Hake et al. 2003, Oikos (Lund University)
quote: All adults crossed the Mediterranean Sea at the Strait of Gibraltar
In contrast, the juveniles travelled in more southerly directions, crossed the Mediterranean Sea at various places, but still ended up in the same wintering areas as the adults.

de.text: 31 junge Wespenbussarde starteten mit Sendern in Südfinnland. Der Wind verteilte sie quer über Afrika, {3340 km|2080 mi} von West nach Ost.

source.title: Vansteelant et al. 2017, Proceedings of the Royal Society B
quote: satellite-tagging 31 fledgling honey buzzards
from southern Finland
the birds eventually spread out across 3340 km of longitude.

de.text: Wespenbussarde sind gegen Stiche gepanzert: Verhornte Federn schützen Augen und Schnabel, die Nasenlöcher verengen sich zu Schlitzen.

source.title: Die Rheinpfalz, Ganz wild auf stechende Insekten (2018)
quote: Um Augen und Schnabel schützen ihn verhornte Federn.
Die Nasenlöcher kann er zu einem Schlitz verengen und die beschuppten Füße bieten ebenfalls keinen Angriffspunkt für die stechenden Insekten.

de.text: Wespenbussarde merken sich, wo sie ein Wespennest geplündert haben, und schauen immer wieder nach, ob dort neue Waben gewachsen sind.

source.title: Die Rheinpfalz, Ganz wild auf stechende Insekten (2018)

with 89.3% of attacked nests destroyed.

source.title: Strandberg et al. 2012, Ardea (Lund University)

en.text: Turtle dove parents feed their chicks milk, made in their own throats.

source.title: Smithsonian Science Education Center (Qrius), Pigeons and Doves: Parental Care
quote: Distinct from mammal milk, it is made in a pouch on the bird's throat (the crop).
Males and females both start to make crop milk just before eggs hatch.

en.text: The 'turtle' in turtle dove comes from its purring 'turr turr' call.

source.title: RSPB, Turtle Dove
source.quote: Its iconic purring ‘turr turr’ call is where the ‘Turtle’ name came from.

en.text: Egyptian wall reliefs from 4,500 years ago show turtle doves being caught in nets.

source.title: Operation Turtle Dove, Turtle Doves in culture
source.quote: Wall reliefs in Egypt from 4,500 years ago show the birds being trapped in nets.

en.text: In Greek myth, turtle doves pulled the chariot of Aphrodite, goddess of love.

source.title: Operation Turtle Dove, Turtle Doves in culture
source.quote: In Greek mythology, the birds pulled the chariot of Aphrodite, the goddess of love.

en.text: Britain's turtle dove population has fallen by almost 99% since the 1960s.

source.title: RSPB, Turtle Dove
source.quote: Turtle Dove numbers have plummeted by almost 99% since the 1960s.

en.text: A courting turtle dove cracks its wings like a whip.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), European turtle dove
source.quote: The nuptial flight, high and circling, is like that of the common wood pigeon , but the undulations are less decided; it is accompanied by the whip-crack of the downward flicked wings.

en.text: Turtle doves fly south by night, up to {700 km|435 mi} at a stretch, at up to {60 km/h|37 mph}.

source.title: Operation Turtle Dove (RSPB and partners), Titan
source.quote: And he travelled around 500-700 km per night, flying at a maximum speed of 60 km per hour.

en.text: Botticelli's portrait of the murdered Giuliano de' Medici includes a turtle dove. It's said to stand for his partner, in mourning.

source.title: Operation Turtle Dove, Turtle Doves in culture
quote: A posthumous portrait of him by Botticelli includes a perched turtle dove.
It’s said that Medici’s partner commissioned the picture, with the bird representing her, in mourning.

en.text: The 'snow white turtle doves' in the Coca-Cola song 'I'd like to teach the world to sing' were probably plain domestic white doves.

source.title: Operation Turtle Dove, Turtle Doves in culture
quote: Turtle doves also feature in the lyrics of “I’d like to teach the world to sing (in perfect harmony)”, a pop song from the 1970s which began life in a Coca-Cola advert.
However the “snow white turtle doves” mentioned are probably domesticated white doves!

en.text: Up to four million turtle doves were shot yearly around the Mediterranean. After a 2021 hunting pause, western Europe's doves rose 47%.

source.title: Wikipedia, European turtle dove
quote: According to a 2001 study cited by the European Commission, between two and four million turtle doves are shot annually in Malta, Cyprus, France, Italy, Spain and Greece.
Following the hunting moratorium, the western European breeding population increased by approximately 47% between 2021 and 2025.

en.text: When Linnaeus named the turtle dove in 1758, he said it came from India. That was a mistake: the species' official home is now England.

source.title: Wikipedia, European turtle dove
quote: Linnaeus gave the locality as "India".
This was an error, and the type locality has been designated as England.

en.text: Young turtle doves leave the nest before they can fly, staying among nearby branches instead.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Turteltaube
quote: Jungvögel verlassen in einem Lebensalter von etwa 14 Tagen das Nest.
Sie sind zu dem Zeitpunkt noch nicht flugfähig und halten sich in den Ästen in der Nähe des Nestes auf.

de.text: Der Name Turteltaube kommt vom schnurrenden Ruf des Vogels: „turr turr“.

source.title: t-online (dpa), Vogel des Jahres 2020: Die Turteltaube ist ein Symbol der Liebe
quote: Turteltauben haben ihren Namen vor allem wegen ihrer Laute, die sie von sich geben
was sich auch wie eine Art Schnurren anhört.

de.text: Verliebte heißen Turteltauben, weil Männchen und Weibchen oft unzertrennlich sind.

source.title: t-online (dpa), Vogel des Jahres 2020: Die Turteltaube ist ein Symbol der Liebe
source.quote: Da männliche und weibliche Tiere oft unzertrennlich sind, wurde die Bezeichnung auch auf Menschen übertragen.

de.text: Unsere kleinste Taube, die Turteltaube, zieht als einzige bis südlich der Sahara.

source.title: Sonntagsblatt, Turteltaube ist Vogel des Jahres 2020 (2019)
quote: Unsere kleinste Taube findet kaum noch geeignete Lebensräume.
Turteltauben ziehen im Winter als einzige mitteleuropäische Taubenart eine Langstrecke: bis südlich der Sahara.

de.text: Die Turteltaube war 2020 der erste weltweit gefährdete Vogel des Jahres.

source.title: t-online (dpa), Vogel des Jahres 2020: Die Turteltaube ist ein Symbol der Liebe
source.quote: Zum ersten Mal sei ein Vogel gekürt worden, der als global gefährdete Art auf der weltweiten Roten Liste stehe

de.text: Seit 1980 schrumpfte der Bestand um fast 90 %. Ganze Landstriche sind turteltaubenfrei.

source.title: t-online (dpa), Vogel des Jahres 2020: Die Turteltaube ist ein Symbol der Liebe
source.quote: Seit 1980 haben wir fast 90 Prozent dieser Art verloren, ganze Landstriche sind turteltaubenfrei.

de.text: Turteltauben ziehen nachts. Eine besenderte Taube schaffte bis zu {700 km|435 mi} in einer Nacht.

source.title: Operation Turtle Dove (RSPB and partners), Titan
source.quote: And he travelled around 500-700 km per night, flying at a maximum speed of 60 km per hour.

de.text: Junge Turteltauben tragen noch keinen schwarz-weißen Halsstreifen-Kragen.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Turteltaube
source.quote: Die für die adulten Vögel charakteristischen Halsquerbinden entwickeln sich erst nach einigen Monaten.

de.text: Wegen des Gefieders und eines Volksglaubens hielt man Turteltauben in Volieren: Die Vögel sollten Krankheiten der Menschen an sich ziehen.

source.title: t-online (dpa), Vogel des Jahres 2020: Die Turteltaube ist ein Symbol der Liebe
quote: Doch nicht nur deswegen wurde sie damals von Menschen in Volieren gehalten.
der Volksglaube, dass die Tiere die Krankheiten der Menschen an sich ziehen

de.text: Turteltauben-Küken wachsen mit Milch auf: Kurz vor dem Schlüpfen beginnen Vater und Mutter, sie im Kropf zu bilden, einer Tasche am Hals.

source.title: Smithsonian Science Education Center (Qrius), Pigeons and Doves: Parental Care
quote: Distinct from mammal milk, it is made in a pouch on the bird's throat (the crop).
Males and females both start to make crop milk just before eggs hatch.

de.text: Früher hörte man das Gurren der Turteltaube an jedem Dorfrand. Heute brüten die Vögel oft auf alten Truppenübungsplätzen oder in Weinbergen.

source.title: Sonntagsblatt, Turteltaube ist Vogel des Jahres 2020 (2019)
quote: Früher sei das markante Gurren der Turteltaube an jedem Dorfrand oder Flussufer zu hören gewesen
Heute brüteten Turteltauben häufig auf ehemaligen Truppenübungsplätzen oder in Weinbauregionen

de.text: Auf Malta werden jedes Frühjahr in zwei Wochen offiziell 20.000 Turteltauben gefangen: etwa ein Drittel aller, die in Deutschland brüten.

source.title: Wikipedia, Turteltaube
quote: innerhalb eines Zeitraums von zwei Wochen 20.000 Turteltauben von den rund 14.000 registrierten Jägern des Landes offiziell in Fangnetzen gefangen.
Das entspricht etwa einem Drittel des gesamten deutschen Brutbestands an Turteltauben.

de.text: Turteltauben ziehen nach der Rückkehr aus Afrika noch wochenlang umher. Der Ort der Balz muss nicht der spätere Brutplatz sein.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Turteltaube
quote: Rückkehrende Turteltauben schreiten nicht sofort zur Brut, sondern ziehen einzeln und als Paar über mehrere Wochen umher.
Selbst eine Balz ist kein Indiz dafür, dass das Paar an diesem Ort auch zur Brut schreiten wird. [ 15 ]

en.text: Lesser black-backed gulls eat fish, worms and abandoned chips.

source.title: RSPB, Lesser Black-backed Gull
source.quote: They feed on a large variety of food including fish, worms, and edible rubbish (and abandoned chips).

en.text: Female gulls dawdle in fall and arrive about 15 days after the males.

source.title: Baert et al. 2018, Scientific Reports
source.quote: arrived 15 days later at their wintering areas, than males.

en.text: City gulls barely visit the sea {10 km|6 mi} away: towns and fields feed them.

source.title: Spelt et al. 2019, Scientific Reports
source.quote: Despite the proximity of marine areas (~10 km), the birds only made significant use of terrestrial environments

en.text: The oldest known lesser black-backed gull lived to almost 35.

source.title: BTO, BirdFacts: Lesser Black-backed Gull
source.quote: Maximum age from a ringed bird 34 years, 10 months, 27 days

en.text: This gull's 'laughing' cry sounds like a herring gull's, only much deeper.

source.title: Wikipedia, Lesser black-backed gull
source.quote: Their call is a "laughing" cry like that of the herring gull, but with a markedly deeper pitch.

en.text: Once just a winter guest, this gull is now seen in North America all year round.

source.title: Wikipedia, Lesser black-backed gull
source.quote: Formerly just a winter visitor to North America, it now occurs in large numbers some winters and birds are recorded year-round.

en.text: These gulls eat almost anything: starfish, berries, eggs, chicks, offal, even pigeons.

source.title: Wikipedia, Lesser black-backed gull
quote: Lesser black-backed gull preying upon a feral pigeon
eat fish, insects, crustaceans, worms, starfish, molluscs, seeds, berries, small mammals, eggs, small birds, chicks, scraps, offal

en.text: Gull chicks peck the red spot on a parent's bill to ask for food.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Lesser black-backed gull
source.quote: The bill is yellow with a red spot at which the young peck, inducing feeding (see fixed action pattern ).

en.text: A satellite-tagged lesser black-backed gull flew its last {3500 km|2200 mi} to Lake Victoria non-stop: 92 hours, ending near Kampala.

source.title: Kube et al., Hop or jump: autumn migration strategies of lesser black-backed gulls (Microwave Telemetry newsletter, 2000)
quote: The other bird went further south to Lake Victoria.
It reached its wintering grounds near Kampala, Uganda, on 29 September.
Its final nonstop journey of about 3500 km lasted 92 hours (38 km/h).

en.text: Gull forms blend into each other around the Pole, yet at the ring's two ends, herring and lesser black-backed gulls are distinct species.

source.title: Wikipedia, Lesser black-backed gull
source.quote: Differences between adjacent forms in this ring are fairly small, but by the time the circuit is completed, the end members, herring gull and lesser black-backed gull, are clearly different species.

en.text: North America's first lesser black-backed gull outside Greenland turned up in New Jersey in 1934. By the 1980s they reached every US coast.

source.title: Sanibel-Captiva Conservation Foundation, Lesser Black-Backed Gulls Increasing on Sanibel and Captiva (2024)
quote: the first record in North America outside of Greenland wasn't until 1934 in New Jersey.
By the 1980s, lesser black-backed gulls had been observed across all the Great Lakes and the entirety of the Atlantic and Gulf coast of the U.S.,

en.text: Where do America's lesser black-backed gulls come from? Thousands are seen each year, yet only two banded birds from Europe ever turned up.

source.title: Sanibel-Captiva Conservation Foundation, Lesser Black-Backed Gulls Increasing on Sanibel and Captiva (2024)
quote: only two banded lesser black-backed gulls have been re-sighted in North America — one in 1997, and one in 2002.
despite thousands of observations of these gulls year after year,

en.text: These gulls crept west: they settled in Iceland in the 1920s and Greenland in the 1990s. Most of America's probably come from there.

source.title: Sanibel-Captiva Conservation Foundation, Lesser Black-Backed Gulls Increasing on Sanibel and Captiva (2024)
quote: In the 1920s, lesser black-backed gulls established breeding grounds in Iceland, which by 2004 had reached 40,000 breeding pairs.
In the 1990s, lesser black-backed gulls (likely from Iceland) were confirmed breeding in Greenland
the researchers propose that most lesser black-backed gulls seen in North America come from western Iceland and Greenland.

en.text: Young lesser black-backed gulls start out scaly brown, not black-backed. The journey to adulthood takes four years.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Lesser black-backed gull
quote: Young birds have scaly black-brown upperparts and a neat wing pattern.
They take four years to reach maturity.

de.text: Heringsmöwen fressen Fisch, Würmer und Essensreste, auch liegen gelassene Pommes.

source.title: RSPB, Lesser Black-backed Gull
source.quote: They feed on a large variety of food including fish, worms, and edible rubbish (and abandoned chips).

de.text: Die älteste bekannte Heringsmöwe, ein beringter Vogel, wurde fast 35 Jahre alt.

source.title: BTO, BirdFacts: Lesser Black-backed Gull
source.quote: Maximum age from a ringed bird 34 years, 10 months, 27 days

source.title: Baert et al. 2018, Scientific Reports

source.title: Schutzstation Wattenmeer, Tier des Monats: Die Heringsmöwe
source.quote: nach Nordafrika, wo sie im Winter die häufigste Möwenart sind.

source.quote: der wissenschaftliche Name übersetzt einfach "dunkle Möwe" bedeutet?

source.title: Schutzstation Wattenmeer, Tier des Monats: Die Heringsmöwe

de.text: Heringsmöwen tauchen bei der Fischjagd manchmal vollständig unter.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Heringsmöwe
source.quote: Fische werden auf dem Meer oft stoßtauchend aus dem Suchflug aus 10–12 m Höhe heraus erbeutet, wobei der Vogel im 45°-Winkel etwa 8 m herabfliegt, rüttelnd abbremst, hinabstößt und völlig untertaucht.

de.text: Vorsicht, Verwechslung: Die „herring gull“ der Briten ist unsere Silbermöwe. Unsere Heringsmöwe heißt dort „Kleine Schwarzrückenmöwe“.

source.title: Schutzstation Wattenmeer, Tier des Monats: Die Heringsmöwe
quote: die Heringsmöwe (herring gull) der Briten unsere Silbermöwe ist, während unsere Heringsmöwe dort
Kleine Schwarzrückenmöwe

de.text: Anders als Silbermöwen suchen Heringsmöwen ihr Futter nicht im Watt, sondern bis zu {130 km|80 mi} draußen auf See, hinter den Fischkuttern.

Sie fliegen täglich 50-80, mitunter 130 km weit hinaus, um Fische und Krebse zu erbeuten

de.text: Nach dem Treibnetzverbot im westlichen Mittelmeer suchten Heringsmöwen neue Nahrung: auch in Olivenhainen und Reisfeldern.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Heringsmöwe
source.quote: So führte ein 1991 von der UN erlassenes Moratorium zur Treibnetzfischerei im westlichen Mittelmeer dazu, dass die Art auf andere Nahrungsquellen umsteigen musste und zwischenzeitlich vermehrt auf Mülldeponien, in Olivenhainen und auf Reisfeldern anzutreffen war.

en.text: Shrikes keep a larder: leftover prey, impaled on thorns for later.

source.title: RSPB, Red-backed Shrike
source.quote: Their catches are taken to their 'larder' where they are impaled on a thorn or wedged into branches for later.

en.text: The red-backed shrike laces its song with other birds' calls.

source.title: Museum für Naturkunde Berlin, Naturblick: Red-backed shrike
source.quote: They imitate the song of other birds.

en.text: Lanius, the red-backed shrike's Latin name, means 'butcher'.

source.title: Wikipedia, Red-backed shrike
source.quote: The genus name, Lanius , is derived from the Latin word for " butcher ", and some shrikes are also known as "butcher birds" because of their feeding habits.

en.text: This little songbird is a hunter: it catches frogs, lizards, mice and even small birds.

source.title: Wikipedia, Red-backed shrike
source.quote: This 16–18 cm-long (6.3–7.1 in) migratory bird eats large insects , small birds , frogs , rodents and lizards .

en.text: A shrike's thorn larder is also for show: it tells females how good a male's territory is.

source.title: Wikipedia, Shrike
source.quote: The primary function of conspicuously impaling prey on thorny vegetation is however thought to be for males to display their fitness and the quality of the territory held to prospective mates.

en.text: The word 'shrike' comes from the Old English for 'shriek', after the bird's shrill call.

source.title: Wikipedia, Red-backed shrike
source.quote: The common English name "shrike" is from Middle English *schrike , *schryke , from Old English sċrīc , "shriek", from the same root as shriek and screech , referring to the bird's shrill cry or call.

en.text: Red-backed shrikes hang their larder on barbed-wire fences as readily as on thorns.

source.title: Wikipedia, Red-backed shrike
source.quote: Like other shrikes it hunts from prominent perches, and impales corpses on thorns or barbed wire as a

en.text: A red-backed shrike coughs up pellets of indigestible leftovers.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Neuntöter
source.quote: Unverdauliche Bestandteile werden als Speiballen ausgewürgt.

en.text: Though a songbird, the red-backed shrike has a hooked bill like a bird of prey's, made for tearing meat.

source.title: Wikipedia, Shrike
source.quote: Their beaks are hooked, like those of a bird of prey , reflecting their carnivorous nature; their calls are strident.

en.text: Red-backed shrikes were once among the cuckoo's top hosts. Now they attack cuckoos so fiercely that in places no cuckoo chicks are left.

source.title: Hromada et al. 2022, Ecology and Evolution
quote: Nevertheless, during the last 30 years, there is increasing evidence from Central Europe that the occurrence of cuckoo chicks in shrike nests has become scarcer, and that in some locations they have disappeared completely.
Our results show that shrikes defending their nests attacked cuckoos very vigorously, more often, and more intensively than they did sparrowhawks.

en.text: In 1575 the poet George Turberville wrote that a shrike fakes cries of distress to lure other birds close, then 'devoureth them'.

source.title: Wikipedia, Shrike
quote: Shrikes vocally imitate their prey to lure them for capture.
In 1575, this was noted by the English poet George Turberville

en.text: Chaucer described a crooked summoner as full of venom as a 'wariangle': an old name for the shrike, once thought to be poisonous.

source.title: Chaucer Bibliography Online (UTSA): Harrison, Chaucer's 'Wariangles' (1954)
source.quote: Offers historical "bird-lore" as evidence of the poisonousness of the "wariangles" (shrikes, or butcher-birds), cited in the description of the summoner in FrT 3.1408).

en.text: By 1988 just one pair of red-backed shrikes was left in Britain. The next year, for the first time, no nest was found anywhere in the UK.

source.title: Wikipedia, Red-backed shrike
quote: The bird's last stronghold was in Breckland but by 1988 just a single pair remained
The following year for the first time no nests were recorded in the UK.

en.text: America has its own 'butcherbird': the loggerhead shrike. Like its red-backed cousin, it stores prey on display, for example in a tree.

source.title: Wikipedia, Loggerhead shrike
source.quote: It is nicknamed the butcherbird after its carnivorous tendencies, as it consumes prey such as insects, amphibians, lizards, small mammals and small birds, and some prey end up displayed and stored at a site, for example in a tree.

en.text: Some unattached male shrikes help feed another pair's young, or join in as extra singers.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Neuntöter
source.quote: Lediglich zum Ende der Brutsaison, nach dem Ausfliegen der Jungvögel, schließen sich manchmal nichtbrütende Männchen den Familien an, beteiligen sich an der Fütterung der Jungen oder betätigen sich als „Vorsänger“.

de.text: Den Namen gab der Volksglaube: Der Neuntöter fresse erst, wenn neun Beutetiere tot seien.

source.title: LBV, Artenporträt Neuntöter
quote: Der Volksglaube gab dem Neuntöter seinen Namen.
also neunmal Beute gemacht hat.

de.text: Für Regentage spießen Neuntöter Beute auf Dornen oder auf Stacheldraht an Weidezäunen.

source.title: Wikipedia, Neuntöter
quote: Um beispielsweise mehrere Regentage oder feuchtkalte Morgenstunden
auf Dornen oder Stacheln sowie auf Stacheldraht von Weidezäunen spießt.

de.text: Der Neuntöter mischt die Stimmen anderer Vögel in seinen Gesang.

source.title: Wikipedia, Neuntöter
source.quote: Diese werden oft mit Imitationen anderer Arten

de.text: Ein besonders begabtes Neuntöter-Männchen sang lange Passagen aus dem Lied der Feldlerche.

source.title: Wikipedia, Neuntöter
source.quote: Berichten zufolge beherrschte ein offensichtlich besonders begabtes Männchen längere Passagen des Feldlerchengesangs

de.text: Neuntöter ziehen nur nachts und jeder für sich. Der Tag gehört dem Fressen.

source.title: Wikipedia, Neuntöter
source.quote: Den Tag zur Nahrungsaufnahme nutzend, zieht der Neuntöter ausschließlich nachts und einzeln.

de.text: Der zuwachsende Todesstreifen der deutsch-deutschen Grenze bot Neuntötern gute Jahre.

source.title: Wikipedia, Neuntöter
quote: nach der Wiedervereinigung zuwachsende ehemalige
an der innerdeutschen Grenze
bieten für den Neuntöter nur wenige Jahre günstige Bedingungen.

de.text: Neuntöter singen oft mit fast geschlossenem Schnabel.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Neuntöter
source.quote: Der Gesang wird meist in aufrecht sitzender Haltung mit kaum geöffnetem Schnabel vorgetragen.

de.text: Neuntöter, Negenmörder, Dorndreher, Dorntreter: Die alten Volksnamen erzählen alle vom Töten und Aufspießen.

source.title: Wikipedia, Neuntöter
quote: Hieraus entstanden auch ähnliche Namen wie Neunmörder ( niederdeutsch Negenmörder )
Ebenfalls auf das „Spießen“ bezieht sich der Name Dorndreher
oder Dorntreter .

de.text: Sperbergrasmücken bauen ihr Nest gern im selben Busch wie der Neuntöter. Vermutlich hält der wehrhafte Nachbar auch von ihnen Feinde fern.

source.title: Wikipedia, Neuntöter

en.text: Wheatears love rabbits: they keep the grass short and dig their nest holes.

en.text: Young Alaskan wheatears find their way to Africa alone: they're born knowing the route.

source.title: University of Alaska Fairbanks Geophysical Institute, Ned Rozell: Northern wheatears now on remarkable journey (2019)
quote: How do birds that pecked from eggshells on Alaska tundra just this summer know how to make it to Africa?
The birds are born with that knowledge, maybe tied to the Earth's magnetic field and geographic landforms.

en.text: The wheatear's song crackles and pops, and borrows the calls of other birds.

source.title: National Park Service, Gates of the Arctic: Northern Wheatear
source.quote: The Northern Wheatear's song is complex and composed of a variety of crackling and popping sounds and, like the Bluethroat, the mimicked vocalizations of other bird species.

en.text: A wheatear's white tail carries a bold black, upside-down T.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Northern wheatear
source.quote: Both sexes have a white rump and tail, with a black inverted T-pattern at the end of the tail.

en.text: Alaska's wheatears don't head south to the Americas. They fly west, over the Bering Strait and across the whole of Asia, to Africa.

source.title: Audubon Field Guide, Northern Wheatear
source.quote: Birds from Alaska and northwestern Canada cross Bering Strait and make long westward flight across Asia, also going to wintering grounds mostly in Africa.

en.text: Alaska's wheatears spend the summer on the tundra among muskoxen, and the winter in East Africa among zebras and giraffes.

source.title: University of Alaska Fairbanks Geophysical Institute, Ned Rozell: Northern wheatears now on remarkable journey (2019)
quote: Birds that spent their summer next to muskoxen are now leaving Alaska to spend winter with zebras.
After four months in the sub-Sahara with giraffes, they will again feel the urge, and hop from an acacia tree branch.

en.text: North America's two wheatear groups probably never meet: Alaska's birds winter in East Africa, Baffin Island's in West Africa.

source.title: University of Alaska Fairbanks Geophysical Institute, Ned Rozell: Northern wheatears now on remarkable journey (2019)
quote: The Alaska and Baffin Island populations of wheatears probably never meet, either on the tundra or on the savanna.
The one bird whose geolocator they were able to recover on Baffin Island spent its winter in Mauritania, in western Africa.
until the birds stop for the winter months in eastern Africa: Sudan, Uganda or Kenya.

en.text: After the Ice Age, wheatears may have spread from the Middle East both ways: northeast to Alaska, and northwest to Canada via Europe.

source.title: University of Alaska Fairbanks Geophysical Institute, Ned Rozell: Northern wheatears now on remarkable journey (2019)
quote: Bairlein said that during the last great glacial period, during which much of the far north was ice-covered, wheatears may have been holed up in the Middle East.
When the glaciers shrank from the continents, one group of wheatears may have expanded to the northeast, reaching Alaska, while the other drifted northwest, reaching Canada via Europe and Greenland.

en.text: Northern wheatears can make a nursery in a pipe or a wall cavity; the female builds while the male sings nearby.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Northern wheatear
quote: The nest is built entirely by the female while the male perches nearby, sings and sometimes performs song-flights.
The nest is placed in a cavity such as a rabbit burrow, a crevice among rocks or in a man-made object such as a wall or pipe.

sondern wandern quer durch Asien bis nach Südwestafrika

en.text: The Far Eastern curlew has the longest bill of any wader: about {20 cm|8 in}.

source.title: Birds New Zealand / Te Papa, New Zealand Birds Online: Eastern curlew
source.quote: has the longest bill of any wader at around 20 cm in length.

en.text: It is the largest migratory shorebird in the world.

source.title: Australian Government DCCEEW (2023), Conservation Advice for Numenius madagascariensis (far eastern curlew)
source.quote: Far eastern curlews are the largest migratory shorebird species in the world.

en.text: Young curlews stay two or three years in Australia before their first trip north.

source.title: Australian Government DCCEEW (2023), Conservation Advice for Numenius madagascariensis (far eastern curlew)
source.quote: young far eastern curlews might spend their second austral winter in Australia, and some might also spend their third winter in Australia before undertaking their first northward migration

en.text: Females have longer bills and feed on sandier flats; males stick to the mud.

source.title: Australian Government DCCEEW (2023), Conservation Advice for Numenius madagascariensis (far eastern curlew)
quote: females tend to be larger and have a longer bill.
with females utilising more sandy areas and males utilising more muddy areas

en.text: About 80% of all Far Eastern curlews refuel on the Yellow Sea.

source.title: Australian Government DCCEEW (2023), Conservation Advice for Numenius madagascariensis (far eastern curlew)
source.quote: It supports approximately 80 percent of the species' estimated flyway population during their northward migration

en.text: Its Latin name means 'from Madagascar', but this curlew has never been seen there.

source.title: Wikipedia, Far Eastern curlew
source.quote: The name madagascariensis , referring to Madagascar , was an error by Brisson, with the type locality now known to have been Makassar on Sulawesi, Indonesia, where it winters; the species has never been recorded in Madagascar.

en.text: A Far Eastern curlew eats a crab by snapping off the legs first, then swallowing the lot.

source.title: New Zealand Birds Online, Eastern curlew
source.quote: They usually break crabs legs off first before swallowing the legs and body.

en.text: A Far Eastern curlew sometimes swaps its seafood diet for berries while on migration.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Far Eastern curlew
source.quote: During migration it also feeds on berries.

en.text: Three curlews tracked from Victoria, Australia, all flew {8500 km|5300 mi} non-stop to the Yellow Sea: 7 to 8 days without landing.

source.title: Victorian Wader Study Group, Eastern Curlew geolocator study
source.quote: The three Eastern Curlews departed from their non-breeding area during 4–14 Mar and all flew 8,500 km nonstop to the western shores of the Yellow Sea taking 7–8 days.

en.text: In 1997 a typhoon swept migrating curlews far east of their route. They still found their way back to their own wintering grounds.

source.title: Bird Research News 1(3), Eastern Curlew (2004)
quote: The tracked birds were hit by a typhoon on migration and some of them were swept east- wards from the normal route in 1997.
These birds returned to the wintering grounds.

en.text: Two Darwin curlews reached the Yellow Sea. The adult flew on to breed in Kamchatka; the younger one surprised everyone by staying in China.

source.title: NESP Threatened Species Recovery Hub, Curlew globe-trotting update
quote: Both birds left Darwin in April 2018 and reached the Yellow Sea to refuel for the next leg of the migration.
Only one of the birds, Bird A, travelled further north to the breeding grounds on the Kamchatka Peninsula in south-east Russia.
Bird B, the other, younger, bird surprised us by staying in China.

en.text: More than 65% of the Yellow Sea mudflats where these curlews refuel have been turned into land, and the curlew has declined with them.

source.title: Wikipedia, Far Eastern curlew
source.quote: to the massive tidal flat reclamations by China, North Korea and South Korea along the coasts of the Yellow Sea , which have caused a greater than 65% loss of mudflats

en.text: Numenius, the curlew's scientific genus name, is linked to Greek words for a new moon: a nod to the crescent-shaped bill.

source.title: Wikipedia, Curlew
quote: The name Numenius is from Ancient Greek noumenios , a bird mentioned by Hesychius .
It is associated with the curlews because it appears to be derived from neos , "new" and mene , "moon", referring to the crescent-shaped bill.

en.text: 'Kettles' of tens of thousands of hawks can circle over the Great Lakes shores.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, Broad-winged Hawk
source.quote: flocks or “kettles” of tens of thousands of Broad-winged Hawks can be seen along the shorelines of the Great Lakes

en.text: Broad-winged hawks on Cuba and Puerto Rico stay home all year.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, Broad-winged Hawk
source.quote: Non-migratory subspecies of broadwings inhabit Cuba, Puerto Rico, and several other islands in the West Indies.

en.text: On one September day in 2003, 101,698 broad-winged hawks flew past Duluth, Minnesota.

source.title: Laura Erickson, For the Birds: Record-breaking Day at Hawk Ridge (2003)
quote: Yesterday, September 15, 2003, came as close to that vision as I’ve ever seen, right here in Duluth.
By the end of the day, the final count was 102,329 hawks, 101,698 of which were Broad-winged Hawks.

en.text: On the way south, broad-winged hawks snack on migrating dragonflies.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, Broad-winged Hawk
source.quote: During migration, broadwings will feed opportunistically on insects, including migrating dragonflies

en.text: Broad-winged hawks are fussy eaters: they skin frogs and snakes before eating them.

source.title: Wikipedia, Broad-winged hawk
source.quote: They give special attention to preparing their food for consumption, skinning frogs and snakes and plucking prey birds' feathers.

en.text: Broad-winged hawks rarely drink: the water in their prey is all they need.

source.title: Wikipedia, Broad-winged hawk
source.quote: They rarely drink water and are able to survive solely with the water present in their prey.

en.text: Hawk watchers in Corpus Christi, Texas, count 700,000 raptors a year, mostly broad-wings.

source.title: Texas Parks & Wildlife magazine, Hawk Watch (May 2013)
quote: During its 16-year existence, it has racked up a mind-boggling tally of more than 10 million raptors, averaging more than 700,000 a year.
of the 23 species recorded, broad-winged hawks dominated the tally

en.text: A broad-winged hawk sounds more like a thin whistle than a fierce scream.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Broad-winged hawk
source.quote: Their call sounds like a very high-pitched kee-ee , almost like a whistle.

en.text: In a kettle the adults tend to lead and the young follow. Young broad-wings that go astray may end up wintering in Florida, far off course.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, Broad-winged Hawk
quote: in mixed-aged flocks adults are more likely to be the leading bird or in the leading half of the flock.

Observations of juveniles wintering in Florida, a location off the migration route and north of the typical wintering grounds, appears to support the idea that juveniles are more likely than adults to have difficulty with navigation and orientation.

en.text: Broad-wings race the sun. They leave in mid-September because later in fall the sun is too low to make the warm updrafts they travel on.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, Broad-winged Hawk
quote: Broad-winged Hawks need to leave their nesting grounds as soon as possible in order to migrate when thermal activity is most predictable.
Birds that leave later in the season, when the days are shorter and the sun is not as high in the sky, will face conditions that are less favorable for thermal migration.

en.text: Satellite tags from Hawk Mountain held a surprise: broad-wings that nest a few miles apart may spend the winter {1600 km|1000 mi} apart.

source.title: Northern Woodlands, There and Back Again: Tracking Broad-Winged Hawk Migration (2024)
source.quote: One of the most surprising findings of this study is that birds who summer within a few miles of each other might spend their winters a thousand miles apart.

en.text: Broad-wings from all over merge on the way south. In Veracruz, Mexico, one kettle can hold more hawks than pass New Hampshire all fall.

source.title: Northern Woodlands, There and Back Again: Tracking Broad-Winged Hawk Migration (2024)
source.quote: daily counts can top 200,000 birds, with more hawks whirling in a single kettle on a warm October afternoon than across the entirety of the New Hampshire migration season.

en.text: Flocks of soaring broad-wings are called kettles: they look like steam rising from a kettle, or soup swirling in a pot.

source.title: Northern Woodlands, There and Back Again: Tracking Broad-Winged Hawk Migration (2024)
source.quote: soaring on thermals in groups called “kettles,” named for their resemblance to steam rising from a kettle or soup swirling in a pot.

en.text: Courting broad-winged hawks can hook their feet together in midair and spiral down as a pair.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Broad-winged hawk
source.quote: Birds meet in the air, hook their feet together and spiral down together.

en.text: A threatened baby turkey vulture fights back with projectile vomit.

en.text: No voice box: turkey vultures can only hiss and grunt.

source.title: Missouri Department of Conservation, Turkey Vulture
source.quote: They have no voice box (syrinx), so they can only hiss and grunt when they vocalize.

en.text: Turkey vultures can eat carrion with anthrax or rabies, and stop it spreading.

source.title: Missouri Department of Conservation, Turkey Vulture
source.quote: Their ability to safely eat carrion containing pathogens such as anthrax and rabies helps reduce the spread of these diseases.

en.text: Black vultures can barely smell, so they follow turkey vultures to dinner.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, Turkey Vulture
source.quote: Other vultures, such as Black Vultures, lack a keen sense of smell and often follow Turkey Vultures to carcasses.

en.text: Turkey vultures have such a good sense of smell that they help find gas leaks.

source.title: Chesapeake Bay Program, Turkey Vulture
source.quote: Turkey vultures have such a strong sense of smell that they can help gas companies detect gas leaks.

en.text: Like storks, turkey vultures cool off by pooping on their own legs.

source.title: Wikipedia, Turkey vulture
source.quote: Like storks, the turkey vulture often defecates on its own legs, using the evaporation of the water in the feces and/or urine to cool itself, a process known as urohidrosis .

en.text: Lord Richard, a captive turkey vulture in California, was 51 years old in 2025.

source.title: Wikipedia, Turkey vulture
quote: As of 2025, there is one captive bird which is 51 years
a male named Lord Richard that lives at the Lindsay Wildlife Experience in Walnut Creek, California

en.text: Turkey vultures chill out at night: their body temperature drops by about {6 °C|11 °F}.

source.title: Wikipedia, Turkey vulture
source.quote: The turkey vulture lowers its night-time body temperature by about 6 °C or 11 °F to 34 °C (93 °F) , becoming slightly hypothermic .

en.text: Turkey vultures are named for their bald red head and dark feathers, like a male turkey's.

source.title: Wikipedia, Turkey vulture
source.quote: The turkey vulture received its common name from the resemblance of the adult's bald red head and dark plumage to that of the male wild turkey .

en.text: A turkey vulture's claws are blunt and poorly suited to grabbing prey.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Turkey vulture
source.quote: The feet are flat, relatively weak, and poorly adapted to grasping; the talons are also not designed for grasping, as they are relatively blunt.

en.text: Courting turkey vultures play follow-the-leader in the air, one copying the other's flight path exactly.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, Turkey Vulture
source.quote: Vultures perform aerial courtship displays during which one bird follows the other and precisely mimics the lead bird's flight path.

en.text: A bald head keeps a vulture clean: no feathers for bacteria to lodge in, and the sun disinfects the bare skin.

source.title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, Vulture
source.quote: New World vultures have a distinctive bald head, an adaptation that helps reduce the risks of disease, because bacteria could become lodged in feathers, while the bald head and neck may be disinfected by the sun's rays.

en.text: Turkey vultures often stand with their wings spread wide, especially after damp nights: to dry off, warm up and bake off bacteria.

source.title: Wikipedia, Turkey vulture
quote: This vulture is often seen standing in a spread-winged or horaltic stance.
The stance is believed to serve multiple functions: drying the wings, warming the body, and baking off bacteria.
It is practiced more often following damp or rainy nights.

en.text: Ranchers sometimes blame turkey vultures for dead calves. But they never kill: black vultures do, and turkey vultures eat the leftovers.

source.title: Wikipedia, Turkey vulture
quote: This species also may be perceived as a threat by farmers due to the similar black vulture's tendency to attack and kill newborn cattle.
The turkey vulture does not kill live animals but will mix with flocks of black vultures and will scavenge what they leave behind.

en.text: America's vultures look like Africa's, but they aren't close kin: the two groups evolved on different continents from different ancestors.

source.title: Wikipedia, Turkey vulture
source.quote: Though they are similar in appearance and have similar ecological roles , the New World and Old World vultures evolved in different parts of the world and from different ancestors.

en.text: Courting turkey vultures gather in a circle and hop around its edge with their wings half spread.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Turkey vulture
source.quote: Courtship rituals of the turkey vulture involve several individuals gathering in a circle, where they perform hopping movements around the perimeter of the circle with wings partially spread.

en.text: Ospreys carry their fish head first, like a torpedo.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, Osprey
source.quote: Carry fish head first to make them more aerodynamic in flight.

en.text: An extra eyelid works like swimming goggles when an osprey dives.

source.title: RSPB, Osprey
source.quote: They have a special extra eyelid – a bit like a contact lens – that helps to protect their eyes when they hunt under water.

en.text: Courting male ospreys 'sky dance' up to {90 m|300 ft} high, often holding a fish.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, Osprey
quote: males usually carry a fish or nesting material and call repeatedly.
which sometimes reach heights of 300 feet or more.

en.text: Young ospreys spend over a year in Africa or South America before flying north.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, Osprey
source.quote: Most Ospreys do not return to their breeding grounds until the spring of their second year

en.text: Ospreys add to their nest every year, until it weighs up to {180 kg|400 lb}.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, Osprey
source.quote: Ospreys add material to their nests each year, and sometimes build massive structures weighing up to 400 pounds.

en.text: The osprey is in a family of its own: no other living bird shares it.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, Osprey
source.quote: Ospreys are the only member of the family Pandionidae.

en.text: 'Sea hawk' is an old name for the osprey, as in the Seattle Seahawks.

source.title: Wikipedia, Osprey
quote: historically known as sea hawk , river hawk , and fish hawk
"Seahawks", another term for osprey, is also common among sports teams.

en.text: Ospreys can close their nostrils to keep the water out when they dive.

source.title: Wikipedia, Osprey
source.quote: closable nostrils to keep out water during dives

en.text: The oldest known wild osprey in Europe lived to 26 years and 11 months.

source.title: Wikipedia, Osprey
source.quote: The oldest European wild osprey on record lived to be 26 years and 11 months of age.

en.text: Medieval writers claimed the osprey had one webbed foot and one taloned foot.

source.title: Wikipedia, Osprey
source.quote: Another odd legend regarding this fish-eating bird of prey, derived from the writings of Gerald of Wales and later Albertus Magnus and recorded in Holinshed 's Chronicles , was that it had one webbed foot and one taloned foot.

en.text: On one Australian island, some osprey nests have been reused for 70 years.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Osprey
quote: Rocky outcrops just offshore are used in Rottnest Island off the coast of Western Australia , where 14 or so similar nesting sites are known, of which five to seven are used in any one year.
Many are renovated each season, and some have been used for 70 years.

en.text: Pliny the Elder claimed that osprey parents made their young fly up toward the sun as a test, and got rid of any that failed.

source.title: Wikipedia, Osprey
source.quote: Roman writer Pliny the Elder reported that parent ospreys made their young fly up to the sun as a test and dispatched any that failed.

en.text: Victorian hats were trimmed with 'osprey' plumes, a big item in the 19th-century feather trade. In fact, the feathers came from egrets.

source.title: Wikipedia, Osprey
quote: So-called "osprey" plumes were an important item in the plume trade of the late 19th century and used in hats
Despite their name, these plumes were actually obtained from egrets .

en.text: Like an owl, an osprey can swing its outer toe backward to grip a fish two toes in front, two behind. Spiky soles stop the fish slipping.

source.title: Wikipedia, Osprey
quote: The osprey and owls are the only raptors whose outer toes are reversible, allowing them to grasp their prey with two toes in front and two behind.
sharp spicules on the underside of the toes

en.text: About a quarter of all ospreys in the lower 48 states nest around Chesapeake Bay, many on channel markers and utility poles.

source.title: Chesapeake Bay Program, Field Guide: Osprey
quote: Approximately one-quarter of all ospreys in the contiguous United States nest in the Chesapeake Bay region
Nests are often located near the water on tall structures like dead snags, utility poles, channel markers and nesting platforms.

en.text: Water bends light, so a fish is never quite where it looks. A diving osprey corrects for this, adjusting its angle on the way down.

source.title: Wikipedia, Osprey
source.quote: As an osprey dives, it adjusts the angle of its flight to account for the distortion of the fish's image caused by refraction .

en.text: New Jersey has an official osprey nest-platform design, created by local conservationists and copied far beyond the state.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Osprey
quote: The nesting platform design developed by Citizens United to Protect the Maurice River and its Tributaries, Inc. has become the official design of the State of New Jersey , U.S.
The nesting platform plans and materials list, available online, have been used by people from a number of different geographical regions.

en.text: Greater snow geese bark like dogs: the noisiest of all waterfowl.

source.title: Hinterland Who's Who (Canadian Wildlife Service), Greater Snow Goose

en.text: The 'blue goose' is just a snow goose in a darker coat.

source.title: Audubon Field Guide, Snow Goose
source.quote: now known to be only a color morph of the smaller race of Snow (Lesser Snow Goose)

en.text: Over half a million snow geese gather at Baie-du-Febvre, Quebec, each April.

source.title: Hinterland Who's Who (Canadian Wildlife Service), Greater Snow Goose
source.quote: Striking concentrations of more than 500 000 Greater Snow Geese can be seen in early April at Baie-du-Febvre

en.text: In the Arctic summer, snow geese eat around the clock in 24-hour daylight.

source.title: Hinterland Who's Who (Canadian Wildlife Service), Greater Snow Goose
source.quote: 24 hours a day in the Arctic's round-the-clock summer daylight.

en.text: Snow goose chicks leave the nest hours after hatching and feed themselves.

source.title: Audubon Field Guide, Snow Goose
source.quote: A young Snow Goose will usually leave nest within a few hours after hatching; they find their own food

en.text: A snow goose seems to smile: a dark 'grinning patch' runs along each side of its bill.

source.title: Hinterland Who's Who, Greater Snow Goose
source.quote: These cutting edges form a blackish arc, called a “grinning patch” or “smile,” along each side of the bill on both the upper and lower mandibles.

en.text: Digging in iron-rich mud often stains a snow goose's white head rusty orange.

source.title: Hinterland Who's Who, Greater Snow Goose
source.quote: Because the goose constantly digs in the mud in search of food, its head often becomes stained rusty-orange from the traces of iron in the mud.

en.text: Snow geese mate for life, and only take a new partner if theirs dies.

source.title: Hinterland Who's Who, Greater Snow Goose
source.quote: They mate for life, taking another mate only if their partner dies.

en.text: Snow goose youngsters can stay with their parents for two or three years.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snow goose
source.quote: After 42 to 50 days, they can fly, but they remain with their family until they are 2 to 3 years old.

en.text: On Canada's Bylot Island, snow goose chicks just a day old set off on a {30 km|19 mi} walk with their families.

source.title: Hinterland Who's Who (Canadian Wildlife Service), Greater Snow Goose
quote: the distance between the birds' nesting and breeding sites is more than 30 km.
Within a day of hatching, many young geese set off on this trek with their families, reaching their destination within four days.

en.text: Snow geese like to nest near snowy owls. The owls chase off the foxes and jaegers that raid goose nests, and they seldom attack goslings.

source.title: Hinterland Who's Who, Greater Snow Goose
quote: For protection, snow geese will readily nest near Snowy Owls’ nests.
The owls’ intolerance of foxes and jaegers on their territory is beneficial to the geese, and owls seldom attack goslings.

en.text: Young snow geese usually pick a mate that looks like their parents, white or blue. Geese raised by a mixed pair pair up with either color.

source.title: Wikipedia, Snow goose
quote: When choosing a mate, young birds most often select a mate that resembles their parents' coloring.
If the birds were hatched into a mixed pair, they mate with either color phase.

en.text: At New Mexico's Bosque del Apache, birders brave the predawn cold to watch tens of thousands of snow geese rise from the marsh all at once.

source.title: NPR, Cranes And Geese Flock To New Mexico (2008)
quote: Bird enthusiasts come out before dawn each morning during the five-day Festival of the Cranes to watch as thousands of birds fly into the sunrise.
As if on cue, tens of thousands of geese rose simultaneously from the marsh, their white bodies shimmering against the desert landscape.

en.text: Snow geese can have chicks with Ross's geese, and those hybrids can have chicks of their own.

source.quote: Where snow geese and Ross's geese breed together, as at La Pérouse, they hybridize at times, and hybrids are fertile.
