en.text: Hawaii's own goose, the nene, descends from Canada geese that reached the islands.

source.title: Wikipedia, Nene (bird)
quote: It is thought that the nene evolved from the Canada goose ( Branta canadensis ), which most likely arrived on the Hawaiian islands about 500,000 years ago

en.text: With a good tailwind, a Canada goose can fly {2400 km|1500 mi} in a day.

source.title: National Geographic, Canada Goose
source.quote: They can cover 1,500 miles in just 24 hours with a favorable wind

en.text: Canada geese honk in duets: he calls 'a-honk!', she answers 'hink!'.

source.title: Missouri Department of Conservation, Canada Goose
source.quote: while the females make a faster, higher-pitched

en.text: Every summer Canada geese lose all their flight feathers and are grounded for a month.

source.title: Missouri Department of Conservation, Canada Goose
source.quote: Adults lose their flight feathers during incubation and cannot fly for nearly a month.

en.text: Goose families stick together: the young fly south and back with their parents.

source.title: Missouri Department of Conservation, Canada Goose
source.quote: The goslings stay with their parents all the time and do not leave them until after the spring migration.

en.text: The biggest wild goose ever recorded was a giant Canada goose of {10.9 kg|24 lb}.

source.title: Wikipedia, Canada goose
quote: weighed 10.9 kg (24 lb) and had a wingspan of 2.24 m (7 ft 4 in)
This specimen is the largest wild goose ever recorded of any species.

en.text: Canada geese have been reported flying as high as {9 km|29000 ft}.

source.title: Wikipedia, Canada goose
source.quote: The maximum flight ceiling of Canada geese is unknown, but they have been reported at 9 km (29,000 feet).

en.text: A Canada goose can live to be at least 33 years old.

source.title: Missouri Department of Conservation, Canada Goose
source.quote: A Canada goose can live to be at least 33 years old.

en.text: Canada goose parents escort goslings with one adult in front and one behind.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Canada goose
source.quote: Parents are often seen leading their goslings in a line, usually with one adult at the front and the other at the back.

en.text: Goslings leave the nest the day after hatching, wherever it is. In Edmonton a brood jumped nine floors from a balcony to their parents.

source.title: CBC News, Oliver balcony goslings hatch, jump off 10th floor balcony the next day (2015)
quote: the day-old goslings took Lavin by surprise.

The goslings' quick departure was especially surprising given that Lavin lives on the 10th floor — and they jumped all the way to the roof of the parkade where their parents were waiting, 9 floors below.

en.text: Canada geese migrate in a V about {1 km|3000 ft} up. Flying in front takes the most energy, so the birds take turns in the lead.

source.title: Wikipedia, Canada goose
quote: Canada geese fly in a distinctive V-shaped flight formation, with an altitude of 1 km (3,000 feet) for migration flight.
The front position is rotated since flying in front consumes the most energy.

en.text: Britain's Canada geese go back to a royal whim: in the late 17th century they were added to the king's waterfowl in St James's Park, London.

source.title: Wikipedia, Canada goose
source.quote: The geese were introduced into Great Britain in the late 17th century as an addition to King James II 's waterfowl collection in St James's Park .

en.text: In 2004 the smallest 'Canada geese' became a species of their own, the cackling goose. Some weigh just {1.4 kg|3.1 lb}.

source.title: Wikipedia, Cackling goose
quote: in July 2004 the American Ornithologists' Union 's (AOU) Committee on Classification and Nomenclature split the two into two species
The smallest 1.4 kg (3.1 lb) cackling geese

en.text: Canada goose parents may pool their goslings into a 'crèche': a big group of youngsters watched over by just a few adults.

source.title: Wikipedia, Canada goose
source.quote: Although parents are hostile to unfamiliar geese, they may form groups of a number of goslings and a few adults, called crèches .

en.text: In 2009 a flock of Canada geese knocked out both engines of US Airways Flight 1549. The crew landed it on the Hudson River, and no one died.

en.text: Loggerheads are named for their big heads, with jaws strong enough to crush conchs.

source.title: NOAA Fisheries, Loggerhead Turtle

en.text: Adult male loggerheads weigh about {113 kg|250 lb}, but some over {450 kg|1000 lb} have been found.

en.text: A loggerhead's apparent tears are a way of getting rid of salt.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Loggerhead sea turtle
source.quote: Lachrymal glands located behind each eye allow the loggerhead to maintain osmotic balance by eliminating the excess salt obtained from ingesting ocean water.

en.text: A loggerhead's shell is a whole world: more than a hundred kinds of living things, from barnacles to crabs and algae, live on it.

source.title: National Geographic, Loggerhead sea turtle

en.text: Bright lights can lead loggerhead hatchlings astray on their dash from nest to sea, so some coastal towns limit lights near nesting beaches.

source.title: National Geographic, Loggerhead sea turtle

Sargassum habitat harbors food sources for juvenile turtles.

en.text: Loggerheads are the sea turtle that nests most in the US: over 10,000 females nest in Florida alone each year.

source.title: NOAA Fisheries, Loggerhead Turtle
quote: Loggerheads are the most abundant species of sea turtle that nests in the United States.

en.text: The loggerhead is South Carolina's state reptile and Florida's state saltwater reptile; it also appears on a Colombian coin.

en.text: Peregrines migrate leap-frog style: the most northern birds winter furthest south.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, Peregrine Falcon

source.quote: According to a National Geographic TV program, in 2005 Ken Franklin recorded a falcon stooping at a top speed of 389 km/h (242 mph) .

en.text: Falconers call the male peregrine a 'tiercel'; only the female is 'the falcon'.

source.title: Wikipedia, Peregrine falcon

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Peregrine falcon
source.quote: A 2021 study of photos from around the world showed that the malar stripe is larger in areas that receive more sunlight, and concluded that the stripe serves to improve the falcon's vision by reducing glare. [ 20 ]

en.text: DDT made peregrines lay eggs that broke. By 1975 only 324 pairs were left in North America; after DDT was banned they bounced back.

source.title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, The peregrine falcon is back (2000)
quote: The pesticide DDT caused peregrines to lay thin-shelled eggs that broke during incubation.
By 1975, the population reached an all-time low of 324 nesting pairs in North America.
The banning of DDT made the recovery of the peregrine falcon possible.

en.text: Courting male peregrines show off with power dives, roller-coaster flights, loop-the-loops and figure eights.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, Peregrine Falcon

en.text: Female peregrines are much bigger: up to {1500 g|3.3 lb}, against as little as {450 g|1 lb} for a male.

source.title: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, Peregrine Falcon
source.quote: Male Peregrine Falcons weigh as little as 450 grams; females weigh as much as 1,500 grams.

en.text: Tiny bony bumps in a peregrine's nostrils may steer the blast of air aside in a dive, so the falcon can still breathe at full speed.

source.title: Wikipedia, Peregrine falcon
source.quote: small bony tubercles on a falcon's nostrils are theorized to guide the powerful airflow away from the nostrils, enabling the bird to breathe more easily while diving by reducing the change in air pressure.

en.text: A male snowy owl can be whiter than a polar bear or an Arctic fox.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: They are purer white than predatory mammals such as polar bears ( Ursus maritimus ) and Arctic fox ( Vulpes lagopus ).

en.text: Snowy owls sometimes follow polar bears to pick at the leftovers of their kills.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: A wide variety of accrued reports show that the snowy owl that scavenging on carrion is not uncommon (despite having once been thought to be very rare in all owls), including instances of reindeer ( Rangifer tarandus ) body parts brought to nests and owls following polar bears to secondarily feed on their kills.

en.text: Young snowy owls toddle around the tundra for nearly a month before they can fly.

source.title: Owl Research Institute, Snowy Owl
source.quote: Fledglings leave the nest and spend nearly a month hiding & toddling around the tundra before they are able to fly

en.text: Unlike most owls, snowy owls are not night hunters: they hunt at any hour.

source.title: Owl Research Institute, Snowy Owl
source.quote: Unlike many other owls, Snowy owls are not nocturnal, and can be seen hunting any time of the day or night.

en.text: A snowy owl's toes are wrapped in thick white feathers, with black claws poking out.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: The toes of the snowy owl are extremely thickly feathered white, while the claws are black.

en.text: Male snowy owls get whiter with age; some aren't fully white until about 10.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: Evidence indicates that snowy owls may attain adult plumage at 3 to 4 years of age, but fragmentary information suggests that some males are not fully mature and/or as fully white in plumage that they can attain until the 9th or 10th year.

en.text: Airports suit wintering snowy owls: flat and grassy like the tundra, and full of prey.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: Perhaps the most consistently attractive habitat in North America to wintering snowy owls in modern times may be airports, which not only tend to have the flat, grassy characteristics of their preferred habitats but also by winter host a particular diversity of prey, both pests which rely on humans as well as wildlife attracted to the extensively grassy and marshy strips that dot the large airport vicinities.

en.text: In the Ice Age, snowy owls lived as far south as Spain, Italy and Sardinia.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: Fossil records shows that snowy owls once could be found in Austria, Azerbaijan, Czechoslovakia , England, France, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Poland, Sardinia and Spain as well as in the Americas in Cape Prince of Wales , Little Kiska Island , St.

en.text: No owl in North America has longer wings than the snowy owl: a female's can span {1.8 m|6 ft}.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
quote: This species is the heaviest and longest winged owl (as well as the second longest) in North America, the second heaviest and longest winged owl in Europe (and third longest) but is outsized in bulk by 3 or 4 other species in Asia.
Female wingspans have reportedly measured from 146 to 183 cm (4 ft 9 in to 6 ft 0 in) , with a mean of 159 cm (5 ft 3 in) .

en.text: A snowy owl's dense feather coat makes it one of the best-insulated animals of the Arctic.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: The snowy owl has perhaps the second lowest thermal conduction to the plumage on average of any bird after only the Adelie penguin ( Pygoscelis adeliae ) and rivals the best insulated mammals, such as Dall sheep ( Ovis dalli ) and Arctic fox , as the best insulated polar creature.

en.text: Males are near-white, females heavily spotted: naturalists once took them for two species.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
quote: Linnaeus originally described the different plumages of this owl as separate species, with the male specimens of snowy owls being considered Strix scandiaca and the likely females considered as Strix nyctea .
The adult female is usually considerably more spotted and often slightly barred with dark brown on the crown and the underparts.

en.text: A snowy owl's huge eyes are built to spot prey far away rather than up close.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
quote: Owls' eyes are large and round, which are nearly the same size in large species such as the snowy owl as those of humans.

Based on the study of dioptres in different owl species, the snowy owl was determined to have eyesight better suited to long-range perception than to close discrimination, while some related species such as great horned owls could probably more successfully perceive closer objects.

en.text: A snowy owl's hoot sounds like a barking dog: 'krooh krooh krooh krooh'.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: The main vocalization is a monotonous sequence that normally contains 2–6 (but occasionally more), rough notes similar to the rhythm of a barking dog: krooh krooh krooh krooh .

en.text: Snowy owls are nomads: they rarely nest in the same place, or with the same mate, twice.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: The snowy owl is a nomadic bird, rarely breeding at the same locations or with the same mates on an annual basis and often not breeding at all if prey is unavailable.

en.text: Guarding its nest, a snowy owl flies with stiff raised wings, like an enormous white moth.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: Nesting territory defense displays, not highly different from courtship displays, include undulating flight and stiffly raised wings with bouts of exaggerated, delayed wing beats, looking like enormous white moths exposing their white wings under the sun.

en.text: In winter, a female snowy owl may hold one spot for 80 days; males move on within days.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: It is known that during winter in Alberta that female snowy owls are territorial towards one another and may not leave an area for up to 80 days but males are nomadic, usually only staying 1–2 days in an area (seldom to 3–17 days).

en.text: The snowy owl is one of the few owls that builds a nest of its own.

source.title: Owl Research Institute, Snowy Owl
source.quote: One of the few species of owl that builds its own nest

en.text: Since 1981 Norman Smith of Mass Audubon has caught over 900 snowy owls at Boston's Logan Airport and moved them away from the planes.

source.title: WUSF/NPR, Meet the man who protects snowy owls that migrate to Boston's Logan Airport (2025)
quote: In 1981, Smith wrote a letter to the airport asking if he could take a different approach, a more humane approach.
And I've relocated over 900 snowy owls, so far, from Logan Airport.

en.text: Some snowy owls don't fly south at all. They spend the winter out on the Arctic sea ice, hunting seabirds in patches of open water.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: Since at least the 1970s, research indicated that snowy owls regularly winter in several of the northern seas during wintertime, following the leads of sea ice as perching sites and presumably hunting mostly seabirds in polynyas .

en.text: Three snowy owls from one Arctic nest went separate ways: a year on, one was in Ontario, one at Hudson Bay, one on Russia's Sakhalin Island.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
quote: Three siblings that hatched in same nest in
were recovered in drastically different spots at least a year later: one in eastern Ontario , one in Hudson Bay and one in Sakhalin Island .

en.text: Snowy owl eggs are laid days apart, so a clutch of 11 can take 20 to 30 days. The oldest chick may be weeks older than the youngest.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
quote: The snowy owl lays a very large clutch of eggs , often from about 5 to 11, with the laying and hatching of eggs considerably staggered.
The laying of a clutch of 11 eggs can take 20–30 days, while a more typical nest of around 8 takes about up to 16 days.

en.text: The biggest prey on record for a snowy owl: an adult red fox of about {6 kg|13 lb}, taken by a wintering owl in Saskatchewan.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: A wintering snowy owl in Saskatchewan was observed to have preyed on an adult red fox ( Vulpes vulpes ) weighing around 6 kg (13 lb) which may be the largest known prey known for snowy owls.

en.text: Snowy owl fathers guard the nest by raising their feathers, fanning their wings and marching at intruders, then slashing with feet and bill.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: At times, humans are forcefully dive-bombed upon, while other potential threats are dealt with in a "forward-threat" where the male walks towards the intruders, engaging in impressive feather-raising and fanning out of half-spread wings until they run forward and slash with both their feet and bill.

en.text: On a bitterly cold winter day, a snowy owl may need to eat as many as seven rodents just to get through it.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: Presumably as many as seven rodents would need to be eaten daily to survive an extremely cold winter's day.

de.text: Anders als die meisten Eulen jagen Schneeeulen auch am helllichten Tag.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Schneeeule
source.quote: Schneeeulen jagen anders als die meisten übrigen Eulen auch tagsüber

de.text: Dicht befiederte Zehen wirken wie Schneeschuhe: Die Schneeeule sinkt nicht im Schnee ein.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Schneeeule
source.quote: Die Füße und Zehen sind dicht befiedert – diese dichte, schneeschuhartige Befiederung dient der Wärmeisolation und verhindert, dass die Eule im Schnee einsinkt.

de.text: Schneeeulen-Männchen werden mit den Jahren immer weißer, bis kaum ein Fleck übrig ist.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Schneeeule
source.quote: Das Federkleid ausgewachsener Männchen wird mit zunehmendem Alter fast völlig weiß.

de.text: Eine erwachsene Schneeeule frisst drei bis fünf Lemminge am Tag.

source.title: Tierpark Hellabrunn, Schneeeule
source.quote: Ausgewachsene Eulen fressen drei bis fünf Lemminge pro Tag.

de.text: Québec hat sich die Schneeeule als offiziellen Provinzvogel ausgesucht.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Schneeeule
source.quote: Die Schneeeule ist der offizielle Vogel der kanadischen Provinz Québec

de.text: Genetisch ist die Schneeeule ein Uhu, eng verwandt mit dem amerikanischen Virginia-Uhu.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Schneeeule
source.quote: Molekularbiologische Untersuchungen haben jedoch gezeigt, dass sie zu den Uhus ( Bubo ) gehört und nah mit dem Virginia-Uhu ( B. virginianus ) und dem Magellanuhu ( B. magellanicus ) verwandt ist.

de.text: Regen und Schnee sitzen Schneeeulen aus. Schutz suchen die Vögel nur vor praller Sonne.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Schneeeule
source.quote: Die Eulen suchen nur bei starker Sonnenbestrahlung einen Unterstand auf, bei Regen und Schneefall bleiben sie sitzen.

de.text: Je mehr Lemminge es gibt, desto mehr Eier legt eine Schneeeule: zwischen 3 und 11.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Schneeeule
source.quote: legt je nach Nahrungsangebot 3–11 Eier

de.text: Ob das Weiß tarnt, ist umstritten: Im schneefreien Sommer fallen Schneeeulen stark auf.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Schneeeule
source.quote: Ob die weiße Färbung zusätzliche Tarnfunktion hat, ist umstritten, da die Tiere besonders während der Brutsaison in der schneefreien Jahreszeit durch das weiße Gefieder besonders auffällig sind.

de.text: Wird das Futter knapp, jagen Schneeeulen sogar Eisfüchsen die Beute ab.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Schneeeule
source.quote: Bei sehr ungünstigen Nahrungsbedingungen jagen sie auch Eisfüchsen oder Kornweihen die Beute ab

de.text: Feine weiße Federn bedecken den schwarzen Schnabel der Schneeeule fast ganz.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Schneeeule
quote: Auffällig ist, dass der schwarze Schnabel überwiegend von so genannten Vibrissen bedeckt ist.
Dies sind dichte, feine weiße Federn.

de.text: Die Balzrufe eines Schneeeulen-Männchens sind in der Tundra kilometerweit zu hören.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Schneeeule
source.quote: Diese Rufe sind in der Tundra über mehrere Kilometer hinweg zu hören.

de.text: Zur Balz fliegt das Männchen mit einem toten Lemming im Schnabel, als Geschenk fürs Weibchen. Ohne so ein Geschenk gibt es keine Paarung.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Schneeeule
quote: Während des Balzfluges trägt das Männchen in der Regel einen toten Lemming im Schnabel, den es nach Ende des Balzfluges dem Weibchen vorlegt.
Ohne die Übergabe eines solchen Futtergeschenks kommt es nicht zur Verpaarung.

de.text: Mögliche Nistplätze zeigt das Männchen in der „Engelstellung“: Mit gehobenen Flügeln steht das Männchen darüber, das Beutegeschenk zu Füßen.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Schneeeule
source.quote: das Männchen zeigt dem Weibchen potentielle Brutplätze, indem es sich in einer „Engelstellung“ mit gehobenen, aber nicht geöffneten Flügeln darüber stellt und das Beutegeschenk ablegt.

de.text: Manche Schneeeulen überwintern auf Eis: junge weit draußen auf den zugefrorenen Großen Seen, alte auf dem Packeis der Arktis.

source.title: Audubon Magazine, The Return of the SNOWstorm (Scott Weidensaul, 2015)
quote: We were also astonished to learn that several of our tagged owls spent the bulk of the winter on the frozen surface of the Great Lakes, far off shore.
While wintering on the Arctic pack ice, those adult birds hunt flocks of sea ducks that squeeze into permanent, open-water cracks called polynyas.

de.text: Kälte macht Schneeeulen kaum etwas aus: Eine saß bei minus {62.5 °C|80.5 °F}, ohne Unbehagen zu zeigen. Das Gefieder isoliert wie ein Eisfuchspelz.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
quote: having been recorded in temperatures as low as minus 62.5 degrees Celsius with no obvious discomfort
rivals the best insulated mammals, such as Dall sheep ( Ovis dalli ) and Arctic fox , as the best insulated polar creature.

de.text: Schneeeulen verschmähen kein Aas. Manche folgen sogar Eisbären übers Eis und fressen an deren Beute mit, wenn die Bären satt sind.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: including instances of reindeer ( Rangifer tarandus ) body parts brought to nests and owls following polar bears to secondarily feed on their kills.

de.text: Junge Schneeeulen verlassen das Nest lange vor dem ersten Flug. Fast einen Monat lang tapsen die Küken durch die Tundra und verstecken sich.

source.title: Owl Research Institute, Snowy Owl
source.quote: Fledglings leave the nest and spend nearly a month hiding & toddling around the tundra before they are able to fly

de.text: In der Eiszeit lebten Schneeeulen mitten in Europa: Fossilien fand man in Deutschland, Österreich und Frankreich, sogar in Spanien.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: Fossil records shows that snowy owls once could be found in Austria, Azerbaijan, Czechoslovakia , England, France, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Poland, Sardinia and Spain

de.text: Die größte bekannte Beute einer Schneeeule: ein ausgewachsener Rotfuchs von rund {6 kg|13 lb}, geschlagen im Winter in Kanada.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Snowy owl
source.quote: A wintering snowy owl in Saskatchewan was observed to have preyed on an adult red fox ( Vulpes vulpes ) weighing around 6 kg (13 lb) which may be the largest known prey known for snowy owls.

en.text: The whimbrel is named after the sound of its call.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Hudsonian whimbrel
source.quote: The English name is imitative of the bird's call.

en.text: Its Latin name, Numenius, means 'new moon', after its crescent-shaped bill.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Hudsonian whimbrel
source.quote: It is associated with the curlews because it appears to be derived from neos , "new" and mene , "moon", referring to the crescent-shaped bill.

en.text: On Virginia's Eastern Shore, whimbrels fatten up on fiddler crabs before flying north.

source.title: William & Mary News, Winnie the whimbrel flies 3,200 miles in 146 hours (2008)
source.quote: The birds stop over on the Eastern Shore to feed on abundant fiddler crabs before continuing their long journey to their northern breeding grounds.

en.text: Whimbrel mothers leave early; the fathers stay behind to look after the young.

source.title: Alaska Science Forum (UAF Geophysical Institute), Flight of the Kanuti whimbrel
source.quote: The whimbrels had already bred and reared young in Kanuti, with the father birds lingering to help the fledglings after the mothers had moved on.

en.text: Alaska's whimbrels can fly non-stop for more than seven days.

source.title: All Hands Ecology, Diverse patterns of migratory behavior seen in Alaska-breeding Whimbrels (2021)
source.quote: The tagged Whimbrels moved entirely within the Pacific Americas Flyway—some making nonstop flights that exceeded 7 days across nearly 5,400 miles

en.text: Whimbrels resting in Virginia in spring can put on half their weight again in three weeks.

source.title: NPR, A Bird Flies Into A Hurricane. Does It Fly Out? (2011, transcript)
quote: One factor clearly is, the birds that come and stop here in the spring, for example, might come in at 350 to 400 grams.
But over a period of three weeks, the add 50 percent of that.

en.text: Alaska's whimbrels often refuel in the farm fields of California's Central Valley.

source.title: All Hands Ecology, Diverse patterns of migratory behavior seen in Alaska-breeding Whimbrels (2021)
source.quote: they were less risk-adverse about stop-over sites, often choosing human-modified environments, like agricultural lands in the Central and Imperial valleys of California, that may provide abundant, high-energy food resources during migration.

en.text: After a long flight, a whimbrel's heart can shrink by a quarter.

source.title: Audubon magazine, An Ecologist and an Extreme Athlete Are Biking More Than 18,000 Miles on the Trail of a Migrating Whimbrel (2026)
source.quote: “Even the heart can shrink by 25 percent.”

en.text: Whimbrels get ahead of storm systems to ride their tailwinds.

source.title: Alaska Science Forum (UAF Geophysical Institute), Flight of the Kanuti whimbrel
source.quote: “They get ahead of these storm systems and get these great tailwinds.”

en.text: A whimbrel can fly over {8000 km|5000 mi} without stopping to eat, drink or sleep.

source.title: Audubon magazine, An Ecologist and an Extreme Athlete Are Biking More Than 18,000 Miles on the Trail of a Migrating Whimbrel (2026)
source.quote: Whimbrels, meanwhile, can fly more than 5,000 miles without stopping to eat, drink, or sleep, and reach speeds of up to 50 miles per hour.

en.text: In 2011 a whimbrel named Hope battled Tropical Storm Gert for 27 hours at {14 km/h|9 mph}. Out of the storm, tailwinds pushed it past {145 km/h|90 mph}.

source.title: William & Mary News, national news highlights bird's heroic flight (2011)
quote: Hope encountered high headwinds for 27 hours, averaging only 9 miles per hour.
Once through the storm, her flight speed increased to more than 90 miles per hour as the bird was pushed by significant tail winds and made it back to Cape Cod.

en.text: In August 2011 a whimbrel named Chinquapin flew straight through the fiercest part of Hurricane Irene, and turned up safe in the Bahamas.

source.title: William & Mary News, national news highlights bird's heroic flight (2011)
source.quote: Satellite tracking revealed that Chinquapin left upper Hudson Bay on Aug. 20 and entered Hurricane Irene’s northeast quadrant—the most severe part of the storm—on Aug. 24.

en.text: Blown off course by Tropical Storm Erika in 2015, a whimbrel named Upinraaq landed in Suriname, {1600 km|1000 mi} short of its Brazil winter home.

source.title: Center for Conservation Biology, whimbrel Upinraaq and Tropical Storm Erika (2015)
source.quote: She made landfall near Paramaribo, Suriname roughly 1,000 miles west of her winter range in Brazil.

en.text: In 2008 a whimbrel named Winnie surprised scientists: instead of following the Atlantic coast, it flew {5000 km|3200 mi} across the continent.

source.title: William & Mary News, Winnie the whimbrel flies 3,200 miles in 146 hours (2008)
quote: Winnie left the study area on May 23, flying northwest at an average flight speed of nearly 22 miles per hour, covering more than 5,000 kilometers (3,200 miles) in no more than 146 hours.
Winnie surprised scientists by making a transcontinental flight, northwest toward Alaska, rather than taking the route expected for a bird belonging to the eastern population of whimbrels.

en.text: On paper, a whimbrel should run out of fuel after three or four days in the air. Yet tracked whimbrels fly non-stop for over a week.

source.title: Audubon magazine, An Ecologist and an Extreme Athlete Are Biking More Than 18,000 Miles on the Trail of a Migrating Whimbrel (2026)
quote: On paper, whimbrels should run out of fuel after three or four days, based on how much fat they can store and how much energy flight requires, says Chris Guglielmo, co-director of the Advanced Facility for Avian Research at Western University.
But satellite tracking confirms that the birds can fly nonstop for over a week.

en.text: In 2026 two Canadians set off to cycle {29900 km|18600 mi} from Alaska's Arctic coast to Patagonia, following one GPS-tagged whimbrel.

source.title: Audubon magazine, An Ecologist and an Extreme Athlete Are Biking More Than 18,000 Miles on the Trail of a Migrating Whimbrel (2026)
quote: On August 1, University of Alberta ecologist Timm Döbert and his partner, extreme athlete Leanna Carriere, set off from Prudhoe Bay on Alaska’s Arctic coast, on a pair of bicycles.
They had around 18,600 miles to go.
They’re now 98 days and more than 5,000 miles into a planned 9-month journey, which will loosely follow the path of one GPS-tracked Hudsonian Whimbrel as it migrates south to Patagonia.

en.text: Hope the whimbrel became a children's book, 'Hope is Here', read in schools in the US Virgin Islands and Virginia, both stops on its route.

source.title: Center for Conservation Biology, Farewell to Hope (2019)
quote: The story of Hope was immortalized in the book “ Hope is Here ” written by well-known children’s author Cristina Kessler of St. John.

The book tells a conservation story to children and has been used as a teaching tool on the U.S. Virgin Islands where Hope spent the winter months and in schools on the Delmarva Peninsula where Hope stopped during spring migration.

de.text: Der Hudsonbrachvogel Hope flog 100 Stunden nonstop von der Hudson Bay bis in die Karibik.

source.title: Center for Conservation Biology (William & Mary), Azalea vs. Hope (the Whimbrel), 2009
source.quote: She (Hope is an adult female) flew non-stop for 100 hours (August 10-15) from the upper shore of Hudson Bay to St. Croix, a flight of 5,720 km (3,550 mi).

de.text: Über den Hudsonbrachvogel Hope gibt es ein Kinderbuch: „Hope is Here“.

source.title: Center for Conservation Biology (William & Mary), Hope, 2019
source.quote: The story of Hope was immortalized in the book “ Hope is Here ” written by well-known children's author Cristina Kessler of St. John.

de.text: Auf dem Weg nach Norden fraß sich Hope in Virginia drei Wochen lang an Winkerkrabben satt.

source.title: Audubon, Hope (the Whimbrel) Returns (2012)
source.quote: For the next three weeks, she'll stay in Virginia eating fiddler crabs.

de.text: Erst seit 2019 gilt der Hudsonbrachvogel als eigene Art, getrennt vom Regenbrachvogel.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Hudsonian whimbrel
source.quote: This species and the Eurasian whimbrel were split in 2019 based on genetic and morphological differences and separate breeding ranges.

de.text: Manche Hudsonbrachvögel aus Alaska fliegen über sieben Tage am Stück, ohne Landung.

source.title: All Hands Ecology, Diverse patterns of migratory behavior seen in Alaska-breeding Whimbrels (2021)
source.quote: some making nonstop flights that exceeded 7 days across nearly 5,400 miles

de.text: Numenius, der Gattungsname, heißt „Neumond“: wegen des sichelförmig gebogenen Schnabels.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Hudsonian whimbrel
source.quote: It is associated with the curlews because it appears to be derived from neos , "new" and mene , "moon", referring to the crescent-shaped bill.

de.text: Bei drei Wochen Rast in Virginia legen Hudsonbrachvögel die Hälfte an Gewicht zu.

source.title: NPR Weekend Edition, interview with Bryan Watts on whimbrel migration
quote: She comes here to Virginia and stages to build fat reserves for migration
the birds that come and stop here in the spring, for example, might come in at 350 to 400 grams.
But over a period of three weeks, the add 50 percent of that.

de.text: Hudsonbrachvögel starten kurz vor einer Sturmfront und lassen sich vom Rückenwind tragen.

source.title: University of Alaska Fairbanks, Alaska Science Forum: The Flight of the Kanuti whimbrel (2009)
source.quote: They get ahead of these storm systems and get these great tailwinds.

de.text: Chinquapin wurde 2011 kurz zum Medienstar: Der Hudsonbrachvogel flog durch den schlimmsten Teil von Hurrikan Irene und kam heil heraus.

source.title: William & Mary News, There's always Hope (2013)
source.quote: One bird, Chinquapin, was a media star briefly in 2011 after successfully flying through the worst of Hurricane Irene.

de.text: Upinraaq war schon drei Tage nonstop unterwegs, als der Tropensturm Erika kam. Der Hudsonbrachvogel flog mitten hindurch bis Suriname.

source.title: Center for Conservation Biology (William & Mary), Whimbrel tracked into Tropical Storm Erika, 2015
source.quote: Amazingly, Upinraaq had been flying non-stop for more than 3 days and 2,700 miles (4,300 kilometers) when she successfully flew directly through the heart of the storm and continued on to the coast of Suriname.

de.text: Hope kehrte jeden Winter in dieselben Mangroven auf St. Croix zurück. Diese Treue des berühmten Vogels half, das Gebiet zu schützen.

source.title: Center for Conservation Biology (William & Mary), Hope, 2019
quote: Her high fidelity to Great Pond was an important factor in preserving habitat around the site, demonstrating the value of a celebrity but also illustrating the great importance of local actions to larger conservation movements.
Photo of mangrove habitat within Hope's winter territory on St. Croix.

en.text: You can hear the air whistle through a flying tundra swan's wings from {30 m|100 ft} below.

source.title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bird of the Month: Tundra Swan (2024)
source.quote: Air whistling through tundra swans’ wings as they fly can be heard from about 100 feet above.

en.text: Tundra swans living on iron-rich bog lakes can get golden or rusty-stained heads.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
source.quote: In birds living in waters that contains large amounts of iron ions (e.g. bog lakes), the head and neck plumage acquires a golden or rusty hue.

en.text: The old name 'whistling swan' misleads: in flight it gives a high bark, 'wow-wow-wow'.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
quote: Contrary to its common name, the ground calls of the whistling swan are not a whistle and neither notably different from that of Bewick's swan.
the whistling swan gives a markedly high-pitched trisyllabic bark like wow-wow-wow in flight.

en.text: Tundra swans spend almost a year together before mating, and then they pair for life.

source.title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bird of the Month: Tundra Swan (2024)
source.quote: Tundra swans spend almost a year together before mating -- and once they mate, it’s for life.

en.text: A tundra swan that loses its mate may stay single for years, even for life.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
source.quote: Should one partner die long before the other, the surviving bird often will not mate again for some years, or even for its entire life.

en.text: In winter, tundra swans glean leftover grain and even potatoes from harvested fields.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
source.quote: At other times of year, leftover grains and other crops such as potatoes , picked up in open fields after harvest, make up much of their diet.

en.text: The tundra swan is the most common swan in North America.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
source.quote: The whistling swan is the most common swan species of North America, estimated to number almost 170,000 individuals around 1990.

en.text: Tundra swans guard their nests fiercely and can fight off animals as big as wolves.

source.title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bird of the Month: Tundra Swan (2024)
source.quote: Tundra swans fiercely protect their nests and can fight off large animals like wolves.

en.text: Tundra swans can fly as high as {2700 m|9000 ft} and as fast as {80 km/h|50 mph}.

source.title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bird of the Month: Tundra Swan (2024)
source.quote: They can fly as high up as 9,000 feet and as fast as 50 miles per hour.

en.text: The oldest tundra swan on record lived to more than 24.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
source.quote: The oldest recorded tundra swan was over 24 years old.

en.text: Its scientific name, columbianus, is for the Columbia River, where it was first described.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
source.quote: Cygnus is the Latin for "swan", and columbianus comes from the Columbia River , the type locality .

en.text: Tundra swan families fly south together. On the wintering grounds, older brothers and sisters from earlier years sometimes join them.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
quote: The fledglings stay with their parents for the first winter migration.
The family is sometimes even joined by their offspring from previous breeding seasons while on the wintering grounds;

en.text: When a bear or another big mammal comes near, tundra swan parents lead their cygnets into deep water and stand still until it passes.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
source.quote: Small or avian predators usually elicit either an aggressive response or the behavior of sitting tight on nests while larger mammals, perhaps more dangerous to adults, usually elicit the response of leading the cygnets into deep waters and standing still until they pass.

en.text: Arctic summers are short, so tundra swan cygnets grow fast: they fly 60 to 75 days after hatching, twice as fast as young mute swans.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
source.quote: Since they nest in cold regions, tundra swan cygnets grow faster than those of swans breeding in warmer climates; those of the whistling swan take about 60–75 days to fledge—twice as fast as those of the mute swan for example—while those of Bewick's swan, about which little breeding data is known, may fledge a record 40–45 days after hatching already.

en.text: Western Alaska's tundra swans winter by the Pacific. Arctic coast swans cross the continent to winter from Maryland to North Carolina.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
quote: Birds breeding in western Alaska winter along the Pacific coast from southern Alaska to California ;

The birds breeding along the Arctic Ocean coast migrate via Canada and the Great Lakes region to winter at the Atlantic coast of the United States, mainly from Maryland to North Carolina , but some move as far south as Florida .

en.text: In winter, tundra swans sleep almost only on the water, and they need a running start across the surface to take off.

source.title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bird of the Month: Tundra Swan (2024)
quote: Because the tundra swans are such strong swimmers, they can take off from the water with a running start.
In winter they sleep almost exclusively on water.

en.text: Lewis and Clark met this swan on their expedition west, on the Columbia River. Meriwether Lewis named it the 'whistling swan' for its call.

source.title: Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition, March 9, 1806
quote: from the peculiar whistleing of the note of this bird I have called it the whistleing swan it's habits colour and contour appear to be precisely those of the large Swan.
we first saw them below the great narrows of the Columbia near the Chilluckkittequaw nation.
The tundra, or whistling, swan.

en.text: Young tundra swans fly south as big as their parents but brownish-gray. By the time they fly back to the tundra in spring, they are white.

source.title: Chesapeake Bay Program, Field Guide: Tundra Swan
quote: Cygnets are as large as adults but are brownish-gray.
They molt to white by late winter or early spring, when the swans return to the tundra to breed.

en.text: Tundra swan pairs build their nest together: a mound of plants, lichens and moss. They keep adding to it and often reuse it for years.

source.title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Tundra Swan species profile
quote: Both the male and female build the nest.
The nest consists of mounded vegetation made of a variety of plants, lichens and moss.
The pair will continue to work on the nest through incubation, and with such effort put into the nest, they frequently use the nest for multiple seasons.

en.text: Tundra swans migrate in V-shaped or ribbon-like flocks that you often hear before you see: a high, whooping 'woo-hoo, woo-hoo'.

source.title: Chesapeake Bay Program, Field Guide: Tundra Swan
quote: Tundra swans migrate in large V-shaped or ribbon-like flocks.
Flocks are often heard before they can be seen.
The tundra swan makes a high, whooping woo-hoo, woo-hoo, woo-hoo.

en.text: To reach underwater grasses, a tundra swan plunges its head and long neck below the surface, often tipping its tail up in the air.

source.title: Chesapeake Bay Program, Field Guide: Tundra Swan
source.quote: It feeds by submerging its head and neck underwater to reach its food, sometimes “tipping up” its tail in the process.

en.text: On Chesapeake Bay, a tundra swan is easy to tell from the year-round mute swan: black bill, straight neck, and gone again by spring.

source.title: Chesapeake Bay Program, Field Guide: Tundra Swan
quote: You can distinguish a tundra swan by its black bill and straight neck.
Also, tundra swans are only found in the Bay region from late autumn through early spring, while mute swans live here year-round.

where Lewis and Clark first saw these birds

source.title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bird of the Month: Tundra Swan (2024)
source.quote: Tundra swans fiercely protect their nests and can fight off large animals like wolves.

de.text: Zwergschwäne fliegen bis zu {2700 m|9000 ft} hoch und bis zu {80 km/h|50 mph} schnell.

source.title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bird of the Month: Tundra Swan (2024)
source.quote: They can fly as high up as 9,000 feet and as fast as 50 miles per hour.

de.text: Der Zwergschwan heißt zu Recht so: Kein Schwan der Nordhalbkugel ist kleiner.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
source.quote: It is the smallest of the Holarctic swans, at 115–150 cm (45–59 in) in length

de.text: Im Sommer leben Zwergschwan-Paare allein in der Tundra, im Winter in Scharen zu Hunderten.

source.title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bird of the Month: Tundra Swan (2024)
quote: During breeding season, the pairs spend their time alone in the Arctic Tundra.
Seeing hundreds of tundra swans gathered is a winter delight.

de.text: Zwergschwäne bleiben ein Leben lang zusammen. Stirbt ein Partner früh, bleibt der andere oft jahrelang allein, manchmal für immer.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
quote: they pair monogamously until one partner dies.
Should one partner die long before the other, the surviving bird often will not mate again for some years, or even for its entire life.

de.text: Naht ein Braunbär, führen Zwergschwäne die Küken ins tiefe Wasser und verharren dort reglos, bis die Gefahr vorüber ist.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
quote: Another surprisingly serious nest predator for tundra swans are brown bears
larger mammals, perhaps more dangerous to adults, usually elicit the response of leading the cygnets into deep waters and standing still until they pass.

de.text: Zwergschwan-Familien halten lange zusammen: Im Winterquartier stoßen manchmal sogar ältere Geschwister aus früheren Jahren wieder dazu.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
source.quote: The family is sometimes even joined by their offspring from previous breeding seasons while on the wintering grounds

de.text: Den amerikanischen Zwergschwan verrät ein kleiner gelber Fleck vor dem Auge. Dem Trompeterschwan fehlt er, der Bewick-Schwan hat mehr Gelb.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Zwergschwan
quote: Er unterscheidet sich vom Trompeterschwan ( Cygnus buccinator ) durch die geringere Körpergröße und einen kleinen gelben Fleck an der Schnabelbasis vor dem Auge.

Die im Winter regelmäßig in Mitteleuropa erscheinende Unterart Cygnus columbianus bewickii ist etwas größer und schwerer als die Nominatform und weist eine, individuell unterschiedliche, aber immer deutliche, Gelbfärbung an der Schnabelbasis auf, die meist etwa ein Drittel des Schnabels bedeckt.

de.text: Im Winter schlafen Zwergschwäne fast nur auf dem Wasser. Zum Abheben nehmen die kräftigen Schwimmer Anlauf und rennen übers Wasser.

source.title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bird of the Month: Tundra Swan (2024)
quote: Because the tundra swans are such strong swimmers, they can take off from the water with a running start.
In winter they sleep almost exclusively on water.

de.text: Im Winter treffen sich Hunderte Zwergschwäne in North Carolina, etwa am Lake Mattamuskeet, dem größten natürlichen See des Bundesstaats.

source.title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Bird of the Month: Tundra Swan (2024)
quote: Seeing hundreds of tundra swans gathered is a winter delight.
Lake Mattamuskeet National Wildlife Refuge, North Carolina : Featuring the largest natural freshwater lake in North Carolina

de.text: Die europäische Form, der Bewick-Schwan, zieht aus Sibirien über Ostsee und Elbmündung bis nach Dänemark, Holland und England.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Tundra swan
source.quote: The populations west of the Taymyr Peninsula migrate via the White Sea , Baltic Sea and the estuary of the Elbe to winter in Denmark, the Netherlands and the British Isles .

en.text: The bowhead has the largest mouth of any animal: almost a third of its body.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Bowhead whale
source.quote: Bowheads have the largest mouth of any animal, representing almost one-third of the length of the body.

en.text: A bowhead's blubber is {43-48 cm|17-19 in} thick, thicker than any other whale's.

source.title: NOAA Fisheries, Bowhead Whale
source.quote: The bowhead whale also has a 17- to 19-inch thick blubber layer—thicker than that of any other whale.

en.text: Bowheads have the longest baleen plates of any whale.

source.title: NOAA Fisheries, Bowhead Whale
source.quote: Bowhead whales have the longest baleen plates of all whales and feed almost exclusively on marine invertebrates, including small to moderately sized crustaceans, such as shrimp-like euphausiids (i.e., krill) and copepods.

en.text: A newborn bowhead calf can swim on its own within 30 minutes.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Bowhead whale
source.quote: Within 30 minutes of birth, bowhead calves are able to swim on their own.

en.text: Bowhead mothers may be able to have calves for 100 years.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Bowhead whale
source.quote: Female bowheads may be capable of producing calves for 100 years.

en.text: Bowheads may live over 200 years, perhaps thanks to genes that repair damaged DNA.

source.title: NOAA Fisheries, Bowhead Whale
quote: However, new techniques allow for more precise estimation of bowhead whale age, and studies suggest they may live to be over 200 years old.
Genes that allow for repair of damaged DNA may be responsible for their longevity.

en.text: Isabella Bay, Nunavut, was the world's first sanctuary designed for bowhead whales.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Bowhead whale
source.quote: Isabella Bay in Niginganiq National Wildlife Area is the first wildlife sanctuary in the world to be designed specially for bowhead whales.

en.text: A bowhead eats about {100 t|220000 lb} of krill, copepods and other small prey a year.

source.title: NOAA Fisheries, Bowhead Whale
source.quote: Scientists estimate that a bowhead whale needs to eat about 100 metric tons (over 220,000 pounds) of prey per year including copepods, euphausiids/krill, other invertebrates, and fish.

en.text: Each summer, eastern Arctic bowheads scrub off dead skin on boulders, like a pumice stone.

source.title: Hakai Magazine, Bowhead Whales Like to Exfoliate, Too (2017)
quote: That’s where bowheads from the Eastern Canada-West Greenland population gather in late summer to rub themselves on large rocks just below the water’s surface.
Think of it as using a pumice stone to get a callus off your foot, using the physical environment to help exfoliate the skin.

en.text: Scientists tell bowheads apart by the scars on their skin, many from breaking ice.

source.title: NOAA Fisheries, Bowhead Whale
quote: Bowhead whales often accumulate scars on their bodies from breaking ice, killer whale encounters, entanglement in fishing gear, and propellers.
Scientists use these scars to identify individual whales.

en.text: A bowhead's huge skull can smash through {20 cm|8 in} of sea ice, and Alaska Native whalers have seen bowheads surface through {60 cm|2 ft}.

source.title: NOAA Fisheries, Bowhead Whale
quote: The bowhead’s large, thick skull allows them to break through 8-inch-thick sea ice.
Some Alaska Native whalers have even reported whales surfacing through 2 feet of ice.

en.text: Whalers in the 1800s called bowheads 'rock-nose whales'. In 2016 a drone showed why: the whales were rubbing on rocks to scrub off old skin.

source.title: Hakai Magazine, Bowhead Whales Like to Exfoliate, Too (2017)
quote: The findings provide a scientific answer to a mystery that dates back to at least the mid-1800s, when European whalers nicknamed the animals rock-nose whales, due to their close proximity to the rocks.

The research team returned in August 2016 for further investigation—this time with a drone—and gathered conclusive evidence of what they had suspected: the whales were rubbing against rocks in water less than 10 meters deep as a way of removing dead skin.

en.text: A hard-working bowhead can overheat. An organ in its mouth fills with blood, and cold seawater cools the blood when the whale opens wide.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Bowhead whale
quote: During physical exertion, the whale must cool itself to prevent hyperthermia (and ultimately brain damage).
This organ becomes engorged with blood, and as the whale opens its mouth cold seawater flows over the organ, thus cooling the blood.

en.text: A bowhead's arched skull can be over {5 m|16.5 ft} long, about a third of the whale. It gives the bowhead its name and its icebreaking head.

source.title: NOAA Fisheries, Bowhead Whale
source.quote: The bow-shaped skull can be over 16.5 feet long—about a third of a bowhead’s body length.

en.text: A newborn bowhead calf is already about {4 m|13 ft} long and {900 kg|2000 lb}, and can swim at birth. Mother and calf stay very close.

source.title: NOAA Fisheries, Bowhead Whale
quote: Calves are usually about 13 feet long, weigh about 2,000 pounds, and can swim at birth.
Mothers and calves form a very close attachment.

en.text: Killer whales hunt bowheads, but bowheads fight back: some have killed attacking orcas with blows of their tails.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Bowhead whale
quote: However, there are also cases where bowhead whales have killed attacking orcas by striking their heads with the tip of their tail fins.
Inuit have a traditional word for this behavior to give historical context that this is not a new phenomenon.

en.text: In summer, northern Foxe Basin in Nunavut is a bowhead nursery: most of the whales gathered there are mothers with calves and young whales.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Bowhead whale
source.quote: Cow – calf pairs and juveniles up to 13.5 m (44 ft) in length make up the majority of summering aggregation in the northern Foxe Basin, while matured males and noncalving females may use the northwestern part of Hudson Bay.

en.text: Bowheads are chatty whales. On migration they listen to the echoes of their own calls to find food and to find a way through the sea ice.

source.title: NOAA Fisheries, Bowhead Whale
quote: Bowhead whales are highly vocal and have a large variety of calls.
The echoes of some of their calls are used to help the whales find food and navigate through the ice as they migrate.

en.text: A bowhead is born with its white chin patch, which grows with the whale. Its other white patches, on the tail and by the eyes, come later.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Bowhead whale
quote: The skin is mostly black with white patches around the flukes, tail, eyes, and chin.

These patches develop throughout life, with the exception of the patch surrounding the chin, which is usually visible in newborn calves, and increases in size at the same rate as the whale's overall growth.

en.text: A bowhead can stay under for up to an hour, though most dives last 9 to 18 minutes. It is no deep diver: about {150 m|500 ft} at most.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Bowhead whale
quote: It is able to dive and remain submerged under water for up to an hour.
The time spent under water in a single dive is usually limited to 9–18 minutes.
The bowhead is not thought to be a deep diver, but can reach a depth down to 150 m (500 ft) .

de.text: Der Kopf eines Grönlandwals macht fast ein Drittel der gesamten Körperlänge aus.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Grönlandwal
source.quote: Der Kopf ist im Verhältnis zum Körper sehr groß, fast ein Drittel der Gesamtlänge wird vom Kopf eingenommen

de.text: Mit dem Kopf durchbrechen Grönlandwale bis zu {60 cm|24 in} dickes Eis.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Grönlandwal
source.quote: und ermöglicht ein Durchbrechen von bis zu 60 Zentimeter dicken Eisschichten.

de.text: Grönlandwale haben zwei Blaslöcher und blasen zwei Fontänen über {4 m|13 ft} hoch.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Grönlandwal
source.quote: Der Wal besitzt zwei Blaslöcher, aus denen er zwei Fontänen über vier Meter weit in die Luft blasen kann.

de.text: Gegen die Kälte schützt den Grönlandwal eine bis zu {28 cm|11 in} dicke Speckschicht.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Grönlandwal
quote: Der Grönlandwal hat eine bis zu 28 Zentimeter
dicke Fettschicht , die ihn vor der eisigen Kälte schützt.

de.text: Kein anderes Lebewesen hat ein so großes Maul wie der Grönlandwal.

source.title: SRF Wissen, Musikalischer Grönlandwal: Die Jazzer unter den Walen (2018)
source.quote: Sie können bis zu 200 Jahre alt werden und besitzen das grösste Maul aller Lebewesen.

de.text: Die Barten eines Grönlandwals werden bis zu {4 m|13 ft} lang, manche sogar {5.2 m|17 ft}.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Grönlandwal
source.quote: Diese Bartenplatten sind dunkelgrau bis bräunlich-schwarz und normalerweise bis zu 4 Meter lang, können aber eine Maximallänge von 5,2 Metern erreichen.

de.text: 1931 stellte der Völkerbund den Grönlandwal als weltweit erste Wildtierart unter Schutz.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Grönlandwal
source.quote: Im Jahr 1931 wurde der Grönlandwal als weltweit erste Wildtierart überhaupt vom Völkerbund unter Schutz gestellt.

de.text: Auf Wanderung schwimmen Grönlandwale in Gruppen von bis zu 14 Tieren in V-Formation.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Grönlandwal
source.quote: Während der Wanderungen im Frühling und Herbst bilden Grönlandwale Gruppen von bis zu 14 Tieren, die in einer v-förmigen Formation schwimmen.

de.text: Forscher nennen Grönlandwale „Nachtigallen der Meere“: Jedes Jahr gibt es neue Lieder.

source.title: wissenschaft.de (Bild der Wissenschaft), Nachtigallen der Meere (2009)
quote: Das Team um Outi Tervo fand heraus, dass die Meeressäuger während der Paarungszeit mehrstimmig singen und ihr Repertoire jedes Jahr ändern.
Die Forscher gaben den Walen wegen ihrer Gesangskünste den Spitznamen „ Nachtigallen der Meere”

de.text: Ein Grönlandwal kann bis zu einer Stunde lang unter Wasser bleiben.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Grönlandwal
source.quote: allerdings kann der Grönlandwal auch bis zu einer Stunde lang abtauchen.

de.text: Grönlandwale lassen sich Zeit: Geschlechtsreif wird die Art erst mit 18 bis 31 Jahren.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Grönlandwal
source.quote: Sowohl Weibchen als auch Männchen erreichen im Alter von 18 bis 31 Jahren die Geschlechtsreife.

de.text: Ein Grönlandwal wiegt rund tausendmal so viel wie ein Mensch.

source.title: Nordkurier (dpa), 200 Jahre alt und selten Krebs (2025)
source.quote: Sie wiegen rund tausendmal so viel wie wir Menschen und leben oft mehr als doppelt so lange

de.text: Im Spätsommer häuten sich Grönlandwale im Cumberland Sound in Kanada und scheuern sich an Felsen im flachen Wasser, wie beim Peeling.

source.title: Fortune et al. 2017, PLOS ONE: Evidence of molting and the function of rock-nosing behavior in bowhead whales
quote: We opportunistically observed whales in Cumberland Sound, Nunavut, Canada with skin irregularities consistent with molting during August 2014
The video images captured bowhead whales rubbing on large rocks in shallow, coastal areas-likely to facilitate molting.

de.text: Auf Borkum stehen bis heute Zäune aus Kieferknochen von Grönlandwalen. Auf den baumlosen Inseln war Walknochen einst das beste Baumaterial.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Grönlandwal
quote: In der Regel handelte es sich um Knochen aus der Kinnlade des meist bejagten Grönlandwals.
Bis heute erhalten sind davon zwei Zäune auf Borkum
vielmehr war dies auf den einstmals ganz unbewaldeten Inseln schlicht das am besten verfügbare Baumaterial.

de.text: Die Zellen von Grönlandwalen reparieren Schäden am Erbgut besonders gründlich. Das erklärt wohl, warum die Riesen so selten Krebs bekommen.

source.title: Nordkurier (dpa), 200 Jahre alt und selten Krebs (2025)
quote: Mehr als 200 Jahre Lebenserwartung und selten Krebs: Forscher haben entschlüsselt, wie Grönlandwale ihre DNA schützen.
Dies erklären die Forschenden damit, dass die Wale ihre DNA besonders erfolgreich reparieren.

de.text: Eine halbe Stunde nach der Geburt schwimmt ein Grönlandwalkalb schon allein. Gegen das Eiswasser hilft dicker Speck, gleich von Geburt an.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Bowhead whale
quote: To survive in the cold water immediately after birth, calves are born with a thick layer of blubber .
Within 30 minutes of birth, bowhead calves are able to swim on their own.

de.text: Grönlandwal-Weibchen werden erst spät Mutter, können dann aber womöglich hundert Jahre lang Kälber bekommen.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Bowhead whale
source.quote: Female bowheads may be capable of producing calves for 100 years.

de.text: Rund {100 t|220000 lb} Nahrung frisst ein Grönlandwal im Jahr, fast nur winzige Krebstierchen wie Ruderfußkrebse und Krill.

source.title: NOAA Fisheries, Bowhead Whale
source.quote: Scientists estimate that a bowhead whale needs to eat about 100 metric tons (over 220,000 pounds) of prey per year including copepods, euphausiids/krill, other invertebrates, and fish.

de.text: In der Isabella Bay in Nunavut, Kanada, liegt das erste Schutzgebiet der Welt, das eigens für Grönlandwale geschaffen wurde.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Bowhead whale
source.quote: Isabella Bay in Niginganiq National Wildlife Area is the first wildlife sanctuary in the world to be designed specially for bowhead whales.

de.text: Grönlandwale tragen Narben vom Eis, von Orcas und Schiffsschrauben. Daran erkennen Forscher einzelne Wale wieder, wie am Fingerabdruck.

source.title: NOAA Fisheries, Bowhead Whale
quote: Bowhead whales often accumulate scars on their bodies from breaking ice, killer whale encounters, entanglement in fishing gear, and propellers.
Scientists use these scars to identify individual whales.

namesSource.title: IOC World Bird List 15.2, multilingual version (German names: Peter Barthel)

en.text: In a dive, a golden eagle may match or even beat a peregrine falcon's speed.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: Although less agile and manoeuvrable, the golden eagle is apparently quite the equal and possibly even the superior of the peregrine falcon 's stooping and gliding speeds.

en.text: The eagle on Mexico's coat of arms, with a snake in its beak, is a golden eagle.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: Mexico's Coat of Arms depicts a golden eagle perched on a prickly pear cactus, with a rattlesnake in its beak.

en.text: Some 4,000 golden eagles pass Mount Lorette, Alberta, in fall: the world's biggest flight.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: At Mount Lorette in Alberta , approximately 4,000 golden eagles may pass during the fall, the largest recorded migration of golden eagles on earth.

en.text: The oldest known wild golden eagle was found 32 years after it was banded.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: The oldest known wild golden eagle was a bird banded in Sweden which was recovered 32 years later.

en.text: Golden eagles build several nests in their territory and take turns using them.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: Golden eagles typically build several eyries within their territory (preferring cliffs) and use them alternately for several years.

en.text: After the chicks hatch, the father brings in about 80% of their food.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: After hatching, 80% of food items and 90% of food biomass is captured and brought to the nest by the adult male.

en.text: The 'golden' in golden eagle is the gleaming patch of long feathers on its nape.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: The nape patch is often gleaming golden in color and the feathers here are exceptionally long.

en.text: A golden eagle's home range can be as big as {200 km²|77 sq mi}.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: Golden eagles maintain home ranges or territories that may be as large as 200 km 2 (77 sq mi) .

en.text: Idaho's golden eagles hunt from an hour before sunrise to an hour after sunset.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: Golden eagles usually hunt during daylight hours, but were recorded hunting from one hour before sunrise to one hour after sunset during the breeding season in southwestern Idaho .

en.text: Golden eagles are 'booted eagles': their legs are feathered, unlike most hawks' bare legs.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: The golden eagle is part of a broad group of raptors called "booted eagles" which are defined by the feature that all species have feathering over their tarsus , unlike many other accipitrids which have bare legs.

en.text: A female golden eagle has double the wingspan of a midsize hawk and five times its weight.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: However, a mid-sized Buteo is dwarfed by a golden eagle, as an adult female eagle has about double the wingspan and about five times the weight.

en.text: A golden eagle soars at about {50 km/h|30 mph}, but hunting, it can glide at {190 km/h|120 mph}.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
quote: A typical, unhurried soaring speed in golden eagles is around 45–52 kilometres per hour (28–32 mph) .
When hunting or displaying, the golden eagle can glide very fast, reaching speeds of up to 190 kilometres per hour (120 mph) .

en.text: Courting golden eagles play catch: one picks up a rock or stick, drops it, dives after it and catches it in midair, three times or more.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: This courtship includes undulating displays by both in the pair, with the male bird picking up a piece of rock or a small stick, and dropping it only to enter into a steep dive and catch it in mid-air, repeating the maneuver three or more times.

en.text: Diving at prey, a golden eagle tucks its legs against its tail and its wings tight to its body, and can reach {240-320 km/h|150-200 mph}.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
quote: When stooping (diving) in the direction of prey or during territorial displays, the eagle holds its legs up against its tail, and holds its wings tight and partially closed against its body.
When diving after prey, a golden eagle can reach 240 to 320 kilometres per hour (150 to 200 mph) .

en.text: American golden eagles are usually smaller than Eurasian ones. Yet the heaviest wild golden eagle on record was a Wyoming female: {7.7 kg|17 lb}.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: American golden eagles are typically somewhat smaller than the large Eurasian species, but a massive female that was banded and released in 2006 around Wyoming's Bridger-Teton National Forest became the heaviest wild golden eagle on record, at 7.7 kg (17 lb) .

en.text: Since the early 1970s, the National Eagle Repository has given feathers of dead golden and bald eagles to Native Americans for ceremonies.

source.title: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, National Eagle Repository
quote: Native Americans have long used eagle remains, parts and feathers for religious and cultural purposes, including in ceremonies and as part of traditional regalia.

Fish and Wildlife Service (Service) established the National Eagle Repository (Repository) in the early 1970s to provide enrolled members of federal recognized Native American Tribes with the remains, parts, and feathers of bald and golden eagles for spiritual and religious use.

en.text: The eastern US has lost its nesting golden eagles: the last known pair, in Maine, was still nesting in 1999. None are known there now.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: Until 1999, a pair of golden eagles were still known to nest in Maine but they are now believed to be absent as a breeding bird from the Eastern United States .

en.text: Young golden eagles go independent in their first fall, then wander widely for four to five years before claiming a territory of their own.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: These juvenile golden eagles usually attain full independence in the fall, after which they wander widely until establishing a territory for themselves in four to five years.

en.text: Faced with an intruder, a golden eagle may turn away, lower its head and freeze. On the nest, adults even freeze for people and helicopters.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: When approached by an intruder, the defending eagle turns away, partially spreads tail, lowers head, and remains still; adults on the nest may lower head and "freeze" when approached by a person or a helicopter.

de.text: Echte Adleraugen: Ein Steinadler erspäht Beute noch aus {1 km|0.6 mi} Entfernung.

source.title: NABU, Vogelporträt Steinadler
source.quote: Er hat wirklich Adleraugen, denn seine Beute kann er aus bis zu einem Kilometer Entfernung erkennen.

de.text: Nur etwa jeder siebte Überraschungsangriff eines Steinadlers führt zum Erfolg.

source.title: NABU, Vogelporträt Steinadler
source.quote: Wenn er seine Beute erspäht hat, unternimmt er einen Überraschungsangriff, von denen etwa jeder siebte erfolgreich ist.

de.text: Der Steinadler ist das Wappentier vieler Staaten, auch der Bundesrepublik Deutschland.

source.title: Bayerisches Landesamt für Umwelt, Artenhilfsprogramm Steinadler
source.quote: wurde er von vielen Staaten als Wappentier auserkoren - so auch von der Bundesrepublik Deutschland.

de.text: Im Sturzflug erreicht ein Steinadler {240-320 km/h|150-200 mph}.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Golden eagle
source.quote: When diving after prey, a golden eagle can reach 240 to 320 kilometres per hour (150 to 200 mph)

de.text: Über die Jahre wachsen Steinadlerhorste auf mehr als {2 m|6.6 ft} Höhe und Breite.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steinadler
source.quote: so dass über Jahre hinweg mächtige, nicht selten mehr als zwei Meter in Höhe und Breite messende Horste entstehen.

de.text: Im Gebirge liegt der Horst meist unter dem Jagdgebiet: Bergab trägt sich Beute leichter.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steinadler
source.quote: Im Gebirge liegen die Horstplätze meist unterhalb der Jagdgebiete, da der Transport der Beute nach unten einfacher ist als nach oben.

de.text: Als einziger Echter Adler hebt der Steinadler beim Segeln die Flügel leicht zum V an.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steinadler
source.quote: Im Gegensatz zu allen anderen Vertretern der Gattung hebt der Steinadler seine Flügel im Segelflug leicht an, so dass ein leicht V-förmiges Flugbild zustande kommt.

de.text: Im Süden lassen Steinadler Landschildkröten auf Felsen fallen, um den Panzer zu knacken.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steinadler
source.quote: dort lassen Steinadler ähnlich wie Bartgeier auch Landschildkröten auf Felsen fallen, um so deren harten Panzer zu zerbrechen.

de.text: Ein beringter Steinadler in Schweden wurde 32 Jahre alt.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steinadler
source.quote: Die durch Vogelberingung nachgewiesenen Maximalwerte waren 26 Jahre (Schweiz) und 32 Jahre (Schweden).

de.text: Junge Steinadler haben weiße Flügelflecken, ausgefärbt sind die Vögel erst mit 5 bis 7.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steinadler
quote: Steinadler im ersten Lebensjahr sind insgesamt dunkler braun und haben auffallende, weiße Federpartien
Steinadler sind erst ab dem 5. bis 7. Lebensjahr voll ausgefärbt.

de.text: Steinadler-Weibchen sind größer als die Männchen und erreichen bis zu {230 cm|7.5 ft} Spannweite.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steinadler
source.quote: Die Flügelspannweite variiert zwischen 190 und 210 cm beim Männchen und zwischen 200 und 230 cm beim Weibchen.

de.text: Steinadler-Paare bleiben meist ein Leben lang zusammen und haben oft mehrere Horste.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steinadler
quote: Brutpaare führen, soweit bekannt, eine monogame Dauerehe.
meist hat ein Paar mehrere sogenannte Wechselhorste.

quote: Auf Grund der unterschiedlichen Färbung war bis ca. 1900 auch die Bezeichnung Goldadler

en.text: Its Latin name, flavipes, means 'yellow foot'.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Lesser yellowlegs
source.quote: The specific epithet flavipes combines the Latin flavus meaning "yellow" with pes meaning "foot".

en.text: Lesser yellowlegs chicks leave the nest a few hours after hatching and feed themselves.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Lesser yellowlegs
quote: Both parents brood and care for the precocial young, which leave the nest a few hours after hatching.
They can feed themselves upon departure from the nest.

en.text: A nesting lesser yellowlegs won't budge until a predator is within {1 m|3 ft}, then fights.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Lesser yellowlegs
source.quote: Nesting lesser yellowlegs are very reluctant to leave their nests, only leaving when a predator is less than 1 metre away to fight and keep the predators away from their nest.

en.text: Lesser yellowlegs nest only in the north, from Alaska across Canada to Labrador.

source.title: Boothbay Register (Jeffrey and Allison Wells), Yellowlegs Making Heroic Journeys (2022)
source.quote: Lesser yellowlegs, like their close relatives, greater yellowlegs and solitary sandpiper, in the breeding season occur nowhere else but the region that extends from Alaska across Canada to Newfoundland and Labrador.

en.text: Lesser yellowlegs hunt at a high-stepping trot, neck stretched out, jabbing with the bill.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Lesser yellowlegs
source.quote: They are very active when foraging, moving quickly with a high-stepping gait, neck outstretched, to pick at prey with quick jabs of the bill.

en.text: In Alaska, lesser yellowlegs sing from the tops of spruce trees, like backyard robins.

source.title: BirdNote, Singing Sandpipers
source.quote: That’s right – a sandpiper perched at the top of a tree like our backyard robins – singing its caroling song.

en.text: A lesser yellowlegs may dig up to 75 nest scrapes before settling on one.

source.title: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan), Tringa flavipes
source.quote: They may dig and line up to 75 nest scrapes before deciding on a final one.

en.text: Alarmed, a lesser yellowlegs gives a sharp 'kip' call and bobs its head and tail.

source.title: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan), Tringa flavipes
source.quote: They use a sharp "kip" alarm call that is accompanied by bobbing of the tail and head.

en.text: A lesser yellowlegs is about the size of a robin, perched on long, bright yellow legs.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Lesser Yellowlegs
quote: Size About the size of a Robin
The Lesser Yellowlegs is slender, with bright yellow legs.

en.text: Its flight looks lazy, but a lesser yellowlegs can fly at up to {75 km/h|47 mph}.

source.title: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan), Tringa flavipes
source.quote: Lesser yellowlegs walk with a quick, graceful gait and their flight has been described as languid, although they can fly up to 75 km per hour.

en.text: Parents lead their chicks to food by flying ahead, landing and calling them over.

source.title: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan), Tringa flavipes
source.quote: Parents lead young to foraging areas by flying ahead, landing, and then calling to the young.

en.text: Lesser yellowlegs sleep on one leg, bill tucked in, and droop their wings to sunbathe.

source.title: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan), Tringa flavipes
source.quote: They sleep with one leg and their bill tucked into their feathers and may drop their wings to sun themselves.

en.text: Up to 65% of lesser yellowlegs come back to the same area to nest each year.

source.title: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan), Tringa flavipes
source.quote: Lesser yellowlegs have fairly high site fidelity, with up to 65% of individuals returning to the same area to breed each year.

en.text: Alaska's lesser yellowlegs fly south over land, refueling in the prairie potholes. Eastern Canada's fly for days over the Atlantic instead.

source.title: McDuffie et al. 2022, Ecology and Evolution
quote: Individuals tagged in Alaska and Central Canada followed similar southbound migratory routes, stopping to refuel in the Prairie Pothole Region of North America, whereas birds tagged in Eastern Canada completed multi-day transoceanic flights covering distances of
across the Atlantic between North and South America.

en.text: Lesser yellowlegs parents gang up on predators: they swoop down to attack, or put on distraction displays to lure them away from the chicks.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Lesser yellowlegs
quote: Lesser yellowlegs, when defending their nests and young from predators, will show aggression and fight with invaders, including joining together to fight predators.
They may swoop down to attack the predator or use distraction strategies to lure it away.

en.text: Lesser yellowlegs nest in the remote boreal forest of Canada and Alaska. Their favorite places are bogs full of sphagnum moss.

source.title: Boothbay Register (Jeffrey and Allison Wells), More Yellowlegs Mysteries Revealed
source.quote: Because these birds breed across the remote reaches of the Boreal Forest of Canada and Alaska where there are very, very few MOTUS towers but lots of the sphagnum-filled bogs that are their favorite nesting habitat.

en.text: Lesser yellowlegs mothers usually stay with their chicks for about 11 days. Fathers keep watch for about 26 days, until the young can fly.

source.title: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan), Tringa flavipes
quote: Both parents continue to protect the young until they fledge or a few days longer, although females may abandon males with the young.
Females generally stay with the young for about 11 days after hatching, males stay with them for about 26 days after hatching.

en.text: To claim a territory, a male lesser yellowlegs climbs to {75 m|250 ft}, then glides down, tail spread, legs dangling, singing 'pill-e-wee'.

source.title: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan), Tringa flavipes
quote: Breeding males and females also perform a song, described as "pill-e-wee" repeated, but only males perform a flight display to advertise breeding territories.
Flight displays involve a male flying to 10 to 75 m, then leveling off and gliding down while spreading the tail, dangling the legs, and elevating the head.

en.text: While nesting, a lesser yellowlegs pair commutes together every day to the same feeding spot, up to {13 km|8 mi} from the nest.

source.title: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan), Tringa flavipes
source.quote: During the breeding season, male and female mates travel daily to the same foraging area, up to 13 km from their nest.

en.text: In late summer the lesser yellowlegs leave in turns: females and birds whose nests failed go first, then the males, and the young ones last.

source.title: Animal Diversity Web (University of Michigan), Tringa flavipes
source.quote: Females and individuals who weren't successful breeding begin migrating first, followed by males and then juveniles.

en.text: Lesser and greater yellowlegs look identical but for size, 'as if put on earth only to confuse birdwatchers'. They act differently, though.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Lesser Yellowlegs
quote: At first glance, the two species of yellowlegs look identical except for size, as if they were put on earth only to confuse birdwatchers.
With better acquaintance, they turn out to have different personalities.

en.text: On the nesting grounds, lesser yellowlegs spend much time perched high in spruce trees, and protest loudly if anyone comes near the nest.

source.title: Mark A. Chappell (UC Riverside), Lesser yellowlegs photo gallery
quote: They nest in wet boreal forests and spend a lot of time perched high in spruce trees, as some of these birds are doing.
Nesting birds will protest vigorously if an intruder (such as a person) gets anywhere near their nests.

en.text: Count the notes: a lesser yellowlegs' alarm call usually has two, while its look-alike, the greater yellowlegs, gives three or more.

source.title: Mark A. Chappell (UC Riverside), Lesser yellowlegs photo gallery
source.quote: Also, the two species have different alarm calls: the lesser typically gives a two-note call while the greater gives three or more notes.
