en.text: The wood stork is the only stork that breeds in the United States.

source.title: National Park Service, Everglades: Wood Stork species profile
source.quote: It is the only stork breeding in the United States and was placed on the Federal Endangered Species list in 1984.

en.text: A wood stork's bill snaps shut in 25 milliseconds, the fastest known vertebrate reflex.

source.title: National Park Service, Everglades: Wood Stork species profile
source.quote: Its bill snaps shut with a 25-millisecond reflex action -- the fastest known for vertebrates -- whenever it touches prey.

en.text: Wood storks fish by touch, groping blind through muddy water with their bills.

source.title: National Park Service, Everglades: Wood Stork species profile
source.quote: A stork locates food -- mostly small, freshwater fish -- not by sight but by tactolocation, or groping with its bill in shallow water.

en.text: Old Southern nicknames for the wood stork include 'flinthead' and 'ironhead'.

source.title: Wikipedia, Wood stork
source.quote: Its regional names include "flinthead", "stonehead", "ironhead", "gourdhead", and "preacher".

en.text: Fish come first, but a wood stork will also eat snakes, frogs and baby alligators.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Wood Stork
source.quote: Also crayfish, crabs, aquatic insects, snakes, baby alligators, small turtles, frogs, rodents, some seeds and other plant material.

en.text: Wood storks used to be called 'wood ibises', though they aren't ibises at all.

source.title: Wikipedia, Wood stork
source.quote: Likely because of its decurved bill, the wood stork has formerly been called the "wood ibis", although it is not an ibis .

en.text: Adult wood storks are almost silent: they hiss and clatter their bills instead.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Wood Stork
source.quote: Young Wood Storks have noisy begging calls, but adults are almost silent except for hissing and bill clappering.

en.text: A wood stork will fly more than {80 km|50 mi} to reach a good fishing spot.

source.title: Wikipedia, Wood stork
source.quote: This bird can travel over 80 kilometres (50 mi) to reach foraging sites, lending it access to a wide variety of habitats.

en.text: Mycteria, the wood stork's genus name, comes from the Greek for snout or trunk.

source.title: Wikipedia, Wood stork
source.quote: The accepted generic name Mycteria derives from the Greek μυκτήρ : myktēr , meaning snout or trunk, and the species name americana references the distribution of this stork.

en.text: Wood storks nest in crowds: up to 25 nests can share a single tree.

source.title: Wikipedia, Wood stork
source.quote: It nests colonially , with up to 25 nests in one tree.

en.text: In flight, a wood stork's black and white wings can make it look like a pelican.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Wood Stork
source.quote: In flight, black and white wing pattern may look like an American White Pelican.

en.text: Wood storks aren't born bald: young birds have feathered heads and yellow bills.

source.title: Wikipedia, Wood stork
source.quote: When fledged, they resemble the adult, differing only in that they have a feathered head and a yellow bill.

en.text: In hot weather a wood stork cools off by aiming its watery droppings at its own legs, taking turns with each leg. The evaporation cools it.

source.title: Wikipedia, Wood stork
quote: When weather is hot, though, the adult takes a different position, quickly moving its tail downward and forward while twisting its body around to aim at a leg that is bent backward (this is called urohidrosis ).
Which leg is aimed at is alternated.

en.text: Wood storks only nest when falling water traps fish in shrinking pools. That makes them a living gauge of the health of the Everglades.

source.title: National Park Service, Everglades: Wood Stork species profile
quote: The Wood Stork serves as an indicator species for restoration of the Everglades ecosystem.

In the marsh habitat of the Wood Stork, the effectiveness of this feeding technique increases as fish are concentrated in pools by seasonal water-level declines that result from the prolonged winter dry periods.

en.text: A nesting pair of wood storks needs about {200 kg|440 lb} of fish per season. When food is short, they won't even try to nest.

source.title: National Park Service, Everglades: Wood Stork species profile
quote: Each breeding pair of these large birds requires about 440 pounds (200 kg) of fish per breeding season.

When the natural hydrologic cycle is upset by human-controlled water-management activities, Wood Storks fail to feed and nest successfully because a breeding pair of Wood Storks will not attempt to nest if sufficient food is not available.

en.text: The Everglades once held up to 15,000 wood stork pairs; by 1995 under 500 nested there. Many had moved north to Georgia and South Carolina.

source.title: National Park Service, Everglades: Wood Stork species profile
quote: The Everglades of the 1930s, largely undrained and without complex water-control structures, supported a nesting of population of 5,000 to 15,000 pairs of Wood Storks.
By 1995, fewer than 500 pairs of Wood Storks were nesting in the Everglades National Park and Big Cypress National Preserve area of south Florida.

The dwindling population of Wood Storks in south Florida does not mean that the species is going extinct, but that they have moved to more suitable habitat in other locations such as north Florida, Georgia, and South Carolina.

en.text: Listed as endangered in 1984, the wood stork came back after three decades of conservation work and was downlisted to threatened in 2014.

source.title: National Park Service, Everglades: Wood Stork species profile
source.quote: The species was downlisted from endangered to threatened in June 2014, reflecting a successful conservation and recovery effort spanning three decades.

en.text: On warm, clear days a wood stork flaps up to at least {610 m|2000 ft}, then glides {16-24 km|10-15 mi} on rising air without a single wingbeat.

source.title: Wikipedia, Wood stork
quote: When weather is warm and clear, this bird glides after it gains an altitude of at least 610 metres (2,000 ft) through continuously flapping its wings.
It can then glide for distances ranging from 16 to 24 kilometres (9.9 to 14.9 mi) .
It does not have to flap its wings during this time because the thermals are strong enough to support its weight.

en.text: Under the hot sun on an open treetop nest, wood stork parents spread their wings over the chicks like parasols.

source.title: Wikipedia, Wood stork
source.quote: In hot weather, breeding adults will also shade their chicks with their wings.

en.text: Wood storks don't stop at sticks: they line their nests with fresh green twigs and leaves, which help insulate the nest.

source.title: Wikipedia, Wood stork
quote: The greenery usually starts to be added before the eggs are laid, but after the main structure of twigs is completed.
This greenery functions to help insulate the nest.

en.text: Wood stork parents take turns on the eggs and never leave them alone. The bird off duty flies out to feed, drink and fetch nest material.

source.title: Wikipedia, Wood stork
quote: During the first week of incubation, the parents do not go far from the colony, with the exception of the short trips to forage, drink, and collect nesting material carried out by the nonincubating bird.
After the first week, the nonincubating bird spends less time in the colony, although the eggs are never left unattended.

en.text: Underground in its burrow, a puffin growls like a chainsaw being revved up.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
source.quote: At the breeding colony, it is quiet above ground, but in its burrow makes a growling sound somewhat resembling a chainsaw being revved up.

en.text: Fratercula, the puffin's Latin name, means 'little friar', for its monk-like plumage.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
source.quote: The generic name Fratercula comes from the Medieval Latin fratercula , little friar , a reference to their black and white plumage, which resembles monastic robes.

en.text: A puffin can carry a whole row of fish in its beak, pinned by its grooved tongue.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
quote: It can catch several small fish in one dive, holding the first ones in place in its beak with its muscular, grooved tongue while it catches others.
The two mandibles are hinged in such a way that they can be held parallel to hold a row of fish in place, and these are also retained by inward-facing serrations on the edges of the beak.

en.text: Puffins can't really land: they crash into a wave or do a belly flop.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
source.quote: Landing is awkward; it either crashes into a wave crest or, in calmer water, does a belly flop.

en.text: Wings whirring several times a second, a puffin can fly at {80 km/h|50 mph}.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
quote: To maintain flight, the wings must beat very rapidly at a rate of several times each second.
The bird's flight is direct and low over the surface of the water, and it can travel at 80 km/h (50 mph) .

en.text: A puffin's bright bill isn't permanent: the colorful plates fall off after breeding.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
quote: The characteristic bright orange bill plates and other facial characteristics develop in the spring.
At the close of the breeding season, these special coatings and appendages are shed in a partial moult.

en.text: In winter a puffin sheds all its flight feathers at once and can't fly for a month or two.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
source.quote: Land birds mostly lose their primaries one pair at a time to enable them still to be able to fly, but the puffin sheds all its primaries at one time and dispenses with flight entirely for a month or two.

en.text: A young puffin heads out to sea and doesn't set foot on land again for two or three years.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
source.quote: It does not congregate with others of its kind and does not return to land for 2–3 years.

en.text: With its big painted bill and waddle, the puffin is known as the 'clown of the sea'.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
source.quote: The puffin's striking appearance, large, colourful bill, waddling gait, and behaviour have given rise to nicknames such as "clown of the sea" or "sea parrot".

en.text: Maine's first transplanted puffin chicks traveled from Newfoundland in juice cans.

source.title: Audubon Magazine, A Crazy Idea to Bring Back Atlantic Puffins Is a Success (2013)
source.quote: With the help of nature enthusiast and Intel cofounder Robert Noyce, another early supporter, Kress and research assistant Kathleen Blanchard moved the chicks in juice cans to be hand-reared on Hog Island and then released on Egg Rock.

en.text: At sea, a puffin sometimes dips its head underwater to look around for predators.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
source.quote: Atlantic puffins are probably safer when out at sea, where the dangers are more often from below the water rather than above; puffins can sometimes be seen putting their heads underwater to peer around for predators.

en.text: Puffin pairs renew their bond by 'billing': they wag their heads from side to side, then rattle their beaks together, again and again.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
quote: This is a practice in which the pair approaches each other, each wagging their heads from side to side, and then rattling their beaks together.
This seems to be an important element of their courtship behaviour because it happens repeatedly, and the birds continue to the bill, to a lesser extent, throughout the breeding season.

en.text: Puffins bringing fish home tend to arrive in groups. That makes it harder for skuas to chase any one bird until it drops its catch.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
quote: Adults bringing fish to their chicks tend to arrive in groups.
This is thought to benefit the bird by reducing kleptoparasitism by the Arctic skua, which harasses puffins until they drop their fish loads.

en.text: The name 'puffin' first meant the salted meat of young Manx shearwaters, a different seabird. Atlantic puffins got the name much later.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
quote: The vernacular name "puffin" – puffed in the sense of swollen – was originally applied to the fatty, salted meat of young birds of the unrelated species Manx shearwater ( Puffinus puffinus ), which in 1652 was known as the "Manks puffin".
The Atlantic puffin acquired the name at a much later stage, possibly because of its similar nesting habits,

en.text: In late summer, a Scottish seabird center asks drivers to check under their cars: young puffins confused by street lights may hide there.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
source.quote: Another conservation measure undertaken by the centre is to encourage motorists to check under their cars in late summer before driving off, as young puffins, disoriented by the street lights, may land in the town and take shelter underneath the vehicles.

en.text: Puffins dig their own burrows with beak and feet, but they also move into rabbit burrows, pecking and driving off the owners.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
source.quote: They can excavate their own hole or move into a pre-existing system dug by a rabbit , and have been known to peck and drive off the original occupant.

en.text: A puffin chick leaves its burrow for the first time at night, scrambles down to the sea, and paddles about {3 km|1.9 mi} out by daybreak.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
quote: The chick finally leaves its nest at night, when the risk of predation is at its lowest.
When the moment arrives, it emerges from the burrow, usually for the first time, and walks, runs, and flaps its way to the sea.
It cannot fly properly yet, so descending a cliff is perilous; when it reaches the water, it paddles out to sea, and maybe 3 km (1.9 mi) away from the shore by daybreak.

en.text: Alone in the dark burrow, a puffin chick works out: it flaps its little wings, tugs at roots and pushes hard against the walls.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
source.quote: It rearranges its nesting material, picks up and drops small stones, flaps its immature wings, pulls at protruding root ends, and pushes and strains against the unyielding wall of the burrow.

en.text: If one puffin takes off in a fright, panic can sweep the colony: every bird launches into the air and wheels around in a great circle.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
source.quote: If a bird is startled and takes off unexpectedly, panic can spread through the colony with all the birds launching themselves into the air and wheeling around in a great circle.

en.text: A puffin's black back and white belly are camouflage: from above it blends with the dark sea, from below with the bright sky.

source.title: Wikipedia, Atlantic puffin
source.quote: This provides camouflage , with aerial predators unable to locate the birds against the dark, watery background, and underwater attackers fail to notice them as they blend in with the bright sky above the waves.

en.text: To woo a mate, a male buff-breasted sandpiper flashes its bright white underwings.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Buff-breasted Sandpiper
source.quote: Male displays by raising one wing, showing off white underside.

en.text: Some buff-breasted sandpipers show off their wings on migration, with no audience at all.

source.title: Wikipedia, Buff-breasted sandpiper
source.quote: The male has a display which includes raising the wings to display the white undersides, which is also given on migration, sometimes when no other buff-breasted sandpipers are present.

en.text: This shorebird skips the beach: it stops over on golf courses, cemeteries and airfields.

source.title: BirdWeb (Birds Connect Seattle), Buff-breasted Sandpiper
source.quote: In migration, they can be found on grassy areas such as golf courses, cemeteries, mowed lawns, and airfields.

en.text: Migrating buff-breasted sandpipers have been found resting on baseball diamonds.

source.title: Smithsonian Migratory Bird Center, The Dancing Shorebird (1997)
source.quote: Favorite migration stopovers are short-grass pastures, dry ponds and even baseball diamonds, airports, lawns and other "grasslands".

en.text: Buff-breasted sandpipers catch Arctic bumblebees, to eat or to feed to their chicks.

source.title: Wikipedia, Buff-breasted sandpiper
quote: The buff-breasted sandpipers are known to prey on Bombus polaris , a species of bumblebee found within the Arctic Circle .
They will either eat the bees or feed them to their young.

en.text: A robin-sized buff-breasted sandpiper commutes between the Arctic and Argentina's pampas.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Buff-breasted Sandpiper
quote: About the size of a Robin

Formerly an abundant bird, the Buff-breasted Sandpiper suffered serious declines around the beginning of the 20th century, with many shot during their long migration from the Arctic tundra to the pampas of Argentina.

en.text: With its round head, short bill and dark eye, this sandpiper has a gentle, dovelike face.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Buff-breasted Sandpiper
source.quote: Has dovelike or "gentle" expression, with dark eye on pale face, short bill, round head.

en.text: Instead of fancy feathers like birds-of-paradise, buff-breasted sandpipers woo with dance.

source.title: Smithsonian Migratory Bird Center, The Dancing Shorebird (1997)
source.quote: Buff-breasted Sandpipers have evolved elaborate behavior in their courtship instead of the gaudier plumages of other lekking species such as the manakins and birds-of-paradise.

en.text: Lost buff-breasted sandpipers have turned up in faraway Australia at least eight times.

source.title: Wikipedia, Buff-breasted sandpiper
source.quote: The buff-breasted sandpiper has also been recorded in Australia on at least eight occasions.

en.text: On the Texas coast, migrating buff-breasted sandpipers favor sod farms, where lawns grow.

source.title: USGS Publications Warehouse: Rodkey et al. 2024, Sod farms drive habitat selection of a migratory grassland shorebird
source.quote: Using tracking data from 118 birds compiled over 4 years, we found Buff-breasted Sandpipers selected intensively managed crops such as sod and short-stature crop fields, but generally avoided rangeland and areas near trees and shrubs.

en.text: Buff-breasted sandpipers are often surprisingly tame, so birders can get a close look.

source.title: Wikipedia, Buff-breasted sandpiper
source.quote: They are often very tame.

en.text: A buff-breasted sandpiper hunts with a high-stepping walk, bobbing its head to spot prey.

source.title: BirdWeb (Birds Connect Seattle), Buff-breasted Sandpiper
source.quote: While foraging, they walk steadily along with a high-stepping gait, bobbing their elevated heads looking for prey on the ground.

en.text: Rival male sandpipers play dirty: one may crawl on its belly into a neighbor's display spot, or act like a female to break up a mating.

source.title: Smithsonian Migratory Bird Center, The Dancing Shorebird (1997)
source.quote: Sometimes a renegade male will sneak on his belly into another male's mating post to disrupt the dance of his competitor, sometimes he will simply fly in and chase females away from his rival, and at other times, he will wait until his rival attracts several females then will walk in while mimicking female behavior and disrupt the copulation of the rival male.

en.text: Females often nest near golden-plovers and black-bellied plovers, which may act as lookouts against foxes, jaegers and snowy owls.

source.title: Smithsonian Migratory Bird Center, The Dancing Shorebird (1997)
quote: Meanwhile, females build simple nests in the treeless Arctic tundra, sometimes near the nests of Black-bellied and American Golden-Plovers.

These plovers may act as sentinels thereby providing extra protection for the Buff-breasted Sandpiper young and eggs from Arctic Fox, Ermine, Arctic Ground Squirrels, jaegers, Snowy Owls, ravens, gulls and other predators.

en.text: In November 2011 a buff-breasted sandpiper turned up in Kerala, southern India, probably blown off course from the Great Plains.

source.title: Wikipedia, Buff-breasted sandpiper
quote: It is believed that instead of going to Argentina, this bird might have been wind-blown from the Great Plains Flyway of North America and landed up in South Asia.
In November 2011, this species was sighted near Kannur , Kerala in South India .

en.text: Most buff-breasted sandpipers migrate across the Great Plains, but young birds spread out: many reach the East Coast, some the Pacific.

source.title: BirdWeb (Birds Connect Seattle), Buff-breasted Sandpiper
quote: Most Buff-breasted Sandpipers migrate from Arctic breeding grounds across the Great Plains, to the Pampas of southern South America and back.
Juveniles spread out across the country, many reaching the East Coast and some spreading west to the Pacific.

en.text: Buff-breasted sandpiper chicks leave the nest within hours of hatching and feed themselves. Spread out, they may hide more easily.

source.title: Smithsonian Migratory Bird Center, The Dancing Shorebird (1997)
quote: Defense of the young sandpipers is different from many birds in that these young are precocial-that is, they leave the nest within a few hours of hatching and can run and feed themselves.
This may be an adaptation for the open terrain with lots of predators in that they for part of the day they can spread out and hide easier than a nest full of nestlings.

en.text: In South America, buff-breasted sandpipers winter almost only on pastures, where grazing cattle keep the grass short enough for them.

source.title: USGS Publications Warehouse: Lanctot et al. 2002, Conservation status of the buff-breasted sandpiper in South America
source.quote: Buff-breasted Sandpipers were found almost exclusively in pasturelands and appear to depend heavily upon intensive grazing by livestock, which maintain suitable short grass conditions.

en.text: In Uruguay, cattle still graze on native grasslands. Biologists work with ranchers there to keep pastures good for both cows and sandpipers.

source.title: BirdNote, Ranching and Birding in Uruguay go Hand-in-Hand (2022)
quote: Uruguay, Nicolás is saying here, is a country that does ranching in a natural system.
A kind of approach that makes sure pastures for livestock also help host birds like the Buff-breasted Sandpiper, which spend their winters here.

en.text: Each spring, rice fields on the Gulf Coast of Louisiana and Texas are vital rest stops for buff-breasted sandpipers heading north.

source.title: USGS Publications Warehouse: Norling et al. 2012, Shorebird populations during spring stopover in rice fields of Louisiana and Texas
quote: Greater than 50% of the estimated North American populations were estimated to use rice field habitats for five species, including a species of concern, Buff-breasted Sandpiper (Tryngites subruficollis) at 187%.
Because of predictability of suitable rice field habitat acreage, timing of field preparation and water availability, coastal rice prairies are identified as critical spring migration stopover sites.

en.text: Buff-breasted sandpiper chicks can fly at just 16 to 20 days old. In fall the adults usually head south first, and the young follow later.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Buff-breasted Sandpiper
quote: Age at first flight about 16-20 days.
Adults migrate south earlier in fall than juveniles, on average.

en.text: 'Jaeger' comes from the German word Jäger, meaning hunter.

source.title: Wikipedia, Long-tailed jaeger
source.quote: The word "jaeger" is derived from the German word Jäger , meaning "hunter".

en.text: The long-tailed jaeger is the smallest member of the skua family.

source.title: Wikipedia, Long-tailed jaeger
source.quote: This is the smallest of the skua family at 38–58 cm (15–23 in) , depending on season and age.

en.text: Long-tailed jaeger parents may land on an intruder's head and peck it.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Long-tailed Jaeger
source.quote: Parents defend nest by diving at predators or humans, even landing on intruder's head and pecking.

en.text: Over the tundra, a long-tailed jaeger hovers in the air, then swoops down on its prey.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Long-tailed Jaeger
source.quote: In summer on tundra, hunts by hovering and then swooping down on prey; sometimes picks up items while swimming, or catches insects in flight.

en.text: A hunter with a sweet tooth: long-tailed jaegers also eat berries, especially crowberries.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Long-tailed Jaeger
source.quote: Summer diet is mostly small rodents, especially lemmings and voles when they are in high population cycle; also insects, small birds, fish, squid, carrion, and berries (especially crowberries).

en.text: Young long-tailed jaegers on migration sometimes hunt on golf courses, unafraid of people.

source.title: Wikipedia, Long-tailed jaeger
source.quote: Passage juvenile birds sometimes hunt small prey in ploughed fields or golf-courses, and are typically quite fearless of humans.

en.text: Long-tailed jaegers probably don't breed until they are at least 3 or 4 years old.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Long-tailed Jaeger
source.quote: Probably does not breed until at least 3-4 years old.

en.text: When lemmings are scarce, long-tailed jaegers may skip nesting and go back to sea.

source.title: Bylot Island long-term monitoring (Centre d'études nordiques, Université Laval), Long-tailed jaeger
quote: Their breeding is strongly influenced by the abundance of prey and can choose not to breed when lemming populations are too low.
After a few days defending their territory, if the birds decide not to breed, they will return to the sea.

en.text: Long-tailed jaegers build no nest: their eggs lie in a bare scrape on the tundra.

source.title: Bylot Island long-term monitoring (Centre d'études nordiques, Université Laval), Long-tailed jaeger
quote: They lay eggs in a shallow depression directly on the ground.
They do not use any nest material and do not build any nest structure allowing them to be very cryptic.

en.text: Long-tailed jaeger eggs are so well camouflaged that even experts struggle to find them.

source.title: Bylot Island long-term monitoring (Centre d'études nordiques, Université Laval), Long-tailed jaeger
quote: The greenish color of eggs helps to camouflage the nest.
Even for experimented observers, jaeger eggs are quite difficult to locate in the vast arctic tundra.

en.text: A long-tailed jaeger swallows lemmings whole, then coughs up the bones and fur as pellets.

source.title: Bylot Island long-term monitoring (Centre d'études nordiques, Université Laval), Long-tailed jaeger
source.quote: As with most avian predators, the long-tailed jaeger swallows its prey whole but rejects the indigestible parts (bones, hair, claws, feathers, etc.) in pellets that can be analysed to determine their diet.

en.text: Long-tailed jaeger chicks leave the nest a day or two after hatching to catch insects.

source.title: Bylot Island long-term monitoring (Centre d'études nordiques, Université Laval), Long-tailed jaeger
quote: Newly hatched long-tailed jaegers are ‘precocial’, meaning that they leave the nest and move by themselves only 24 to 48 hours after hatching.
This allows young to feed by themselves on arthropods.

en.text: The jaeger's genus name, Stercorarius, means 'of dung'. People once thought the food other birds dropped when chased was droppings.

source.title: Wikipedia, Long-tailed jaeger
source.quote: The genus name Stercorarius is Latin and means "of dung"; the food disgorged by other birds when pursued by skuas was once thought to be excrement.

en.text: In winter a long-tailed jaeger turns pirate, chasing seabirds until they give up their food. Arctic terns and Sabine's gulls suffer most.

source.title: Wikipedia, Long-tailed jaeger
quote: Like other jaegers and skuas, it is also a kleptoparasite , chasing other seabirds to make them give up their food.
The bird species most commonly "robbed" this way by the long-tailed jaeger are Arctic terns ( Sterna paradisaea ) and Sabine's gulls ( Xema sabini )

en.text: A long-tailed jaeger's summer runs on lemmings. When lemming numbers boom, jaegers feast and are more likely to raise their chicks.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Long-tailed Jaeger
quote: Summer diet is mostly small rodents, especially lemmings and voles when they are in high population cycle; also insects, small birds, fish, squid, carrion, and berries (especially crowberries).
More likely to nest successfully in years when lemmings are abundant.

en.text: Courting long-tailed jaegers fly a spectacular show of swoops and zigzags, often three at once. On the ground, the male feeds the female.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Long-tailed Jaeger
quote: Has spectacular courtship flight, with rapid swoops and zigzags, often three birds together, or one male chasing one female.
In courtship on ground, male feeds female.

en.text: In summer, adult long-tailed jaegers grow tail streamers up to {15 cm|5.9 in} long, which makes them easy to tell from the other jaegers.

source.title: Wikipedia, Long-tailed jaeger
quote: However up to 29 cm (11 in) of its length can be made up by the tail which may include the 15 cm (5.9 in) tail streamers of the summer adult.
This species is unmistakable as an adult, with grey back, dark primary wing feathers without a white "flash", black cap and very long tail.

en.text: Long-tailed jaegers leave the Arctic early: many adults are already heading south by mid-August, before the other jaegers.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Long-tailed Jaeger
source.quote: Fall migration earlier than in other jaegers, with many adults southbound by mid-August.

en.text: Long-tailed jaeger partners migrate separately, then meet again on their tundra territory each summer. Some pairs stay together for years.

source.title: Bylot Island long-term monitoring (Centre d'études nordiques, Université Laval), Long-tailed jaeger
quote: Males and females long-tailed jaegers do not migrate together, but partners meet again each summer on their breeding site.
Some couples will breed together for many years.

en.text: Long-tailed jaegers spend most of their lives at sea, eating fish. But in summer they turn into land birds that hunt lemmings on the tundra.

source.title: Bylot Island long-term monitoring (Centre d'études nordiques, Université Laval), Long-tailed jaeger
quote: Since the long-tailed jaeger is a seabird, it spends most of its life at sea.
However, as the summer approaches, its lifestyle changes drastically to become exclusively terrestrial.
While its winter diet consists mostly of small fishes and surface marine invertebrates, breeding birds feed exclusively on terrestrial prey during the summer.

en.text: A jaeger pair nests on a small mound to keep watch for arctic foxes, and chases off any intruder within about {1 km²|0.4 sq mi} of the nest.

source.title: Bylot Island long-term monitoring (Centre d'études nordiques, Université Laval), Long-tailed jaeger
quote: Their nest is usually found on a small mount where they can keep an eye on their territory and protect their nest from predators, mainly the arctic fox.
Jaegers attack and chase away any intruders that come within an area of approximately 1 km 2 from their nest.

de.text: Bei der Falkenraubmöwe kann der Schwanz bis zu {29 cm|11 in} der Körperlänge ausmachen.

source.title: Wikipedia (English), Long-tailed jaeger
source.quote: However up to 29 cm (11 in) of its length can be made up by the tail which may include the 15 cm (5.9 in) tail streamers of the summer adult.

de.text: Die Falkenraubmöwe steht lange in der Luft und späht. Sieht sie Beute, schlägt sie zu.

source.title: NABU, Vogelporträt Falkenraubmöwe
quote: Auf der Suche nach Beute schwebt die schlanke Raubmöwe für längere Zeit in der Luft und hält Ausschau.
Hat sie ein Tier erspäht, schlägt sie schnell zu.

de.text: In mageren Jahren fressen Falkenraubmöwen in der Tundra auch Beeren.

source.title: NABU, Vogelporträt Falkenraubmöwe
source.quote: Auch Insekten, kleinere Vögel und Eier werden gefressen, in schlechten Jahren auch Beeren.

de.text: Mit viel Glück sieht man Falkenraubmöwen im Mai oder im Spätsommer an der Nordsee.

source.title: NABU, Vogelporträt Falkenraubmöwe
source.quote: Im Mai und August/September kann man mit sehr viel Glück eine Falkenraubmöwe an der Nordseeküste beobachten.

de.text: Unter den Raubmöwen ist die Falkenraubmöwe die wendigste, eleganteste und friedlichste.

source.title: BirdWeb (Seattle Audubon), Long-tailed Jaeger
source.quote: Long-tailed Jaegers are the most agile and graceful of the jaegers, and the least aggressive.

de.text: Falkenraubmöwen-Paare bleiben viele Jahre lang zusammen.

source.title: BirdWeb (Seattle Audubon), Long-tailed Jaeger
source.quote: Long-tailed Jaegers for monogamous long-term pair bonds.

de.text: Die langen Schwanzspieße der Falkenraubmöwe brechen im Herbst oft ab oder fallen aus.

source.title: BirdWeb (Seattle Audubon), Long-tailed Jaeger
source.quote: During the breeding season, the adult has long central tail feathers that extend 5-10" beyond the rest of the tail, but from August to November, these are often broken or missing.

de.text: Auf See sammeln sich Falkenraubmöwen gern um Fischkutter.

source.title: BirdWeb (Seattle Audubon), Long-tailed Jaeger
source.quote: Although Long-tailed Jaegers usually migrate singly over the open ocean, small numbers may congregate around fishing vessels during the non-breeding season.

de.text: Falkenraubmöwen brüten wohl erst, wenn sie mindestens drei oder vier Jahre alt sind.

source.title: Audubon Field Guide, Long-tailed Jaeger
source.quote: Probably does not breed until at least 3-4 years old.

de.text: Junge Falkenraubmöwen jagen auf dem Zug auch auf Äckern und Golfplätzen, ohne viel Scheu.

source.title: Wikipedia (English), Long-tailed jaeger
source.quote: Passage juvenile birds sometimes hunt small prey in ploughed fields or golf-courses, and are typically quite fearless of humans.

de.text: Ihr Nest legt die Falkenraubmöwe gern auf eine kleine Kuppe, mit gutem Überblick.

source.title: NABU, Vogelporträt Falkenraubmöwe
source.quote: Ihr Nest legt sie in Bodenmulden an, gern etwas erhöht mit gutem Überblick.

de.text: Im Winter südlich des Äquators wird die Falkenraubmöwe zur Diebin. Sie jagt dann vor allem Küstenseeschwalben und Schwalbenmöwen Beute ab.

source.title: Wikipedia (English), Long-tailed jaeger
quote: This appears to be an important food source during the winter months, spent south of the equator.
The bird species most commonly "robbed" this way by the long-tailed jaeger are Arctic terns ( Sterna paradisaea ) and Sabine's gulls ( Xema sabini ).

de.text: Raubmöwen sind als Diebe verrufen. Die Falkenraubmöwe jagt im Brutgebiet aber lieber selbst: Rötelmäuse, Wühlmäuse, Insekten, Eier.

source.title: Wikipedia, Falkenraubmöwe
quote: In den Brutgebieten spielt das möwentypische Beuteabjagen bei der Falkenraubmöwe kaum eine Rolle.
Ihre Nahrung besteht hier hauptsächlich aus Rötelmäusen , Wühlmäusen und ähnlichen Kleinsäugern.
Sie frisst hier auch Insekten, Eier und kleinere Vögel.

de.text: Lemminge brauchen lange Winter unter schützendem Schnee. Seit etwa 2000 bleiben ihre Massenjahre oft aus, schlecht für Falkenraubmöwen.

source.title: Justus-Liebig-Universität Gießen, Seevögel als Verlierer des Klimawandels (2018)
quote: Dieser benötigt lange Winter und eine schützende Schneedecke, um sich neun Monate lang zu vermehren.
Die in der Vergangenheit regelmäßig auftretenden Massenvermehrungen sind etwa seit der Jahrtausendwende – offenbar bedingt durch kürzere Winter – deutlich schwächer geworden oder bleiben ganz aus.

de.text: Balzende Falkenraubmöwen zeigen am Himmel Sturzflüge und Zickzack, oft zu dritt. Am Boden füttert das Männchen dann das Weibchen.

source.title: Audubon Field Guide, Long-tailed Jaeger
quote: Has spectacular courtship flight, with rapid swoops and zigzags, often three birds together, or one male chasing one female.
In courtship on ground, male feeds female.

de.text: Bei Falkenraubmöwen jagt meist das Männchen. Es würgt das Futter am Nest wieder hoch, und das Weibchen füttert damit die Küken.

source.title: BirdWeb (Seattle Audubon), Long-tailed Jaeger
source.quote: Typically, the male brings food back, regurgitates, and the female feeds the young.

de.text: Junge Falkenraubmöwen verlassen das Nest nach ein, zwei Tagen. Mit gut drei Wochen fliegen sie, bleiben aber noch eine Weile bei den Eltern.

source.title: BirdWeb (Seattle Audubon), Long-tailed Jaeger
quote: Chicks stay in the nest 1-2 days after hatching.
Young often remain with their parents for 1-3 weeks after fledging, which occurs at 22-27 days.

namesSource.title: IOC World Bird List 15.2, multilingual version (German names: Peter Barthel)

en.text: Sabine's gulls make the longest migration of any gull: up to {39000 km|24200 mi} a year.

source.title: Wikipedia, Sabine's gull
source.quote: They migrate south to the Southern Hemisphere in autumn, covering up to 32,000–39,000 km per year, the longest migration of any gull.

en.text: The Sabine's gull's genus name, Xema, seems to be an invented word with no meaning.

source.title: Wikipedia, Sabine's gull
source.quote: The genus name Xema appears to be an invented name without meaning.

en.text: In shallow water, a Sabine's gull may spin in circles to stir up food from the bottom.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Sabine's Gull
source.quote: In shallow water may spin in circles, stirring up items from bottom.

en.text: Sabine's gulls usually nest in or near colonies of Arctic terns.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Sabine's Gull
source.quote: Usually located in or near a colony of Arctic Terns.

en.text: With its notched white tail, the Sabine's gull was once known as the 'fork-tailed gull'.

source.title: Wikipedia, Sabine's gull
quote: It has also been known historically as fork-tailed gull or xeme (from the genus name).
The white tail is slightly forked.

en.text: The Sabine's gull's closest relative is the ivory gull, another Arctic bird.

source.title: Wikipedia, Sabine's gull
source.quote: Mitochondrial DNA studies confirmed that they are not closely related, and the closest relative of Sabine's gull is now thought to be the ivory gull , another Arctic species.

en.text: Sabine's gulls flutter low over the sea and pick food off the surface, more like terns.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Sabine's Gull
quote: Delicate in its feeding, this species often floats in the air low over the water, dipping down to take food from the surface without landing.
Its flight action may suggest a tern more than a gull.

en.text: Joseph Sabine named Sabine's gull in 1819 after his brother Edward, who had collected it.

source.title: Wikipedia, Sabine's gull
source.quote: Sabine based his description on specimens that had been collected by his brother Captain Edward Sabine , who had accompanied Captain John Ross on a voyage to look for the Northwest Passage .

en.text: Every fall a few young Sabine's gulls go astray and thrill birders on lakes far inland.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Sabine's Gull
quote: A young Sabine's that goes astray in fall may cause excitement by showing up on a pond far inland.
Every fall, a few (mostly young birds) show up on lakes in the interior of North America.

en.text: To protect its nest, a Sabine's gull may dive-bomb intruders or try to lure them away.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Sabine's Gull
source.quote: Parents may defend nest by dive-bombing intruders, or may try to lead predators away with distraction display.

en.text: For a gull, the Sabine's gull has a very high-pitched, squeaky voice.

source.title: Wikipedia, Sabine's gull
source.quote: They have a very high-pitched and squeaking call.

en.text: Sabine's gull honors Edward Sabine, who fought the Americans in the War of 1812 and later led a global effort to measure Earth's magnetism.

source.title: Wikipedia, Edward Sabine
quote: He became a second captain when he was sent to Quebec and fought the Americans in the Niagara campaign .
He led the effort to establish a system of magnetic observatories in various parts of British territory all over the globe.

en.text: Sabine's gull was discovered in July 1818 on John Ross's hunt for the Northwest Passage. The birds were nesting on islands off Greenland.

source.title: Wikipedia, Sabine's gull
quote: Sabine based his description on specimens that had been collected by his brother Captain Edward Sabine , who had accompanied Captain John Ross on a voyage to look for the Northwest Passage .
The birds were found breeding on low-lying islands off the west coast of Greenland in July 1818.

en.text: The Galápagos swallow-tailed gull shares the Sabine's gull's notched tail and yellow-tipped bill. Yet DNA shows they aren't close relatives.

source.title: Wikipedia, Sabine's gull
quote: The yellow-tipped black bill and notched tail are shared only with the swallow-tailed gull of the Galapagos .
Mitochondrial DNA studies confirmed that they are not closely related, and the closest relative of Sabine's gull is now thought to be the ivory gull , another Arctic species.

en.text: Young Sabine's gulls keep their juvenile feathers all the way south and only start to molt once they reach their winter seas.

source.title: Wikipedia, Sabine's gull
source.quote: Fledged birds retain their juvenile plumage through the autumn and do not start moulting into their first winter plumage until they have reached their wintering grounds.

en.text: Sabine's gulls molt backward: adults get a full new set of feathers in spring and only a partial one in fall, the reverse of other gulls.

source.title: Wikipedia, Sabine's gull
source.quote: Adults have their complete moult in the spring prior to the spring migration, and have a partial moult in the autumn after returning to the wintering area, a reversal of the usual pattern for gulls.

en.text: On their way from the Arctic to South Africa, Atlantic Sabine's gulls take a long meal break: about 45 days feeding in the Bay of Biscay.

source.title: Wikipedia, Sabine's gull
quote: The Svalbard , Greenland and eastern Canadian populations of Sabine's gull usually cross the Atlantic Ocean by way of the westernmost coasts of Europe ( Ireland , western Great Britain , northwest Spain , Portugal ) and northwest Africa ( Morocco ) to winter off southwestern Africa in the cold waters of the Benguela Current off Namibia and South Africa .
During their flight south, the birds spend significant time (typically around 45 days) feeding offshore in the Bay of Biscay .

en.text: A male Sabine's gull courts by giving a long call, arching its neck and bowing. Once paired, the male may bring the female food.

source.title: Audubon Guide to North American Birds, Sabine's Gull
quote: Male on territory lures female by giving long call, arching neck, bowing.
In courtship, male may feed female.

de.text: Der Gattungsname Xema ist wohl frei erfunden und bedeutet nichts.

source.title: Wikipedia (English), Sabine's gull
source.quote: The genus name Xema appears to be an invented name without meaning.

de.text: Schwalbenmöwen schweben tief über dem Wasser und picken ihr Futter auf, ohne zu landen.

source.title: Audubon Field Guide, Sabine's Gull
source.quote: Delicate in its feeding, this species often floats in the air low over the water, dipping down to take food from the surface without landing.

de.text: Im flachen Wasser dreht sich die Schwalbenmöwe im Kreis und wirbelt Futter vom Grund auf.

source.title: Audubon Field Guide, Sabine's Gull
source.quote: In shallow water may spin in circles, stirring up items from bottom.

de.text: Schwalbenmöwen brüten meist nahe bei Küstenseeschwalben oder mitten in deren Kolonie.

source.title: Audubon Field Guide, Sabine's Gull
source.quote: Usually located in or near a colony of Arctic Terns.

de.text: Droht Gefahr am Nest, stürzen sich Schwalbenmöwen auf den Feind oder locken ihn fort.

source.title: Audubon Field Guide, Sabine's Gull
source.quote: Parents may defend nest by dive-bombing intruders, or may try to lead predators away with distraction display.

de.text: Für eine Möwe hat die Schwalbenmöwe eine erstaunlich hohe, quietschende Stimme.

source.title: Wikipedia (English), Sabine's gull
source.quote: They have a very high-pitched and squeaking call.

de.text: Bald nach dem Schlüpfen führen Schwalbenmöwen die Küken ans Wasser, wo sie allein fressen.

source.title: BirdWeb (Seattle Audubon), Sabine's Gull
source.quote: Shortly after the young hatch, the parents lead them to water, where they mostly feed themselves.

de.text: Zur Brutzeit trägt die Schwalbenmöwe eine schiefergraue Kapuze mit schwarzem Kragen.

source.title: Wikipedia, Schwalbenmöwe
source.quote: Im Brutkleid ist der Kopf schiefergrau und gegen den weißen Hals durch einen schmalen schwarzen Ring abgesetzt.

de.text: Junge Schwalbenmöwen sind braun statt grau. Erst nach zwei Jahren gleichen sie den Eltern.

source.title: Wikipedia (English), Sabine's gull
quote: Young birds have a similar tricoloured wing pattern, but the grey is replaced by brown, and the tail has a black terminal band.
Juveniles take two years to attain full adult plumage .

de.text: Schwalbenmöwen aus Kanada und Grönland überqueren den Atlantik nach Osten und überwintern im kalten Benguelastrom vor Namibia und Südafrika.

source.title: Wikipedia (English), Sabine's gull
source.quote: The Svalbard , Greenland and eastern Canadian populations of Sabine's gull usually cross the Atlantic Ocean by way of the westernmost coasts of Europe ( Ireland , western Great Britain , northwest Spain , Portugal ) and northwest Africa ( Morocco ) to winter off southwestern Africa in the cold waters of the Benguela Current off Namibia and South Africa .

de.text: Edward Sabine, Namenspate der Schwalbenmöwe, steht auch auf Karten: Es gibt eine Sabine-Insel vor Grönland und einen Krater auf dem Mond.

source.title: Wikipedia, Edward Sabine
quote: Eine Insel vor der Ostküste Grönlands , auf der Sabine 1823 Pendelversuche ausgeführt hatte, heißt seit 1869 Sabine-Insel .
1935 wurde der Mondkrater Sabine nach ihm benannt.

de.text: Zur Brutzeit in der Tundra jagen Schwalbenmöwen nicht nur am Wasser: Auf dem Speiseplan stehen Käfer, Springschwänze, Schnaken und Mücken.

source.title: Wikipedia (English), Sabine's gull
source.quote: In the breeding season, the gulls pursue a range of freshwater and terrestrial prey on the tundra (and within boreal river deltas , estuaries and coastal wetlands ), including both terrestrial and aquatic beetles , springtails , craneflies , mosquitoes , midges , flower flies ( Syrphidae ),

de.text: Junge Schwalbenmöwen fliegen im Jugendkleid bis ans andere Ende der Welt. Neue Federn wachsen erst, wenn sie im Winterquartier sind.

source.title: Wikipedia (English), Sabine's gull
source.quote: Fledged birds retain their juvenile plumage through the autumn and do not start moulting into their first winter plumage until they have reached their wintering grounds.

de.text: Auf dem Weg nach Südafrika schlemmen Schwalbenmöwen ausgiebig: Rund 45 Tage fressen sie sich in der Biskaya vor Frankreich satt.

source.title: Wikipedia (English), Sabine's gull
source.quote: During their flight south, the birds spend significant time (typically around 45 days) feeding offshore in the Bay of Biscay .

windows.note: Too few animals move 500 km or more between summer and winter to give windows (e.g. sea turtles roam rather than shuttle).

en.text: The elk's other name, 'wapiti', is a Shawnee and Cree word meaning 'white rump'.

source.title: Wikipedia, Elk
source.quote: The alternative name "wapiti" derives from the Shawnee and Cree word waapiti

en.text: In Europe, 'elk' means the moose. Colonists in America gave the name to a different deer.

source.title: Wikipedia, Elk
quote: For the species called "elk" in Eurasia ( Alces alces ), see Moose .
The word "elk" originally referred to the European variety of the moose , Alces alces , but was transferred to Cervus canadensis by North American colonists.

en.text: A bull elk's antlers can grow up to {2.5 cm|1 in} a day, and weigh up to {18 kg|40 lb}.

source.title: NPS Rocky Mountain National Park, Elk
quote: Antlers can grow up to an inch a day.
Antlers on a mature male can weigh up to 40 pounds.

en.text: To woo cows, bull elk roll in mud holes they have soaked with their own urine.

source.title: Wikipedia, Elk
quote: Bulls also dig holes in the ground called wallows, in which they urinate and roll their bodies .
The urine soaks into their hair and gives them a distinct smell which attracts cows.

en.text: Banff's elk winter at Ya Ha Tinda, which means 'mountain prairie' in the Nakoda language.

source.title: Wikipedia, Ya Ha Tinda Ranch
quote: Around a thousand elk spend the winter in the ranch.
Ya Ha Tinda means "mountain prairie" in the Nakoda language.

en.text: The elk's winter home is a ranch where Parks Canada raises horses for its mounted rangers.

source.title: Wikipedia, Ya Ha Tinda Ranch
source.quote: The ranch is owned by Parks Canada and used to raise horses for use in the western national parks that request mounted park rangers.

en.text: Elk change their minds: each year about 15% of Ya Ha Tinda elk switch to staying or going.

source.title: Eggeman et al. 2016, Journal of Animal Ecology
source.quote: Individuals switched between migrant and resident strategies at a mean rate of 15% per year

en.text: After snowy winters, Yellowstone's elk head uphill late; in early springs, they go early.

source.title: NPS Yellowstone, Elk
quote: After winters with high snowpack, elk delay migration.
In years with lower snowpack and earlier vegetation green-up, elk migrate earlier.

en.text: Elk had vanished from the Great Smoky Mountains. In 2001, 25 elk were brought back.

source.title: NPS Great Smoky Mountains, Elk
quote: The last elk in North Carolina is believed to have been killed by the late 1700s
The reintroduction of elk to the park began in 2001 with the release of the first group of 25 elk.

en.text: Of all the world's deer, only the moose is bigger than the elk.

source.title: Wikipedia, Elk
source.quote: The elk is the second largest extant species of deer, after the moose .

en.text: An elk's two 'ivory' teeth may be relics of saber-like tusks its ancestors fought with.

source.title: Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation, Elk Facts
quote: An elk’s top two canine teeth are called ivories
Scientists believe ivories are remnants of saber-like tusks that ancestral species of elk used in combat

en.text: An angry elk curls back its upper lip, grinds its teeth and hisses softly.

source.title: Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation, Elk Facts
source.quote: Elk threaten each other by curling back their upper lip, grinding their teeth and hissing softly

en.text: Spring reaches Banff's mountains about 50 days later for every {1000 m|3300 ft} of height. Migrant elk climb with it to find fresh grass all summer.

source.title: Movebank Data Repository, Ya Ha Tinda elk project, Banff National Park (data from Hebblewhite et al. 2008)
quote: was delayed by 50 days for every 1000-m increase in elevation
The expected digestibility for migrant elk in summer was 6.5% higher than for residents

en.text: Banff's elk choose: migrants head into the park, away from wolves. Stay-at-homes keep close to people at the ranch, where wolves rarely go.

source.title: Hebblewhite and Merrill 2009, Ecology
quote: Migration reduced exposure to wolf predation risk by 70% relative to residents at the landscape scale
they reduced predation risk at fine scales to only 15% higher than migrants by using areas close to human activity, which wolves avoided

en.text: After a big forest fire brought fresh grazing east of the Ya Ha Tinda ranch, some elk invented a brand-new migration route there.

source.title: University of Montana, Williams et al. 2024, Journal of Animal Ecology
source.quote: A novel eastern migrant tactic emerged following a large forest fire that enhanced forage in an area with lower predation risk outside of the protected area.

en.text: A bull elk's bugle is two sounds at once: a low note from the vocal cords and a high whistle of air rushing through a narrow throat.

source.title: Reby et al. 2016, Journal of Experimental Biology
source.quote: with one source oscillating at a mean of 145 Hz (F0) and the other oscillating independently at an average of 1426 Hz (G0)

en.text: Each elk has two ivory teeth that outlast everything else. To the Lakota they meant long life, so a newborn child was given an elk tooth.

source.title: Buffalo Bill Center of the West, Top 10 Visitor Questions to the Plains Indian Museum
quote: Two elk teeth remain after everything else has crumbled to dust
When a child is born, its parents desire long life for it and for this reason an elk tooth is given to a child.

en.text: Wyoming's National Elk Refuge was created in 1912 as a winter haven for one of the largest elk herds.

source.title: Wikipedia, National Elk Refuge
quote: It was created in 1912 to protect habitat and provide sanctuary for one of the largest elk (also known as wapiti) herds.

en.text: Warm chinook winds roar down the Ya Ha Tinda valley and blow the snow off its grassland, so the elk can reach the grass all winter.

source.title: Dryad, Ya Ha Tinda elk dataset (Hebblewhite et al.)
source.quote: In winter, Chinooks (warm air and high winds) clear snow from the grassland acting as a refuge for ungulates.

en.text: Coastal Roosevelt elk are named for Theodore Roosevelt. In 1909, as president, he protected their home as Mount Olympus National Monument.

source.title: Wikipedia, Roosevelt elk
quote: Hart Merriam named the subspecies after his friend Theodore Roosevelt
The desire to protect the Roosevelt elk was one of the primary forces behind the establishment of the Mount Olympus National Monument in 1909 by President Theodore Roosevelt.

en.text: Elk are among the noisiest hoofed animals. Cows chat in chirps and mews, bark to warn of danger, and know their calves by their squeals.

source.title: Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation, Elk Facts
quote: Elk are among the noisiest ungulates, communicating danger quickly and identifying each other by sound.
High-pitched squeal: Newborn to its mother, who recognizes her calf by its voice.
Cows bark to warn others of danger

de.text: Wer in Amerika „elk“ sagt, meint den Wapiti. Der Elch heißt dort „moose“.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Wapiti
source.quote: In Nordamerika wird die Art meist elk genannt, während dies im britischen Englisch die Bezeichnung für den Elch ist, welcher in Nordamerika wiederum moose heißt.

de.text: Unter allen Hirschen ist nur der Elch größer als der Wapiti.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Wapiti
source.quote: In der Familie der Hirsche ist lediglich der Elch größer.

de.text: Im Frühjahr wächst ein Wapiti-Geweih um bis zu {2.5 cm|1 in} am Tag.

source.title: National Park Service, Rocky Mountain National Park: Elk
source.quote: Antlers can grow up to an inch a day.

de.text: Wapitis sind die gesprächigsten Hirsche: Kühe und Kälber quieken, zirpen und miauen.

source.title: Parks Canada, Elk in Banff National Park
quote: Elk are the most vocal deer.
Cows and calves keep in contact with squeals, chirps and mews.

de.text: US-Präsident Theodore Roosevelt schenkte Neuseeland eine Herde Wapitis.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Wapiti
source.quote: US-Präsident Theodore Roosevelt schenkte Neuseeland eine Herde Wapitis

de.text: Vor wohl rund 120.000 Jahren kamen Wapitis aus Asien über die Beringstraße nach Amerika.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Wapiti
quote: In Nordamerika erschien der Wapiti vermutlich erst vor 120.000 Jahren
aus Asien über die Beringstraße einwanderte

de.text: Im Sommer leben bis zu 20.000 Wapitis im Yellowstone-Park. Im Winter bleiben keine 2.000.

source.title: National Park Service, Yellowstone National Park: Elk
quote: The high elevation grasslands of the park provide summer habitat for 10,000–20,000 elk.
However, fewer than 2,000 elk spend winter in the park.

de.text: Im Winterquartier Ya Ha Tinda leben auch die Pferde der Parkwächter von Westkanada.

source.title: University of Montana, Ya Ha Tinda Long-Term Elk Monitoring Project: Ya Ha Tinda Ranch
quote: This ranch is the only federally operated working horse ranch in Canada.
Horses are wintered and trained here to be used as working horses for patrolling and protecting Canada's Western National Parks.

de.text: Knirscht ein Wapiti mit den Zähnen und legt die Ohren an, heißt das: Abstand halten!

source.title: Parks Canada, Elk in Banff National Park
source.quote: At any time of the year, an elk will show its discomfort by grinding its teeth, curling its lower lip back, or laying its ears back against its head.

de.text: Anders als Elch und Maultierhirsch fressen Wapitis Gras genauso wie Zweige und Laub.

source.title: Parks Canada, Elk in Banff National Park
quote: Most members of the deer family — such as moose and mule deer — are browsers, feeding almost entirely on the twigs and leaves of shrubs and trees.
In contrast, elk are both grazers and browsers.

de.text: Warme Fallwinde halten Ya Ha Tinda fast schneefrei. Dazu gutes Gras und Menschen, die Raubtiere fernhalten: ein ideales Winterquartier.

source.title: University of Montana, Ya Ha Tinda Long-Term Elk Monitoring Project: Ya Ha Tinda Ranch
quote: The warming downslope winds blow through the valley and prevent much snow accumulation.
Good-quality fescue grasslands, along with the relatively mild weather, and the predatory refuge provided by proximity to humans, makes Ya Ha Tinda the ideal winter range for elk.

de.text: Nach schneereichen Wintern brechen Yellowstones Wapitis später zur Wanderung auf, nach schneearmen Wintern mit frühem Grün früher.

source.title: National Park Service, Yellowstone National Park: Elk
quote: After winters with high snowpack, elk delay migration.
In years with lower snowpack and earlier vegetation green-up, elk migrate earlier.

de.text: Bullen behalten das Geweih über den Winter: Mit Geweih wird gerangelt, ohne kämpfen Bullen mit den Vorderhufen, und das verletzt eher.

source.title: National Park Service, Yellowstone National Park: Elk
quote: Bulls retain their antlers through the winter.
When antlered, bulls usually settle disputes by wrestling with their antlers.
When antlerless, they use their front hooves (as cows do), which is more likely to result in injury to one of the combatants.

de.text: Wapiti-Kälber kommen zur Welt, wenn das frische Grün am nahrhaftesten ist. So können Mutter und Kalb rasch Fettreserven anlegen.

source.title: National Park Service, Yellowstone National Park: Elk
quote: Ungulates that migrate typically give birth around periods of peak vegetation green-up to overlap with high-nutrition plant phases.
Nutritious food allows mothers and calves to build up fat reserves.

studies.name: Ya Ha Tinda elk project, Banff National Park, 2001-2024 (females)
Data from: A multi-scale test of the forage maturation hypothesis in a partially migratory ungulate population

namesSource.title: Wyoming Migration Initiative, Red Desert to Hoback; Wikipedia (de), Maultierhirsch

windows.note: Too few animals move 500 km or more between summer and winter to give windows (e.g. sea turtles roam rather than shuttle).

en.text: Mule deer are named for their big, mule-like ears, which also shed heat to keep them cool.

source.title: NPS Grand Canyon, Mule Deer
quote: The most defining feature of these deer is their large, mule-like ears.
The large ears on mule deer are known to radiate heat away from the deer's body, helping to keep it cool.

en.text: Startled mule deer flee in stiff-legged bounds, all four hooves landing together.

source.title: NPS Theodore Roosevelt National Park, Mule Deer
source.quote: When startled, a mule deer will move in a series of stiff-legged jumps with all four feet hitting the ground together.

en.text: A bounding mule deer can turn right around in the middle of a single leap.

source.title: NPS Theodore Roosevelt National Park, Mule Deer
source.quote: If necessary, they can turn or completely reverse direction in the course of a single bound.

en.text: A mule deer bouncing on all fours is as fast as one at full gallop: about {34 km/h|21 mph}.

source.title: Wild About Utah, Follow the Bouncing Deer
source.quote: Surprisingly, the fastest speeds of a stotting mule deer were just as fast as top galloping speeds—around 9.5 meters per second.

en.text: Red Desert mule deer spend 4 months of every year on the move between their homes.

source.title: Wyoming Migration Initiative, Red Desert to Hoback Migration Assessment
source.quote: The deer that complete this journey spend 4 months of each year migrating

en.text: Wyoming's mule deer summer on high slopes to build the fat they need for winter.

source.title: Wyoming Migration Initiative, Red Desert to Hoback Migration Assessment
source.quote: The performance of these herds is largely dependent on their ability to seasonally migrate from low-elevation winter ranges to high-elevation summer ranges, where they gain fat needed to survive the long Wyoming winters.

en.text: In 2016 the deer's route became one of Wyoming's first official migration corridors.

source.title: University of Wyoming Extension, Landowner and Economic Benefits from Migration Corridor Designation in Wyoming
quote: We quantify landowner benefits specifically related to the Sublette Mule Deer Migration Corridor, commonly known as the Red Desert to Hoback Basin (RD2H), since it was designate d in 2016.
The RD2H corridor was among the first to receive designation status.

en.text: Heading north, some Red Desert mule deer swim right across Fremont Lake, Wyoming.

source.title: WyoFile, America's longest mule deer migration discovered in Wyoming
source.quote: Some swam across Fremont Lake before making their way out of the Green River Basin.

en.text: Mule deer antlers fork into a 'Y', unlike a white-tailed deer's.

source.title: NPS Theodore Roosevelt National Park, Mule Deer
source.quote: Mule deer antlers are distinct from whitetail antlers due to their second tine forking into a “Y.”

en.text: A mule deer's skinny tail has a black tip. Its white-tailed cousin has a bushy white one.

source.title: NPS Theodore Roosevelt National Park, Mule Deer
source.quote: A mule deer’s tail is thin and black-tipped, unlike the bushy white tail of its cousin.

en.text: Mule deer even nibble the pads of prickly pear cactus.

source.title: NPS, Mule Deer
source.quote: They may even browse on the pads of pricklypear cactus.

en.text: On their {240 km|150 mi} trip from the Red Desert to the Hoback Basin, mule deer cross sand dunes, lakes, rivers, highways and over 100 fences.

source.title: Wyoming Migration Initiative, Red Desert to Hoback Migration Assessment
quote: the longest mule deer migration ever recorded (and 2nd longest land migration in North America) was discovered where deer travel a one-way distance of 150 miles
including sand dunes, lake and river crossings, multiple highways, and more than 100 fences

en.text: Mule deer migrate by heart. Memory of the route steers them 2 to 28 times more strongly than fresh green grass or deep snow does.

source.title: Merkle et al. 2019, Ecology Letters
source.quote: Spatial memory had an extraordinary influence on migration, affecting movement 2-28 times more strongly than tracking spring green-up or autumn snow depth.

en.text: In spring, mule deer 'surf' the green wave of new growth up the mountains. Almost a third keep pace as well as a perfect surfer would.

source.title: Aikens et al. 2017, Ecology Letters
quote: The Green Wave Hypothesis posits that herbivore migration manifests in response to waves of spring green-up (i.e. green-wave surfing).
In a population of migratory mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus), 31% surfed plant phenology in spring as well as a theoretically perfect surfer

en.text: Since 2016, ranchers along the deer's corridor have rebuilt or removed {776 km|482 mi} of fence to make it easier for wildlife to cross.

source.title: University of Wyoming Extension, Landowner and Economic Benefits from Migration Corridor Designation in Wyoming
source.quote: Since its designation by the Wyoming Game and Fish Department in 2016, landowners have benefited from at least 482 miles of wildlife friendly fencing projects on private lands related to the RD2H migration corridor.

en.text: When a fawn cries in distress, a mule deer doe comes running, even for a white-tailed fawn. White-tailed does answer only their own kind.

source.title: Teichroeb et al. 2013, Behavioural Processes
quote: white-tailed deer females approach a speaker only when it plays distress calls of conspecific fawns
Mule deer females approach when hearing distress calls of either white-tailed deer or mule deer.

en.text: Why bounce? A mule deer bounding on all fours clears rocks, logs and brush better than a galloping one, and gets a look at the way ahead.

source.title: Wild About Utah, Follow the Bouncing Deer
quote: Stotters can clear rocks, logs and brush more effectively than gallopers.
The height gained during stotting allows the mule deer to check the surrounding vegetation along their escape path.

en.text: Shed mule deer antlers don't go to waste. Mice, porcupines, coyotes, even bison and elk gnaw on them for calcium and other minerals.

source.title: NPS Theodore Roosevelt National Park, Mule Deer
source.quote: Mice, porcupines, coyotes, bison, elk, deer, and many other animals will chew on the the antlers throughout the year to absorb calcium and other minerals.

en.text: A mule deer usually smells or hears a predator before seeing it. Then it raises its head, stares hard and swivels those huge ears forward.

source.title: NPS Yellowstone, Mule Deer
source.quote: They probably smell or hear the approaching predator first; then may raise their heads high and stare hard, rotating ears forward to hear better.

en.text: Black-tailed deer of the Pacific Northwest's rainforests and mule deer of the dry West are one species. Mule deer evolved from blacktails.

source.title: Wikipedia, Mule deer
quote: virtually all recent authorities treat the mule deer and black-tailed deer as conspecific
Mule deer apparently evolved from the black-tailed deer.

de.text: Bis zu {28 cm|11 in} lange Ohren wie ein Maultier gaben dem Maultierhirsch den Namen.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Maultierhirsch
quote: Die Artbezeichnung Maultierhirsch bezieht sich auf die großen Ohren, die an jene von Maultieren erinnern.
Die Ohren erreichen eine Länge von 28 und eine Breite von 15 Zentimetern.

de.text: Fliehende Maultierhirsche springen mit allen vier Beinen zugleich ab, auch steil bergauf.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Maultierhirsch
quote: Dabei stoßen sie sich mit allen vier Läufen zugleich in die Höhe.
auch sehr schnell einen steilen Hang hinauf zu springen

de.text: Vier Monate im Jahr sind die Maultierhirsche der Red Desert auf Wanderschaft.

source.title: Wyoming Migration Initiative, Red Desert to Hoback Migration Assessment
source.quote: The deer that complete this journey spend 4 months of each year migrating

de.text: Zwillinge sind bei Maultierhirschen häufig: ein Zeichen, dass die Mutter gut in Form ist.

source.title: National Park Service, Jewel Cave National Monument: Mule Deer
quote: It is common for mule deer does to give birth to two fawns.
This is a sign of a doe in very good health

de.text: Bei Gefahr warnt ein Maultierhirsch die anderen mit Duft aus einer Drüse am Hinterbein.

source.title: Animal Diversity Web, Odocoileus hemionus
source.quote: The metatarsal gland produces an alarm pheromone

de.text: In Kalifornien picken Gelbschnabelelstern den Maultierhirschen die Zecken aus dem Fell.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Maultierhirsch
source.quote: In Kalifornien sind die Vögel häufig dabei zu beobachten, wie sie Zecken und andere Parasiten aus dem Fell der Hirsche picken.

de.text: Trotz großer Ohren wittert der Maultierhirsch Gefahr vor allem mit der Nase.

source.title: Texas Tech University, The Mammals of Texas: Mule deer
source.quote: Although equipped with acute senses of sight and hearing, these deer rely largely on the sense of smell in detecting danger.

de.text: Die Interstate 80 ist für die Hirsche eine Mauer. Ohne die Autobahn würden sich viele im Winter weiter südlich in der Red Desert verteilen.

source.title: National Geographic, Longest Land Mammal Migration in Lower 48 Discovered (2014)
source.quote: the deer would likely spread out farther south into the Red Desert in winter if they weren't stopped by Interstate 80

de.text: Maultierhirsche wandern aus Erfahrung: Das Gedächtnis lenkt die Tiere 2- bis 28-mal stärker als frisches Grün oder tiefer Schnee.

source.title: Merkle et al. 2019, Ecology Letters
source.quote: Spatial memory had an extraordinary influence on migration, affecting movement 2-28 times more strongly than tracking spring green-up or autumn snow depth.

de.text: Ein Jahr lang folgt das Kalb der Mutter. Kurz bevor die neuen Kälber kommen, schickt die Hirschkuh den Nachwuchs vom Vorjahr fort.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Maultierhirsch
quote: Die enge Bindung an das Muttertier währt etwa ein Jahr.
Gewöhnlich vertreibt das Weibchen den ihr folgenden Nachwuchs zu einem Zeitpunkt, der kurz vor der Geburt des diesjährigen Nachwuchses liegt.

en.text: Zebras can turn back mid-migration when the weather changes the menu.

source.title: Data from: In search of greener pastures: using satellite images to predict the effects of environmental change on zebra migration
source.quote: are able to reverse migration to avoid adverse conditions or exploit renewed resource availability

en.text: For these Botswana zebras, rain changes both when the journey starts and how quickly it unfolds.

source.title: Data from: In search of greener pastures: using satellite images to predict the effects of environmental change on zebra migration
source.quote: influence of environmental conditions, monitored using satellite data, on departure date and movement speed of migrating zebras in Botswana

en.text: No two plains zebras wear exactly the same stripes.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Plains zebra
source.quote: Like all zebras, they are boldly striped in black and white and no two individuals look exactly alike.

en.text: A plains zebra foal is born brown and white; the dark stripes deepen with age.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Plains zebra
source.quote: The natal coat of a foal is brown and white and the brown darkens with age. [ 15 ] [ 14 ] [ 19 ]

en.text: Plains zebras bark: their contact call sounds like a repeated "kwa-ha".

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Plains zebra
source.quote: One is its distinctive, high-pitched, contact call (commonly called " barking ") heard as "a- ha , a- ha , a- ha " or "kwa-ha, kaw-ha, ha, ha" [ 15 ] also transcribed as "kwahaah", [ 30 ] or "oug-ga".

en.text: While a zebra group sleeps, one member keeps watch.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Plains zebra
source.quote: They may rest or sleep laying down, while one individual keeps guard. [ 9 ]

en.text: A mother zebra initially keeps even her older offspring away from her newborn.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Plains zebra
source.quote: Early on, a mother zebra keeps any other zebra away from her foal, including the stallion, the other mares, and even her previous offspring.

en.text: Zebras tackle long, tough grass first, opening the way for fussier grazers such as wildebeest and Thomson's gazelles.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Plains zebra
quote: Plains zebras are adapted for grazing on both long, tough grass stems and newly emerging short grass (stems and sheaths).
The zebra is a pioneer grazer and prepares the way for more specialised grazers such as blue wildebeests and Thomson's gazelles . [ 9 ]

en.text: Zebras groom one another with their teeth and lips, nibbling along the neck and back to strengthen family bonds.

source.title: Wikipedia (en), Plains zebra
quote: Zebras strengthen their social bonds with grooming .
Members of a harem nip and scrape along the neck, withers, and back with their teeth and lips.

de.text: Frisches Grün kann die Zebras sogar dazu bringen, auf dem Zug wieder umzukehren.

source.title: Data from: In search of greener pastures: using satellite images to predict the effects of environmental change on zebra migration
source.quote: are able to reverse migration to avoid adverse conditions or exploit renewed resource availability

de.text: Diese Zebras ziehen zwischen ihren Gebieten für die Trockenzeit und die Regenzeit hin und her.

source.title: Data from: In search of greener pastures: using satellite images to predict the effects of environmental change on zebra migration
source.quote: Daily zebra movements between dry and rainy season ranges

de.text: Steppenzebras suchen nach verloren gegangenen Herdenmitgliedern.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steppenzebra
source.quote: Der Zusammenhalt innerhalb der Herde ist sehr groß, verloren gegangene Mitglieder werden über längere Zeit gesucht.

de.text: Junge Steppenzebra-Hengste leben in eigenen Junggesellengruppen.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steppenzebra
source.quote: Neben den eigentlichen Herden gibt es auch „Junggesellengruppen“ junger männlicher Tiere, die noch keine eigene Herde aufgebaut haben.

de.text: Ein Steppenzebra-Fohlen steht schon rund elf Minuten nach der Geburt.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steppenzebra
source.quote: Nach rund elf Minuten steht das Fohlen bereits, nach im Mittel einer Stunde saugt es erstmals Milch.

de.text: Manche Steppenzebras tragen zusätzliche „Schattenstreifen“ im Fell.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steppenzebra
quote: Die breitesten Streifen besitzt heute die Unterart Böhm-Zebra in Ostafrika, sogenannte „Schattenstreifen“, die manchmal die weißen Streifen überlagern, kommen hier kaum vor.
Die Streifenzeichnungen werden schmaler, aber weniger bei Populationen, die im Süden leben, hier treten dann auch sehr häufig „Schattenstreifen“ auf.

de.text: Bei Gefahr wecken Steppenzebras zuerst die Jungtiere.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steppenzebra
source.quote: Als Schutz vor Beutegreifern hält mindestens ein Tier Wache, Jungtiere werden bei aufziehender Gefahr als erste geweckt.

de.text: Vorn führt meist die ranghöchste Stute, hinten sichert der Hengst. Beim Trinken geht dagegen der Hengst als Erster vor.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steppenzebra
source.quote: In der Regel führt die ranghöchste Stute die Gruppe, während der Hengst am Ende des Zuges die Nachhut bildet; beim Trinken, das meist nachts stattfindet, ist er jedoch der Erste.

de.text: Zur Begrüßung zeigen Steppenzebra-Ohren nach vorn; bei einer Drohung gehen sie zurück und die Zähne kommen zum Vorschein.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steppenzebra
quote: Beim Treffen zweier Herden führen die Hengste eine ritualisierte Begrüßungszeremonie durch, bestehend aus der charakteristischen Grußgeste – erhobene und nach vorn gerichtete Ohren – und gegenseitigem Beschnüffeln der Nase und Genitalien .
Ein Steppenzebra in Bedrängung legt die Ohren an und spreizt bei zunehmender Bedrohung die Lippen und zeigt die Zähne, eine Mimik , die dem Flehmen und dem Rossigkeitsgesicht ähnelt.

de.text: Steppenzebras bereiten Gnus und Gazellen den Tisch: Erst wird das lange Gras abgefressen und niedergetrampelt, dann folgen die anderen.

source.title: Wikipedia (de), Steppenzebra
source.quote: Erst nachdem das Steppenzebra das lange Gras abgefressen und niedergetrampelt hat, folgen Gnus und Gazellen .
